Hence, without receiving even a word of censure from Antony, he nullified the odium raised against him by the embassy.

Again, nearly a hundred Jewish men travelled as far as Antioch with no less spirit to bring accusations. At Daphne they found Antony, already wholly given over to Cleopatra’s love and serving her lust, and there began to denounce the brothers’ intolerable power. Messalla argued against them, with Hyrcanus present, and denounced the insolence of the nation: roused by a faction of a few, it rejected its own and sought outsiders, making Hyrcanus’s injury a pretext when Hyrcanus had preferred what was advantageous to the citizens. After hearing the arguments of both sides, Antony asked Hyrcanus whom he considered better fitted to preside. Hyrcanus’s preference was for Herod and his brother. Finding the answer in accord with his own wish, Antony was greatly delighted, for he was joined to the brothers by a bond of hospitality through their father: when he had come into Judaea with Gabinius, Antipater had received him most warmly as a guest and honoured him with many services. He appointed Herod and Phasael tetrarchs and ordered them to undertake the administration of all Judaea.

From this too the number of complainants increased. Although some of the envoys had been imprisoned and others insulted, a thousand envoys were later ordered, after sedition arose in Jerusalem, to go to Antony, who was staying in the city of Tyre. They did not fail their fellow citizens’ will. Although the protesters had been harshly punished, they dared raise their clamour again. Antony sent the governor of the Tyrians to rebuke those guilty of insolence. The governor, together with Herod and Hyrcanus, sought to prevent them from bringing the heaviest punishments upon themselves, and disturbances and causes of war upon their homeland.

When nothing was achieved and everything began to fall into confusion through irrational strife, Antony sent armed men. Some were killed by them, and many were gravely wounded. From Hyrcanus, however, the dead received the benefit of burial, and those who had managed to escape the benefit of medical care. They thus furnished an occasion for a twofold display of humanity, through which his goodwill towards his fellow citizens became manifest. The others who had escaped so exasperated Antony by keeping the city in turmoil that he ordered the execution even of those whom he was holding in chains.

Insolence had yielded to severity, but when almost two years had passed, a Parthian army poured into Syria, with Pacorus, the king’s son, and Barzaphranes, the Persian satrap, leading the barbarian host. Lysanias, Ptolemy’s son, joined them as an instigator. After the death of his father, whose surname was Mennaeus, he had already been stripped of power. Through the satrap just mentioned, he solicited Pacorus with a promise of a thousand talents of silver and five hundred women, to give Antigonus the kingdom and dissolve Hyrcanus’s priesthood. Pacorus gave part of the cavalry to a royal servant to cross into Judaea, act on Antigonus’s behalf and support his endeavour, since he himself was detained by rebellions within Syria.

But this too would have made little progress had it not been proposed, on Antigonus’s advice, that the Jews should receive Pacorus as a mediator of peace, while they were fighting one another under Herod and Phasael on one side and Antigonus on the other. Phasael, in his easy-going disposition, approved this at the time, despite Herod’s opposition. Soon, finding it ruinous to himself, he learnt that barbarians were unfaithful by nature.

For he was sent to Barzaphranes as though to an agent of peace, and, setting out with Hyrcanus, met the satrap, who was cunningly concealing his ambush beneath an appearance of kindness. Indeed, he gave them gifts as they prepared to leave, and made his arrangements for their entrapment. Men accompanied them more to keep them under guard than to share their dangers. Reports arrived that the Parthian had been bought for a thousand talents to destroy the men just mentioned.

Ofellius too urged flight, since he had learnt from Saramalla, the wealthiest of the Syrians, that a plot had been prepared against them. Yet even so Phasael was not persuaded to abandon Hyrcanus and look to his own safety. Instead, he assailed the satrap with bitter abuse for betraying trust for a price and valuing money more than justice: he himself would give more for their safety than Antigonus was paying for the kingdom. But the Persian tried by perjury to win back the trust he had betrayed and dispel suspicion, and not long afterwards carried out the deception. For when he had departed to Pacorus, those to whom they had entrusted this business seized Phasael and Hyrcanus. Since the captives could now do nothing else, they sought by curses to avenge the barbarians’ perjuries and the faithlessness of their betrayal.

The cupbearer sent into Judaea had likewise laid out his deceptions to capture Herod. But Herod had long suspected the barbarians’ ambushes, and grave concern kept him on his guard; he remained within the fortifications. Nor did he think he should leave the walls and entrust himself to conversations with the enemy in response to feigned instructions from Pacorus, by which the cupbearer would approach Phasael’s brother about Phasael and his insolence.

When he learnt that his brother and Hyrcanus were being held, he sent his people ahead into Idumaea at night, and himself with his servants routed the barbarians in pursuit. After killing many, he hastened to Masada, finding the Jews who had pressed upon him in flight more troublesome than the Parthians. Having avenged himself upon his pursuers, he settled his people within the fortifications. He himself left a garrison to protect his mother and younger brothers, and made for Petra in Arabia.

The Persians poured into Jerusalem, breaking into the houses of those who fled. Everything was turned to plunder, war and tumult. The outrage went so far that the kingdom was handed over to Antigonus, and Phasael and Hyrcanus too were delivered into his power, to undergo whatever he pleased. He could restrain himself no longer, but immediately attacked Hyrcanus and bit off his ears with his own teeth, so that no change of circumstances should ever open the way for his return to the priesthood. For the high priest must be unmutilated, and it is clear that the law does not permit anyone with a mutilated body to perform the supreme office of the priesthood.

Phasael forestalled humiliation by swiftly bringing death upon himself, dashing his head against some rocks that happened to be at hand. He disdained to be preserved for mockery or to die at another’s command, when, even with his hands bound and denied a sword, he could find a way out of life. Yet another account of him also circulated, that Antigonus brought a doctor to the wounded man to pour poison into the wound as though it were medicine. Whichever of these endings occurred, it had its beginning in a defiant spirit. It is alleged that in his last moments, when he was already breathing out his life, on learning that Herod was alive and had escaped the ambush prepared for him by flight, he added that he died with gratitude, leaving alive someone who would bring him vengeance.

Herod, meanwhile, hastened into Arabia, hoping to obtain money, which he believed was the only means of bending barbarian greed, to ransom his brother from captivity. If he found the Arab either forgetful of his father’s affection or too tight-fisted to repay his gifts, he would ask for a loan to pay the ransom, pledging in return the son of the man to be ransomed, a boy of seven whom he had brought with him for this purpose. But Phasael’s death forestalled the endeavour of devoted brotherhood, and Herod was carrying out his brotherly duty with such diligence, all in vain. Yet before he learnt of his brother’s death, he found Bocchus, king of Arabia, hostile, though he had believed him a friend. For Bocchus changed his faithfulness with the times, and forbade Herod to enter when he was already approaching Arabia’s borders. He fabricated a story that Parthian envoys had warned him not to think of receiving their fugitive into the kingdom of Arabia and bringing a most grievous war upon himself.

Offended at this, Herod at once replied with the words that the pain of his just indignation brought forth, and turned from there towards Egypt. Soon, however, Bocchus regretted the violation of their friendship and sent men to recall him, but Herod had gone on ahead. When he entered the regions inhabited by the Rhinocorites, reliable reports made known to him his brother’s death and the captivity of Hyrcanus, who had been taken in chains into Parthyene. He took on as much grief as he laid aside anxiety, and prepared for flight instead of war. He hastened with all eagerness to Alexandria, where Cleopatra received him with honour, thinking that a man of such renown should be sought as a commander for her side. Disregarding the queen’s requests, he sailed from there for Rome. He judged the storms of winter and the disturbances he knew of in Italy less serious than the waves he dreaded in Cleopatra’s inconstancy, more grievous than any shipwreck.

Setting out without waiting for the winds, he encountered danger around Pamphylia, but escaped. Changing ships, he reached Brundisium first, and from there Rome. There, with the advantage of his father’s friendship, he approached Antony. He lamented his own misfortunes and those of his family, who were under siege and for whom he had come to Rome to plead, and moved Antony to pity at so great a reversal of circumstances. A king until recently most powerful, who had often brought aid to the Roman state, had suddenly changed his home for exile, like a shipwrecked man destitute of everything and lacking the help he begged for his people in danger.

Although Antony was strongly inclined towards him by the bond of hospitality he had shared with his father Antipater, and especially because, in making him tetrarch, he had left him destined for kingship, Caesar was still more generous in his natural goodwill. He cherished all the more Antipater’s service in Egypt in all his father Caesar’s battles and their bond of hospitality, as though the pledges of favour had been renewed. Yet he regarded with suspicion the king’s cunning disposition, perversely intent on the advantage of his own affairs rather than on what was fair and good. Herod was granted access to the senate. Before it, Messalla and Atratinus set forth his father’s good deeds and Herod’s own services to the Roman state. By the senators’ authority it was decreed that Herod’s kingship appeared advantageous to Roman rule, since, as Antony supported the proposal, it would be useful in waging war against the Parthians for the Romans to gain the alliance of the king just mentioned. When the senate was dismissed, Caesar, Antony and Herod left the senate house together and were escorted by the magistrates’ attendants. On the first day that kingship was conferred upon Herod by the senate’s decree, Antony prepared a banquet and invited the king.

At about the same time, Josephus, Herod’s brother, had arranged to flee at night because of a shortage of water. But suddenly so great a rain flooded the land that it filled all the water channels. Abandoning the escape he was preparing to the Arab nation, he routed the forces of Antigonus, who was besieging him, partly by ambushes and partly by engagements and open battle. Yet he too often withdrew into the fortress after an adverse outcome.

And now Herod had arrived unexpectedly from Italy at Ptolemais, a city of Syria. Disembarking swiftly, he advanced against Antigonus with a great force of citizens and foreigners. Ventidius and Silo, commanders of the Roman army whom Antony had ordered to assist in escorting Herod, came to meet him. Dellius, sent by Antony for this purpose, had persuaded them to come from nearby to meet him, at least for appearance’s sake, though their sympathies were opposed, since Antigonus had bought them both off. Ventidius was staying in the neighbouring cities to suppress the disturbances of the Parthian war; Silo, stationed within Judaea, was making money in open alliance with Antigonus. Yet Herod did not need help: all the Galilaeans except a few had joined him. His purpose was to rescue his people from the siege at Masada as soon as possible, and he took Joppa by fighting. It lay on the way and was full of enemy troops, whom he did not wish to leave behind him as he advanced further. Although Antigonus wanted to obstruct his march, he recovered Masada without difficulty and rescued his people from danger.

Then he went to Jerusalem. He did everything to avoid the necessity of fighting, declaring that he had undertaken war on behalf of his fellow citizens against rebellion, not against his own people. When Antigonus’s supporters provoked him with arrows and lighter missiles, he forced those assailing him from the wall to flee.

There would have been no delay in victory had Silo, commander of the Roman force, not suborned soldiers to complain of shortages. They alleged that everything around the walls was devastated, that supplies were difficult to obtain and food scarce, and that the time had now come when they should withdraw to winter quarters. They threatened to disobey orders unless their demands were accepted. The mutiny would already have gained strength had Herod not placed himself among the centurions and Roman soldiers alike and begged them not to abandon the man whom Caesar, Antony and the senate had entrusted to their protection, especially since he promised that nothing they needed would be lacking. When he had finished speaking, he went out into the countryside and suddenly had an abundance of everything supplied to the army, leaving Silo no excuse.

With everyone’s spirits thus raised, he recovered Idumaea with two thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry, while the Roman force was now at rest in winter quarters. Josephus was chosen to lead the undertaking, a lighter task, so that he would not think he should attempt anything against Antigonus at greater risk.

Herod himself transferred his people from Masada and settled them in Samaria, providing what he believed would serve for their protection and use. In the icy winter, when all the country was covered with snow, he arrived ahead of the report of his coming and entered without a battle the place called by its ancient name Sepphoris, which they later named Diocaesarea. He thought it suitable for restoring those wearied by the winter frosts and journeys made harsher by ice, for there was also an abundance of food there. When his soldiers had recovered there with food and a spell in camp, he decided to undertake battle against the brigands who ranged throughout the country and wore down its inhabitants no less than an invasion in war. He therefore first sent a detachment of cavalry and infantry ahead to the village of Arbela, and himself arrived with the remaining force forty days later. The brigands were not frightened by the sight of the army, but thought they should meet it in arms, displaying military discipline and the audacity of brigands. When battle was joined, Herod’s left wing gave way, but he quickly restored it, brought up reinforcements and steadied his men, struck the pursuers and broke the attacks of those

who could not withstand Herod fighting at close quarters. He pursued them as they turned away, as far as the Jordan, and put them to death. All the rest were scattered beyond the river, so that Galilee was freed from all fear of raids. Only those who concealed themselves in hiding places and, as it were, buried themselves in caves remained, delaying victory.

On the steep mountain slopes, in the hollow recesses of the rocks, there were fearsome caves among rugged crags, inaccessible from every side and impossible to approach except for the inhabitants of the place. They used cross-paths and narrow tracks, the only usual approaches, and their familiarity with danger made them safer against the danger of being caught. Within were the dark recesses of the caves. In front of them a rock projected like a continuous ridge down to the deep bodies of water, excluding any hope of approach, with slippery ground on every side, water falling from the mountain brow and the crashing course of streams. The rush of the falling waters and the rock overhanging the ravines thus made the precipice more terrifying. For some time the king hesitated in uncertainty, unable to discover how to overcome nature. Later he used the following contrivance: he enclosed his strongest men in protective structures fashioned like chests and lowered them, armed, by ropes to the very mouths of the caves. They easily began to slaughter the unarmed and kill them with all their kin and offspring, and to burn alive any who dared resist by casting fire upon them. There was no place for pity. Indeed, even when Herod wished to rescue many from death and give them confidence to take refuge with him, he drove them further away. No one joined Herod voluntarily, and those compelled by force preferred death to captivity. One of the older men, who had seven sons and a wife with him and could have provided for their safety, killed them all in the following way. Ordering each one to come forward in turn, he stood at the entrance and killed each of his sons as he emerged. Seeing so grievous and pitiable a deed, Herod was gripped by the bond of fatherhood. He tried to stop him with his hand and begged him in words to spare his children, promising immunity. But the man was not moved at all by these words. He even abused the king, killed his wife as well as his sons, and, after throwing his sons’ bodies down from the height, finally hurled himself headlong into the depths.

Antigonus was terrified that Herod had so easily overcome the multitude of brigands and the difficulties of the terrain. He avoided his presence, but turned against Ptolemy, whom Herod had placed over part of the army. A man most adept at the stealthy devices of war, he used those accustomed to disturbing Galilee to have Ptolemy killed in a sudden attack.
He also destroyed Josephus, Herod’s brother, while his brother was occupied in other regions. Josephus resisted vigorously with the Roman soldiers who had come to his aid, hastily assembled.

Not content with so great a triumph, he added to his victory a grievous insult to the dead man, leaving him with his head cut off. Pheroras, the slain man’s brother, offered fifty talents for it, but did not obtain it. This victory again turned the sympathies of many in Galilee towards Antigonus, and the business of war was renewed.

Herod had made for Antioch and was resting there in the very pleasant place called Daphne. On receiving news of his brother’s killing, he groaned briefly at his suffering, deferred his grief and prepared vengeance. Antigonus could not face his raging sorrow, but hid himself within the fortifications.

Herod burst in to pursue the authors of so great a crime, and easily drove back the forces that met him. Very many were killed. The roads were blocked with the bodies of the fallen, so that the very routes were filled with the corpses of the slain. The battle would have been finished, with everyone put to flight, had Herod thought he should march straight to Jerusalem. Antigonus had cast away his spears and dreaded the final punishment.

All were so confounded by fear that, when the harsh winter had recalled Herod from pursuit and he laid aside his arms and entered a bath accompanied by a single servant, three men with drawn swords met him, and then more, who had fled the battle and were seeking hiding places. On seeing the king, they were thrown into confusion by fear, passed him and hurried to the exit of the bath to escape, although they could have killed the king and ended the war. Indeed, there was no one to seize them as they fled. Inferring from this how great the enemy’s fear was, Herod pressed on with the fighting and killed Pappus, the very commander of the opposing force, and ordered his head to be cut off, because he had killed Josephus, the king’s brother.

Meanwhile Antigonus, who had prepared to flee, delayed. As he lingered, Herod surrounded him with his army and besieged him, pressing upon the side in front of the temple, where Pompey too had broken into the city. The king was now so confident of victory that, after beginning the siege, he turned aside to take Alexander’s daughter as his wife, exchanging the battle trumpet for wedding songs and mingling marriage with war. Having gained the opportunity for the union from the occasion of battle, he returned from the festivities to the war.

Sossius too arrived, sent by Antony to aid the king. Their forces were thus united. Although the Romans excelled in experience of war and military discipline, and strove eagerly to please the king, the city was only broken into in the fifth month, when Herod’s men dared to climb the wall and the Roman centurions burst in. Then there was countless slaughter, and everything around the temple was devastated. Some were cut down as they fled to the temple, others gathered inside their houses. There was no pity for old age, none for infancy or women’s weakness. Antigonus presented himself and, forgetful of his position, threw himself at Sossius’s feet. Sossius, whom so great a reversal of circumstances ought to have reminded of pity, abused the prostrate man and called him Antigone. Yet he did not spare him as a woman, but cast him bound into custody.

Herod wavered over how to rescue his homeland from Roman hands, how to preserve the temple undefiled by the gentiles. For the Romans hurried to inspect the inner mysteries and profane the holy of holies. The king drove them away one by one, now with pleas, now with threats, judging victory worse than flight if any of the sacred mysteries were divulged. The Romans pressed on towards plunder; Herod resisted, lest they leave him an empty city and nothing of his kingdom but a desert. Sossius, on the other hand, claimed the plunder of the captured city for the soldiers. But the king promised to give the soldiers money from his own resources, and thus bought back with money what remained of his homeland. To fulfil his promise, he received the soldiers most hospitably, treated the commanders as befitted them, and rewarded Sossius himself with royal generosity. No one left ungrateful. Sossius offered a crown to God and departed, taking Antigonus with him to Antony, who had him struck with an axe as a man of ignoble spirit.

Herod also bestowed very many gifts upon his own people. He gave very many to Antony and his friends, yet could not buy his own security from Antony. For Antony, mortgaged to his love for Cleopatra, was already her servant and, enslaved to her lust, attended upon her. Yet he could not overcome the greed of a woman, especially one practised in killing her relatives: once they were dead, she had added their possessions to her own as spoils. With the same avarice and cruelty, she had any Syrians she heard were particularly wealthy put to death. With Antony already enslaved to her desires, she thought that the kingdoms of Judaea and Arabia too could be added to her avarice, once the rulers of both nations had been killed.

But although drunk with lust and heavy with sleep, Antony came to his senses in this matter and refused to destroy such men and most powerful kings at the command of a most wanton woman. Yet, so as not to let them go unscathed, he struck down their friends, took away the greatest part of their possessions, especially the land that produced balsam, and awarded all the cities on this side of the river Eleutherus, except Tyre and Sidon, to Cleopatra’s greed. Appeased towards her husband by such a payment, she accompanied Antony as far as the Euphrates when he set out against the Parthians, and returned through Judaea. There Herod did not neglect to win the queen’s goodwill towards himself, especially with gifts and presents. Success increased her arrogance, so that her womanly lack of restraint exalted itself beyond measure. Indeed, not long afterwards Artabazes, king of the Parthians and son of the most powerful King Tigranes, was given to her as a gift. Antony held him captive with all the Persian plunder and spoils. Though owed to a triumph, he was assigned to a woman like a worthless slave, so that the more glorious the victory had been, the more shameful was the gift that dishonoured kings with such mockery.

Yet the man who did not know how to use success did not enjoy it for long: through a woman’s insolence, he roused Augustus against himself. Thus the Actian war was being prepared with great movements on both sides. The king was most eager to enter the war with Antony, since Judaea was free from hostile disturbance and he had recovered Hyrcania, long held by Antigonus’s sister. Yet in this too Herod was most fortunate, being begrudged a share in others’ dangers. Cleopatra therefore wished to estrange Antony’s mind from the kings and turn it away. She persuaded her husband that Herod should wage war against the Arabs, so that, if he prevailed, Arabia would fall to the queen, and, if he was defeated, Cleopatra’s dominion would extend into Judaea.

Whichever won would destroy the other. This plan inclined in Herod’s favour in its outcome, rather than its intention. As soon as he began battle, his superior cavalry drove the enemy back, but in the end he was overcome by the enemy’s multitude and surrounded by their numbers. His adversaries’ forces had gathered at Canatha, and he wished to draw up his line closely against them. But his men’s spirits were elated by their earlier success, and for that reason they rushed out against the enemy, leaving him unsupported. Above all, this came through the treachery of Athenion, whom Cleopatra had attached to the commander to abandon Herod at the very moment of need, not to help him. The Arabs then attacked his abandoned army in rocky and inaccessible places, struck it down in grievous slaughter and routed it, pursuing the fugitives to their places of refuge and destroying them.

Herod arrived, later indeed than the need demanded, but nevertheless avenged the disaster. In subsequent battles he so afflicted the Arabs that they repeatedly lamented that single victory of theirs. Added to this was a grievous loss of heart caused by an earthquake, in which very many livestock and about thirty thousand people perished. Yet the entire military force remained unharmed, since it lived in the open air. This too raised the enemy’s spirits: they thought they could more easily invade a deserted Judaea and afflict those stricken by such portents. Herod therefore thought that his men must be roused to their own defence, especially because he had learnt that the envoys he had sent into Arabia had been treacherously killed. He addressed them in their fear with these words:

“After so many successful battles on our side, the enemy’s fortunes have been broken, even by their own admission: driven by frenzied grief, like defeated men, they murdered our envoys. It therefore seems strange to me that an irrational fear has so shaken you that you set the accidents of the elements above the known successes of valour. There has been no encounter in which the Arabs did not immediately give way and turn to flight, thinking they must retreat. As is the way with the stealthy devices of war, they sought remedies in deceit and ambushes, not to win themselves, but to delay our victory. In place of the confidence this should have brought, agitation has arisen, as though the war were terrifying, because the earth shook, although the very men who wage war were alone unharmed. Or, if we wish to consider whom it harmed, we shall judge it to be the Arabs rather, whom it brought back to war so that they should not escape stronger men by fleeing. For I see that they have returned to the battle line relying not on their arms and strength but on the loss of our livestock. Yet frail is the hope that depends not on confidence in one’s own valour but on another’s misery, since nothing on earth is so changeable as prosperity or adversity. For the state of human affairs is renewed by slight turns; prosperity does not endure, nor does hardship persist. Thus neither misery nor its contrary is perpetual: fortunes frequently alternate and vary even for the same people. Indeed, we may take an example from events. In the earlier clash we had the advantage, but as the battle advanced our fortune changed, and we were defeated by those we had defeated. We too therefore have grounds to hope that those who defeated us will be defeated by us. For excessive confidence is always incautious and careless of itself. Fear, however, warns us to look ahead and teaches diligence. In prosperity, audacity steals upon us, and unthinking rashness does not know how to await the commander’s counsel. Indeed, it was when you advanced against my judgement that Athenion’s wickedness found an opportunity to do harm. Now your trembling pledges me the first claim to victory. Raise your spirits, then, and exalt the Jews’ ancient greatness of soul. Do not let the disturbances of insensible things terrify you, nor think that movements of the earth indicate some other disaster. The disturbances of the elements have their own harm: fear nothing other than the injury that lies in them. For an earthquake and the destruction of living creatures are not signs of dangers, but the dangers themselves. There is therefore no reason for us to fear as though we were about to suffer grievous things, when we have already suffered the most grievous. He who has exacted punishment can now be favourable, and gentler than if he had not exacted it. What remains after earthquake and pestilence except mercy, since we have paid for twofold sins? Yet we have intact what is useful for war. For pestilence carried off those outside the war, while our victory took from the enemy those they had chosen as fit for war. Moreover, our livestock have died, but their judgement has died: they thought the envoys we sent should have their throats cut against human and divine law. They have transgressed the law of all human beings, even of the barbarians themselves. Even among those who know nothing of humanity, envoys are held inviolable, through dread of heavenly vengeance and fear of God as the avenger of so great a crime. Our adversaries have therefore committed what neither human nor divine laws leave unavenged. Let us go out, then, to fight not for territory or spoils, but for an injury to God. Let us be roused to war not by love of wife or children, but by our confidence in God’s protection. We carry out not our own decisions, but the sacred precepts of divine law, to exact vengeance for those whom religion requires to be inviolable. Amid hostile arms, an embassy alone mediates peace; one who serves as an envoy lays aside the character of an enemy. Their blood now cries out to God and demands vengeance. Let us hasten to battle, then, while we have God as avenger, vindicator of the slain. They fight better on our behalf and, surrounded by legions of angels, stand before us in the battle line.”

Having exhorted his soldiers with such words, he rushed upon the enemy, seeking every opportunity to fight. The Arabs were superior in number but inferior in spirit, and when battle was joined about five thousand of them fell. The rest withdrew into a fortification and were wearied by a shortage of water, so that they sent an embassy to ask for peace at a price. But when they saw that they were being put off and thirst burned still more fiercely as the water ran out, many came out and offered themselves voluntarily to the enemy, preferring to perish by the sword rather than by thirst. Herod kept them bound, lest there be any ambush. Thus in five days about four thousand were received; when others came out to fight, about seven thousand men were again killed. Humbled by the king through this blow, the Arabs were as superior in judgement as they were inferior in valour: they asked for the very man they had as an adversary to be their defender and helper.

But greater anxiety struck him in victory. Having subjected something to himself, he now dreaded imminent danger not to his territory but to his entire kingdom, for Antony, whom faithful friendship had bound to him, had been defeated. Indeed, Augustus Caesar, victor in the Actian contest, did not yet think Antony overcome while Herod survived the victory. When the anxious king learnt from a reliable report that Caesar had reached Rhodes, he sailed to him, lest rumour outstrip his journey by land. On arrival, he laid aside his diadem and presented himself in the dress of a private man, but with a king’s spirit. Withholding nothing of the truth, he maintained his firmness and preserved his authority. “I confess, Augustus,” he said, “that I was Antony’s faithful ally, since I received my kingdom from him and still do not deny that I am his debtor. I would have proved this by arms had Cleopatra not begrudged it and the Arabs not prevented it. It was through that necessity that I did not bear arms against you, not as one who deserted a friend or feared battle, but as one occupied with affairs at home. Yet Antony did not find me ungrateful to him: although absent, I sent him reinforcements for his army and countless supplies of grain. Nor would you, Caesar, have judged me ungrateful for his benefits had I taken part in the Actian war. See how I withhold nothing. I am more afraid of appearing before you ungrateful to your enemy than an enemy to you. Your judgement weighs more heavily upon me than war, for before you it is crimes that are put in jeopardy, not the deserts of excellence. I too prefer to plead my case before you for faithfulness rather than faithlessness. See, Caesar, how I did not desert Antony when he was unharmed: I did not flee from him when defeated. You defeated Antony, Caesar, with your greatest legions; you defeated him with your counsels; you defeated him with the strength of the Roman dominion, which he abandoned and which he disowned. He was truly defeated by your excellence, but more by his own conduct. His wife Cleopatra defeated him; Egyptian love defeated him; Canopic luxury defeated him. It defeated him because he preferred to be defeated with Cleopatra rather than win without her. A woman more hostile to her own people than to her adversaries defeated him. I had advised the woman’s death, if he wished to look to his own interests. I had promised help to restore him in his affliction, promised forces to protect him in flight, and offered myself as a partner in war; but his mind had been blocked by his desires for Cleopatra. He was defeated because he would not listen to me. I too was defeated with Antony, yet with less disgrace, because Cleopatra defeated him, Antony me. He did not abandon a barbarian woman, I a friend. With him I laid aside my diadem, but I have come to you retaining the credit of a faithful friend. I have put away the insignia of kingship, but have not cast aside the consciousness of excellence. Judge as you will; yet, whatever the outcome of your judgement, I shall take this away with me: what sort of friend I have been will be recognised.”

Caesar answered these words. “Greetings,” he said, “and now enjoy your kingdom all the more, for we do not envy excellence but delight in it. You deserve to rule over more people, since you so defend friendship that you neither disown a man in adversity nor blush to acknowledge him as your friend. But undertake to attach yourself to the more fortunate, and to preserve in prosperity the faithfulness you have amply proved in adversity. Antony may have defeated you, but I shall not consider defeated a man whom friendship has made equal to the victors. We seek you for this reason, that no outcome of war changed you, since you did not desert Antony: Antony deserted you first, trusting himself to Cleopatra rather than to you. His folly gained you for us, because he chose the woman most ruinous to him and rejected a faithful man. Nor is it strange if Antony, defeated, clings to Cleopatra, by whom he was captured in victory. Why are you surprised that Cleopatra made Antony break with you, when she parted him from me and made an enemy out of a partner in rule? You too, therefore, were rejected with us, and so reign with us. Nor is it without benefit that, while we were occupied in civil wars, you subjected the untamed Arab nation, for we count the enemies of the Jews as our own. Those who assail you bear arms against us. You therefore served us as a soldier when you won for yourself, and so we reward you, that your kingdom may be confirmed by our gift. For now, our favour is to have diminished nothing; for the future, we shall endeavour to ensure that you do not miss Antony. For it is not fitting that we should fail to surpass in goodwill the man whom we surpassed in war.”

When he had said this, he placed the diadem on Herod’s head, adding attentiveness to his gift. Encouraged by this mark of Caesar’s regard, Herod wished to rescue Alexas, one of Antony’s friends and a man at whom Caesar was most indignant, from disfavour. He lamented with many pleas, but Caesar’s excessive indignation left no room for pardon. When Caesar departed from there for Egypt, Herod accompanied his journey, supplying everything that would be useful to him or his army. By winning the greatest favour for himself, he secured the commander’s affection, especially because, in the more arid places as far as Pelusium, his royal foresight provided an abundant supply of water. Through these services he inspired such love for himself in everyone that he was judged to have deserved more than he had received, and the power of his kingdom to be less than the generosity of his hospitality. Hence, after events in Egypt had gone as he wished and Antony and Cleopatra were dead, Caesar not only restored what had been taken from Herod, but, besides what Cleopatra had diverted, granted him Gadara, Hippos and Samaria. He also gave him the coastal cities of Gaza, Anthedon, Joppa and Strato’s Tower together. He granted the king four hundred bodyguards from Gaul, surrounded by whom Cleopatra used to walk, to guard his person, and many other things. But the king valued above all these gifts that Caesar loved him more than anyone except Agrippa, and Agrippa loved him more than anyone except Caesar.

In the fifteenth year of his reign, then, to respond to his good fortune and favour, uplifted by so great a course of successes, he turned his attention to devotion. To show himself grateful for the heavenly benefits flowing upon him beyond measure, he adorned the temple. He surrounded the whole circuit of ground around the temple with a wall and enclosed a doubled area, with immense expenditure on building and exquisite beauty. The great porticoes around the sanctuary, which he erected from their foundations, bore witness to this. His concern to protect it was no less than his concern to adorn it: he fortified the stronghold facing north, which he called Antonia on account of Antony’s favour, inferior to none of the earlier palaces. Within the citadel itself he also added two dwellings for the royal house, of the greatest extent and marvellous beauty, with whose charm you would think nothing could compare. One was named Caesarium, the other Agrippium, so that the lasting memory of such great friends might be celebrated in his own buildings.

He also not only built up the city of Sebaste but filled it with inhabitants. Not to pursue every detail, he scarcely passed over any site of an ancient city without renewing what was falling into decay or adorning it by adding the buildings it seemed to lack. Extending his generosity even to the five-yearly contests, he enriched that worthless class of men by pouring out his wealth.

He also built a temple of white marble to Caesar at the sources of the Jordan, so forgetful of religion that he dedicated a temple to a man and introduced the practice of the nations into Judaea. The place is named Panium. There a mountain of lofty height stretches aloft with its highest summit, and in its side a shadowy cavern opens, through which the depth of a foul-smelling chasm exhales a fierce stench. Within was a body of water, a great mass utterly still, so that its profound depth could not be estimated. Outside, however, springs gush out around the roots of the mountain itself. Hence many have thought that the Jordan rises there; yet we think that what the truth holds should be disclosed later.

On the coast there was a city called Strato’s Tower, already worn out by frequent wars and inclining towards ruin through age itself, but outstanding in the convenience and charm of its site. He renewed it in white stone and adorned it with palatial buildings, expressing in it the strength of his greatness of soul and the elegance of his work. For it lies midway between two coastal cities, Dora and Joppa, and on either side is hemmed in by a shore without harbours, so that all who wish to sail from Egypt past Phoenicia are tossed on the open sea. For the sea there is often roused by winds, especially the blast of the south-west wind. Even when it blows more moderately, a wave rises; striking the projecting rocks and rebounding with its force broken, it makes the wild sea rougher as it retreats. Thus the king, setting no limit to expense, overcame nature by greatness of soul and established a harbour larger than Piraeus. Within it, penetrating the vast mass of rock, he made safe anchorages.

He also measured out a space suited to the size of the harbour and cast enormous rocks into the sea, many of them fifty feet in height, others even taller. He marked out the harbour itself with very great towers, one of which he called Drusion, to weave the name of Drusus, who was among Caesar’s ancestors, into his own conspicuous works.

He also inserted shorter flights of steps at more frequented places, by which ships could be hauled up without great labour, and embellished the whole charm of the harbour with three enormous colossi. Again he founded a temple to Caesar on a higher site, and in the middle of the temple set a colossus bearing Augustus’s name, as his image, no smaller in size than the image of Olympian Jupiter or Argive Juno. You would not know whether to think that beauty amid such great difficulties excelled more, or the strength and protection of the work amid such great splendour, since the work remains indestructible against both sea and age. Thus manifold benefits came together in a single work: a very great city was added to the province, a harbour for sailors, and honour for Caesar, from whose name it is called Caesarea to this day.

The pursuit of marriage to a single woman brought low this royal power, which abounded in prosperous successes, and broke it with bitter sorrows, from the time when, contrary to law and right, he thought marriage should be measured by rank of birth rather than love, in a certain royal fashion. He had as his partner a woman of Jerusalem named Dosis, who had been joined to him earlier when he was a private man. She should have been all the dearer because she had brought her husband good fortune: it was with her that he had attained the heights of kingship. But, forgetful of his debt of gratitude, he cast Dosis aside and married Mariamne, Aristobulus’s granddaughter and Alexander’s daughter. Thus, in pursuing noble birth, he fell into turmoil: his own household would not be at one with him, although the manifold people of different provinces obeyed him. Antipater—for that was the name of the young man born to Dosis—was expelled not only from his father’s house but from the whole city, lest the sight of him in the house offend the new bride in her stepmotherly hatred. He made way for the ill-fated marriage, which his father celebrated with the exile of his only son, and was scarcely summoned even for the celebrations on feast days. Seeing her husband comply with her wishes even when it brought his family devotion into disrepute, the woman turned to arrogance. A further cause was added that justly inflamed her spirit: she had learnt that her grandfather Hyrcanus had been killed through her husband’s plots, falsely suspected of desiring the kingdom. He is the man we mentioned above, whom Barzaphranes, who commanded the Persians, had carried off captive when he occupied Syria. He had first been detained in Parthia; then, pitying his fallen lot, Barzaphranes had handed him over at the request of the Jews who lived beyond the Euphrates. If only, just as he had been granted to those who entreated for him, he had also trusted those who warned him not to let the power of his relatives tempt him, in the manner of human nature, to go over to Herod. That power would endanger him, since a man eager to preserve his kingdom harassed none more than those closest to him and guarded against his relatives. But, weary of living abroad and longing for his own people, he crossed the Euphrates and returned to Judaea. This sank deeper into Herod’s heart than anyone had thought, not because Hyrcanus had aspired to the kingdom, but because it was thought uncertain whether a man of royal birth, with the privilege of power long exercised, could refrain from it. His granddaughter’s marriage was therefore the snare of death for Hyrcanus. For its sake he hastened to Herod, unaware that captives lived more safely with an enemy than relatives with a king. Thus, without even a slight suspicion that he sought to reign, he was killed for this reason alone: the kingdom seemed to belong to him.

Meanwhile he loved Mariamne with lavish love and did not wish her to be offended. Her many children had increased his favour towards her. For she had borne him five children, but the youngest of the three males had died in Rome while being instructed in the liberal arts. The other two were honoured with royal splendour beyond the measure of private men. The young men were supported by their mother’s noble birth and their own birth into kingship, since they had been born when their father was already reigning. Above all, however, they were supported by his love for Mariamne, which inflamed the king more and more each day. Although his wife repaid him with no love in return, he nevertheless took care not to sadden her spirit in anything. The woman’s hatred and the man’s love contended against one another in an evenly balanced scale. Yet Mariamne had better cause to hate the husband who loved her than Herod had to love Mariamne, who did not love him. The woman drew hatred from his crime, confidence from his love: she recoiled from the one with a granddaughter’s grief, while the other exalted her through her lover’s submission. She therefore did not refrain even from reproaching him with his crimes: he had wickedly robbed her of her grandfather Hyrcanus and her brother Jonathan. The one was his grandfather by marriage, the other his brother-in-law; the former should have been spared because of the frailty of old age, the latter at least because of his youth. It was an unworthy deed: he had entrusted the high priesthood to a young man of seventeen, and immediately upon conferring honour on him he inflicted death, for no other reason, as we have learnt, than that the people suddenly burst into tears when he first approached the altars on a sacred feast day, clad in priestly robes. Herod found this so suspicious that he believed the people had wept for joy and thereby betrayed their affection for the youth. Those tears revealed their wish; the people’s enthusiasm endangered him, since they had shown from their inmost hearts what enthusiasm they felt for the young man’s dignity. That noble grandson of a king, son of an unrestrained woman, brother of a most insolent queen who disdained her royal husband, would burst forth into power unless he were removed all the sooner. He possessed beauty and the charm of comeliness, so that he was thought rightly to deserve preference over everyone. Herod therefore resolved to kill the young man. The young man’s mother troubled him: most keen in investigation and most vehement in vengeance, she allowed nothing to remain hidden or unavenged. For that reason he considered drawing back and restraining himself. Yet the daily increase in everyone’s love for the young man and the danger to his kingdom troubled him in turn. Hence, roused by headlong fury, he resolved to look to his own interests by whatever means.

The young man was sent by night to the city of Jericho. There, where he was accustomed to delight in swimming, many gathered as though for play; submerged beyond all measure, he was killed in the pool.

His sister did not bear this in silence. Out of affection for her brother, she made it known in reproaches and repeatedly charged her husband with having her brother taken from her at his command. She had been bereft of everyone; her husband’s house was a house of mourning for her, for he had first taken her grandfather from her and afterwards killed her brother. Wretched woman that she was, she had brought destruction upon her own people. She called down dreadful curses upon her husband, her mother-in-law and the king’s sister: the crime was common to them all. She called upon God as avenger, that so great a deed should not be left unpunished. Herod bore this, captive to love and devoted to her every nod, but the women raged. They could not bear her curses as she reviled them or her arrogance in indignation, especially since Herod, overcome by his admiration for her, could not rise against the woman he loved. Thus, to arouse him all the more in his love, a scene of adultery was devised and a charge of this kind was fabricated against the woman: she had sent her portrait to Antony in Egypt. What lack of restraint she had shown, offering her beauty for sale to an absent man prone to lust and, moreover, powerful, one who used power as his right, auctioning off her beauty! In the commerce of this novel auction she had prostituted herself, whether through the force of love or hatred of her husband, whose peril she had demanded as the price of adultery. Through this invention of the women, therefore, Mariamne was assailed before Herod all the more grievously the more she was loved. Yet the accusation itself, although made by indignant women, was not wholly alien to truth. It was nearer the truth to believe that her mother Alexandra, furious that another was being preferred to her son Aristobulus for the priesthood—for she preferred her son Jonathan to be called by this name, to recall that her grandfather had been king—had asked Antony to grant her son the priesthood through a certain musician who acted as intermediary for the letters; and then that, when Antony’s friend Gellius came to Judaea, the young man, upon becoming known to him, had aroused his admiration through the charm of his exceptional comeliness. Mariamne had done so no less: the more illustrious her rank, the more brilliant her reputation. Perhaps he had come to know her through a certain habit of human nature, by which men too wish to show how dear they are to their more intimate friends by allowing them to share a hospitable table with their relatives also present.

There too, Alexandra was said to have been given an opportunity to speak with Sossius, although, as a widow rather free in her conduct, she could not have lacked another opportunity to become acquainted with the guest, especially since she sought occasions and people of this kind. Then, after consulting together, they had decided that portraits of both should be sent to Antony. Dazzled by the splendour of the portraits, and especially by Sossius’s testimony, Antony had written to Herod to send Aristobulus to him without delay. Sossius, acting as a pander to excite Antony’s far from sober desires, had declared that he had never seen anything like them on earth and that their charm was divine, not human. He had passed over Mariamne because she was married to Herod, not because he was accustomed to conceal his lust even for women living with their husbands: he could enjoy them without danger and commit disgrace without shame. Rather, he guarded against Cleopatra’s indignation. She took offence at a rival of either sex, but more so if she discovered a woman attached to Antony, since she thought herself more beautiful than all other women. Upon reading the letter, Herod had therefore excused himself on the grounds that he could not tear the noble young man away from his people without their rising in sedition and the whole nation being thrown into turmoil. To satisfy Alexandra, he had promised Aristobulus the priesthood. But, thinking the promises were being delayed and that she was being cunningly deceived, Alexandra had prepared a ship. While she was making ready to flee, her plan had become known through Sabbion and she had been brought back with her son. Moved by these things, Herod had concealed the affront for a time and hastened the grant of the priesthood to Aristobulus, so as to veil the odium of the murder he had prepared beneath the appearance of honour.

Once the murder had been carried out, as we have said, he was shaken as though struck by lightning, and at the same time by the charge fabricated by his own people that she had sought an adulterous lover. He knew that Antony was prone to lust and, because of his very great power, inflamed his unconcealed desires for every kind of love affair. He also knew that Cleopatra’s implacable resentment, especially of rivalry, and her savagery had killed very many men whom she had found too slow to restrain their wives’ lack of restraint. He shuddered at the danger not only of losing his wife but of facing death as well. He therefore resolved to go himself to Egypt to sway Antony or Cleopatra, whom he feared most. Others report that he went there after being summoned by Antony’s letter to give an account of the young man’s killing.

Before setting out, however, he privately disclosed to his brother-in-law Josephus, whom the king’s sister Salome had married, that he feared being killed because of desire for his wife’s beauty, which the woman was accused of having made known by sending an image of her comeliness. He entrusted this task to him as his brother-in-law: if he himself were killed by Antony, he was to kill Mariamne, so that no reward for the disgrace should survive. Josephus, by no means, I think, from a desire to betray him, but to soothe the woman’s complaints against her husband, in which she said that in her affliction she burned with hatred for him, revealed the instruction. He interpreted it as a lover’s affection: not even in death would Herod allow himself to be separated from his union with his wife. But, far differently from what Josephus had supposed, the woman took it as proof of his still unappeased cruelty towards her. He had charged his own brother-in-law with carrying it out even after his death. He wronged her in his hostility: he did not test his suspicions against any evidence of truth but pressed them through to the destruction of headlong death. There would be no end to hatred that extended beyond the very end of life and safety. But Josephus, forgetful of trouble at home, inflamed his own wife’s suspicions against him while seeking to reconcile another man’s wife to her husband. She thought that her own husband’s conversations with Mariamne and his lingering in the royal palace should not be taken lightly. Indeed, when her brother returned, she did not delay her accusation, adding her own injury to the insults against the king: Mariamne had taken her husband from her too. But Herod, although shaken, was at first by no means greatly moved. He did not show himself hostile to his wife; indeed, broken by the force of love, one day he began to swear to the woman that he loved her with such affection that he had never burned with desire for another woman. He had cast them all from his mind so as to remain faithful to his wife. But she said: “You showed your love for me well enough in the instructions you gave Josephus, ordering him to kill me. How can a man love who can kill?”

The king immediately lost his senses when he heard that his secret had been betrayed. He therefore began to think that Josephus would never have betrayed him unless, captive to love for the woman, he had sought in illicit intercourse the reward for betrayal. What had long been hidden was now revealed; the crime was in the open, the debauchery beyond doubt. His sister had not been roused without reason, for she had detected the injury to her household before anyone else. Thus, raging with excessive indignation and beside himself, he leapt from the bed, fleeing the contamination of shameful debauchery, and the palace could not contain his fury. His sister heard him shouting and at once seized the moment for an accusation, an opportunity to do harm, and confirmed his angry suspicions. Impelled by the pain of the injury and his sister’s accusation, he therefore ordered both to be killed.

Not long afterwards, remorse for his deeds followed. When anger fell away, love succeeded it and passion was revived. Such a heat of desire blazed up that he did not believe she was dead and, out of his mind, spoke to her as though she were alive. He sent servants to her as to a living woman, asking her to lay aside their quarrels, come to him and restore herself to their conjugal affection. Only after much time and instruction did he finally believe that she had died. In his love, he had thought that a woman of such immortal beauty could not die. So great was his affection for the dead woman. Indeed, he is said afterwards to have grown savage and, embittered by hatred of those around him, to have killed many, and to have suffered not only from sickness of mind but also from a grave illness of the body, which they said he had contracted also from the pestilential air. For the corrupted atmosphere brought pestilence upon very many. Hence, after consulting those skilled in medicine, he withdrew into the seclusion of the woods. As his vigour gradually returned, hunting restored both his bodily health and his sobriety of mind.

These things too he added to the wonders with which he revered the dead woman’s charm: he had paid the penalty for his unjust crime, and the destruction of such beauty had been expiated by the sickness of the elements. The death of one woman had been avenged by the world’s ruin and a plague upon peoples, yet with an unequal recompense, as the earth refused its fruits and famine increased the pestilence.

Mariamne met this end with composure, chaste towards her husband but insolent in her awareness of her beauty. She had magnanimity in excess but lacked attentiveness, so that she disdained her husband’s caresses, confident that she could suffer no destruction at the hands of one who loved her beyond measure.

She not only found vengeance for the present but also transmitted hereditary hatred into the future. Her sons succeeded her as executors of their mother’s grief, with an affection indeed devoted to their mother but impious towards their father, although the right of nature should have been discharged towards both parents with equal service. Grief did not find them untrained. For, educated for a long time in Rome in Latin and Greek letters alike, they had acquired no small cunning. On learning of their mother’s death while absent, they were embittered by the many who incited them to hatred of their father. Even upon their return, reverence for their father’s presence had not instilled attentiveness in them; malice grew with age. Marriage added to their presumption: Salome’s daughter, Herod’s niece, had been joined in lawful wedlock to one, and the daughter of Archelaus, who held the kingdom of Cappadocia, to the other. The nobility of these unions had lent authority to their hatred. Herod therefore took offence even at his sons’ unspoken disposition, more agitated than a father’s family devotion could bear, which is often wounded even by a look. Further provocations were added by those who repeatedly warned him, as though out of concern, to guard against his sons’ plots, asserting that they were arming their hands to avenge their mother’s death.

Terrified by these warnings, Herod began to prefer Antipater, Dosis’s son, to his brothers and, with more abundant affection, to draw him into his favour. The royal palace began to burn with greater hatred and to be shaken by rivalry between the brothers, as the others resented a private woman’s son being preferred to them, who had been born into kingship. Cunning in flattery, the lower he saw his maternal standing to be, the more eagerly Antipater commended himself to his father. He did not cease assailing his brothers with fabricated accusations until, by himself and through others he had attached to him, he excluded them from their father’s affection. Indeed, he took away all their hope of reigning, so that in a publicly drawn-up will he alone was designated successor to the rule. Sent to Caesar in Rome, he was supported with every royal adornment and splendour except the distinction of the diadem. Returning from there to Judaea with increased favour from Caesar and very many illustrious men, he gained so much influence in a very short time that he even restored his mother to marriage with his father. With the twin weapons of skill in flattery and cunning in accusation, he began to press his brothers so hard before their father that their father prepared death for his sons.

Indeed, beside himself with fury, he went to Rome, dragging Alexander with him, and arraigned him before Caesar on a charge of magic directed against him. Given the opportunity to lament his misfortune and all his afflictions, Alexander saw that he had the support of so great a judge, who could neither be swayed through favour by Herod nor deceived by Antipater. Thinking nothing should be passed over, he touched upon his father’s crimes with a certain restraint, so as neither to appear to press them as an accuser nor allow them to remain hidden, since it would greatly help his case if he showed that his father’s hatred assailed him because of his grief at his mother’s murder. For in trials of this kind nothing weighs more heavily upon children than nature’s family devotion and the authority of that devotion. If these are discredited by some crime, the prejudgement is diminished and the privileged claim removed. When he came to his father’s charges, however, he refuted them with powerful assertions and first showed that his brother had no part in the crime. He shared his dangers, and Alexander groaned that an innocent man was being accused. The force of his pleading and his skill in speaking supported his clear conscience. He lamented most bitterly that no honour remained to himself and his brother: everything had been taken away through their brother’s wickedness and their father’s pliancy. Death was being inflicted upon him, and his father so eagerly awaited it that he added a charge and attached a crime. With these words he brought everyone to tears and turned the course of the trial so that Caesar rejected the accusation and his father embraced reconciliation. It was most pleasing and distinguished for the Roman ruler not only to have given a kingdom to an illustrious king but also to have restored his children. It was therefore determined after a just examination that reverence for the father’s right should remain inviolate and the sons’ innocence safe. The children were to obey their father, as was fitting, and he was to show his sons the unimpaired affection of nature; nevertheless, he could leave the kingdom to whom he wished.

Alexander returned from the city of Rome with his father, acquitted at trial more than cleared of suspicion. For Antipater did not allow Herod’s mind to be free of hatred for his sons. He himself was the very material of that hatred; yet, out of regard for the reconciler, he restrained his purpose so as not to betray the scene he had staged against his brothers and expose his plots. When they reached Cilicia and put in at Eliusa on their voyage, Archelaus received them with a sumptuous banquet, giving thanks on behalf of his son-in-law Alexander, whom Herod had considered worthy of reconciliation as well as rescue from danger. He himself had also asked his friends, in letters sent through his own people, to assist his son-in-law’s defence. At Herod’s departure he offered thirty talents as gifts of hospitality and accompanied the king as far as Zephyrium.
Upon returning home, the king immediately summoned the people and addressed them in this manner.

“Hebrew citizens, my reason for going to Rome proved both useful and fruitful: Caesar was to judge my sons, so that I, who was angry, should not hear the case alone. I went to Caesar so that the man who had restored my kingdom might pronounce upon my successor. He added to his benefits by doing what was difficult: restoring almost lost sons to their father, and restoring to brothers concord, which stands above kingship. I therefore return richer than when I set out. I have learnt to be a better father, because my sons have learnt to be better children, through Caesar’s benefit. For he determined that my sons’ succession should depend upon my decision: lest the privilege of succession engender arrogance, I myself should appoint as my successor the man I chose, the man who had deserved it, the man who had honoured his father more. I shall imitate Caesar, for by acquitting my younger sons he made them equal to my elder son. Thus today I appoint my three children kings together. Age supports the one, noble birth the others. Let their number trouble no one: the greatness of the kingdom is abundant enough for even more. Let God first judge my decision; then you too should join in. Honour fittingly those whom Caesar has united and their father appointed, so that their honour is neither excessive nor too low. The one inflates, the other exasperates. Let each be granted what is appropriate to his share. For a man does not so much please the person he honours beyond measure as wound the person to whom he denies his due. Often both are offended where flattery shows preference. I am certainly father to them all: honour paid to my sons is surely a favour to their father. Yet if anyone honours my children beyond measure, he is answerable to me also on my children’s behalf, for he brings about their downfall. Excessive honour supplies the means for audacity. Do I envy my children? Far from it. But I prefer them to have less power with goodwill than very great power with sedition. What belongs to arrogance or rapacity soon slips away; what belongs to goodwill is held for a long time. I shall therefore take care to attach relatives and friends to my children as guarantors of concord, through whose exhortation they may clothe themselves in mutual affection. For, while every evil utterance readily infects the hearer’s mind, continual conversations and prolonged familiarity especially tend to pour a plague into minds, which soon passes, as by contagion, into the conduct of those living together. Even if their conduct is tranquil, just as a pool, though calm, can rise in surges when stirred by winds, so a good nature is tossed by wicked advisers. I therefore think that each man ought to place his greatest hope for himself in me, for what accrues to my children is not lost to me. Each tribune or soldier should show greater reverence to the father of his commanders. I am the one, I am the one who will repay you all even for what you have bestowed upon my sons. If I observe upright efforts, I shall reward them in deeds. Ill will will receive its price, losing its reward even with the man it thought it should flatter. But you, good sons, consider first the sacred obligation of nature, whose affection binds even beasts and compels even wild creatures to love their kin. Mutual love remains among untamed animals, and beasts redeem their own by endangering themselves. Revere Caesar too, who has made you friends instead of enemies; and thirdly myself, who prefer to ask when I can command. Remain brothers; do not cast off what you were born. I give you the dress and splendour of rulers, but more precious is the inviolate seal of your love that I urge upon you. If family devotion remains, kingship delights; if affection is absent, rule is worthless and often harmful. Thus, while I put you to the test, for the present you have the honour of kingship, not the kingdom. If you love your father, the right will follow. Yet demonstrate your love for me among yourselves: as rulers you will enjoy everything by which kingship usually delights, while the burdens of rule and the mass of affairs will await me alone, even if I am unwilling. It is therefore to your advantage to wish what I wish, since I both wish for what is yours and consider it mine.” With these words he kissed his sons, so as to bind them to one another with a single kiss of love. Having done so, he dismissed the assembly.

Many departed happy, pleased by the concord between the brothers, but discord returned with the brothers, all the graver because their greater rank aroused more envy and supplied greater power to do harm. Mariamne’s sons resented being placed on an equal footing with the son of a private woman whose lineage knew nothing of kingship. Antipater, on the other hand, disdained having the hope of kingship divided between himself and his brothers, and envied his brothers, for whom even a lower place was scarcely reserved instead of the first. But he concealed and veiled himself, covering his hatred with a show of favour, while their every design lay open in their speech even to those who did not seek it, their tongue too ready and lavish with secrets. Whatever they had said reached Antipater at once; much that they had not said was also fabricated. The messenger added a great deal by way of amplification. Antipater was the architect of everything by which his brothers were assailed. His life was nothing other than a meeting place of cunning devices, a stage of wickedness, a plot of crimes, a mystery of disgraceful deeds. He planted informers, suborned witnesses and feigned a defence, carrying about the mask of a brother as though in a theatre, so as to shake off the lighter charges and yield to the graver ones, thereby deceiving his father more and stirring him more violently against his brothers. Above all, he skilfully aggravated the odium of a plan to kill their father and seize the kingdom, matters more suspicious to kings through fear of danger. Yet, lest the charges seem less credible to the king without anyone to rebut them, he first attempted to refute them himself and then wished to appear constrained by manifest evidence of the facts. With the case pleaded on both sides, as though nothing had been lacking in the trial, their father would be roused all the more against his sons as men convicted. For nothing lent greater credibility to the assertions than that Antipater was thought to be his brothers’ defender. Through this fraud he courted the favour of very many and inclined even his father’s mind towards himself.

Whatever was daily taken from his brothers’ share of their father’s affection was transferred to him. He drew away the king’s friends and relatives, and especially estranged the king’s brother Pheroras and his sister Salome from their nephews, so that they not only failed to defend them but also assailed and hated them. Alexander’s wife Glaphyra added material for hatred. With womanly insolence in her present circumstances, she had begun to exalt herself in proud disdain because she surpassed everyone in the distinction of her lineage. Thus she set herself above everyone in the royal palace as though their mistress, habitually boasting that her father and grandfather were kings, and especially that Darius Hystaspes was the summit of her maternal line. She insulted the king’s sister Salome and his wife Dosis for their low birth, which caused them grief and brought hatred upon herself. She similarly exasperated the other women joined to the king for their beauty rather than the nobility of their birth. For Herod delighted in very many women, not only according to royal custom but also by the practice of the Jews, as though with a certain licence for error: they use the figures of their ancestors as a cover for their own vices. Alexander was therefore burdened by his wife’s insolence.

Aristobulus too assailed his wife with the same words as Glaphyra: she was of lowly standing, could not be compared with royal offspring and was unequal to Glaphyra. It was a reproach to him that his brother enjoyed marriage to a woman of royal birth, while he himself had fallen below his birth by cohabiting with a private woman. Madman, to disturb his own bonds of kinship with abuse! Stung by these insults, Aristobulus’s wife reported them to her mother in tears. Salome in turn reported to King Herod what she had learnt through her daughter.

But he, thinking it better to warn his sons than destroy them, summoned them. In part he terrified them with a commander’s authority, in part he urged them with a father’s affection to love their brother and not be divided as enemies, forgiving past offences and threatening correction for future ones. Lamenting that they were assailed by many fabricated accusations, they pleaded and at the same time promised that henceforth their very deeds would lend credibility to their defence, if only their father would look at what was done and not rashly believe what he heard. For wicked informers would not be lacking so long as a credulous listener was available.

With these and similar words they softened their father. Although for the moment they drove away the fear that threatened them, they nevertheless increased their sorrow, seeing themselves pressed by Pheroras and Salome: the one their paternal uncle, the other their father’s sister, plotting against those whom they should have defended. For a grave fear was added by their very great influence with their brother. Except for the diadem, Herod had shared almost the whole power of the kingdom with his brother, and had bestowed no small wealth upon them both, especially Pheroras. Indeed, he put away a hundred talents each year, apart from the region situated beyond the Euphrates that multiplied his abundant revenues. He had also been appointed tetrarch by Caesar at Herod’s request and granted kinship with the king’s wife, since he had taken the queen’s sister in marriage. After her death, with the king’s elder daughter betrothed to him, he would have gained the favour of a son-in-law had he not, captive to love for a young slave woman, declined marriage to the royal girl. Exasperated by this affront, Herod gave his daughter to a man who later died in the Parthian war.

Nevertheless, when Pheroras was accused before him of having assailed his brother’s life with poison—a suspicion from which he had not been free even while his wife was alive—Herod willingly acquitted him after an interrogation first of very many people and finally of his friends had found him innocent of the deed of which he was accused. He also pardoned his planned flight: the confessions of his household disclosed his intention to carry off the slave woman he loved and flee to the Parthians. Alexander had breathed a little more freely while Pheroras was being assailed and Pheroras himself was assailing Salome for having promised to marry Syllaeus, Obodas’s man, who was the king of Arabia’s procurator and most hostile to Herod.

But when both were pardoned their offence, the storm of the household settled upon Alexander and enveloped him in grave danger. For Antipater, the savage plague and tempest of the whole palace, raged, bearing down upon his brother by every means and even through the concerted action of his relatives. His father’s sober state of mind was so disturbed that he loudly declared Alexander was standing over him with a sword. A scene of this kind had been brought forward: Alexander had enticed three eunuchs with more lavish gifts into his favour and participation in a shameful deed. One of them habitually served the king’s drinks, another brought in the dishes at dinner, and the third watched over the royal bed and never went away once Herod had lain down. When this was revealed, the eunuchs were compelled by torture to disclose the degrading acts of obscene lust. Unable to conceal the amorous promises either, they disclosed the words with which they had been solicited and the reward for illicit intercourse, so that a plan to murder his father might be believed beneath the disgrace. Through the charm of youth he possessed beauty of form and the strength of his years, whereas Herod was weak and already burdened by old age, dyeing his hair lest he reveal his years. Alexander could transfer the right to reign from Herod to himself whenever he wished. He promised immense rewards, and so they should place their hope in a young man, not in a decrepit old man whose end nature itself was hastening.

These things moved Herod deeply, but above all the eunuchs’ disclosure that had informed him that a body of soldiers, commanders of the army and centurions were conspiring with Alexander. Indeed, he was so agitated that he thought no kind of cruelty should be passed over, trusted no one and suspected everyone. Punishments were swifter than the investigation of crimes, and the death of the accused preceded judgement. Everywhere those assailed by any suspicion were seized for punishment. False accusations raged. Many, wishing to please the king, denounced the accused; but immediately the very men who had denounced others were themselves denounced and led to the place of punishment with those they had accused. Thus Herod had grown savage towards everyone, so that anyone left alive was suspect, the king thinking himself safe only if the human race should fail. He was irreconcilable towards the accused, distrustful of friends, arrogant towards his household, pitiless towards those on trial, fearful of everything, so that he frequently changed his quarters and spent sleepless nights. Exasperated by all these things, he suddenly bound Alexander in chains, surrounded him with guards and summoned his friends for interrogation. Those who denied the charges died under torture; those who remained silent in turn were torn with wounds to the very end of life because they confessed nothing that agreed with the suspicions. Yet some, overcome by the bitterness of the tortures and punishments, asserted that the young men had resolved to kill their father while he was intent upon hunting and to go to the city of Rome without delay, so as to evade punishment by flight. Although this was supported by no evidence, their father turned it to the consolation of his savage purpose, wishing to have just grounds for his son’s chains.

Alexander therefore considered that his father’s ears were barred against every defence of him, and that matters could in no way be brought to the point where Alexander could rely on his own innocence, assailed as he was by so great a mass of false accusations.
