Archelaus was far from possessing the right to rule, since among the Jews kingship belonged to no one except a man descended from Judah, as the law said. But this man, of Idumaean stock, with no connection by birth to the royal line, had crept into an honour not owed to him. Antipater had been grandfather to both the speaker and Archelaus, outstanding in wealth and powerful in other accomplishments, especially in his friendship with the Romans, and proven in war to the elder Caesar. Although he could have claimed kingship for himself, he had never sought it; indeed, he had preferred to defend it for others rather than obtain it for himself. He had deservedly been regarded as the best of fathers, having won freedom for Judaea by his wounds, without bringing it into slavery. Herod had aspired to kingship through the testimony of Antony, his father’s guest-friend. From that time the fortunes of the Jews had declined: Herod had acted as an enemy, not a ruler. Since he himself had been an adulterer of kingship, how could a lawful king have been created by him? They did not, however, plead to be free of kingship, but asked to be under Roman rule, whose favour had already been secured for them in the days of the Maccabees. Through the later usurpation of kingship they had declined so far that they were much inferior to those against whom they had sought alliance with Rome. Finally, he said that they begged, “Grant Judaea government by a provincial governor on the same terms as Syria, so that our devotion may be put to the test: whether we, who are called seditious and rebellious, can obey moderate judges.”

Replying to these arguments on Archelaus’s behalf, Nicolaus maintained that a most unruly nation had paid the penalty for its insolence, lest Archelaus should above all incur the odium of an inexcusable crime if they disturbed the peace by sedition and withdrew in mind and arms from alliance with the Romans. On the question of which will should take precedence, he asked who could doubt it, “when a later will is usually preferred to earlier ones, and this one ought to be regarded as much stronger than the rest, since in it Caesar’s prerogative of confirming the royal judgement has been preserved? By this the dignity of the Roman name is increased rather than diminished, if you, Caesar, do not deny kings what private persons are allowed—that their wills should be valid and that in their last writing they should name the person they most wish to succeed them—and if kings in turn preserve this honour for you, that confirmation of their judgement should be sought from you, so that the man whom his father has chosen and you have approved should succeed. When, then, did Herod show greater judgement: when he preserved your prerogative, Caesar, or when he passed you over? Where Antipas is appointed successor, Caesar is passed over; where Archelaus is appointed, Caesar is brought in. Without a foundation nothing is stable. Thus, by divine judgement, where justice was lacking, neither pretence nor intention had a foundation; but where fairness of mind was present, strength was sought to confirm the judgement. Consider, then, whether the man who chose you did you an injury, or whether what he left to be ratified by your arbitration ought to be annulled, when you are lord of all things, to whom even kings rightly yield power. For he who knew whom to choose to confirm his judgement certainly knew whom to choose to rule; nor could he be mistaken in his successor when he was not mistaken in the person who would confirm his judgement. For the man who appointed you arbiter certainly knew that he must appoint a successor whom you would not be displeased to appoint.”

After hearing both sides, Caesar deferred his sentence. Then, after consulting the senate, he placed Archelaus over the nation, to discharge the office of ruler without the honour of kingship. He nevertheless promised to grant him kingship too, if he conducted himself so as to win approval. Attempts at revolt among the people of Israel were already being reported. He appointed two of Herod’s sons as tetrarchs, Philip and Antipas, who had contested the kingship with Archelaus. He preserved the bequest to Herod’s sister, whose name was Salome, and himself added other gifts. He also judged that the thousand talents left to him should be divided between Herod’s two daughters, added another six hundred thousand, and decreed that they should be joined in marriage to Pheroras’s children.

Meanwhile, a young man pretended to be Alexander, claiming that those whom his father Herod had charged with the killing had taken pity and, substituting others in his place, had released him together with his brother Aristobulus. He made for Miletus and from there for Rome, so that it would be harder to recognise him among strangers.

There he would easily have stirred up the Jews, who were most ready for political change, had Caesar not learnt the facts and ordered a certain Celadus, who had known Alexander thoroughly, to bring the man to him at once. When Celadus saw the young man, he hesitated, deceived by the resemblance; but, seeing that the other signs did not agree, he asked where Aristobulus was. The man asserted that he was staying on the island of Cyprus to guard against plots, because it would be easier to kill the brothers if they were together. Then, when he was brought before Caesar, on a promise of impunity he immediately disclosed that, relying upon his resemblance in appearance, he had pretended to be Alexander so as to obtain countless gifts from the Jews as a king’s son. Caesar laughed at the deceit, but let the man himself go unpunished and pronounced those who had given him gifts beyond the measure due to a private person, as though he were a king’s son, sufficiently punished by the immense losses they had borne in unnecessary expenditure.

Archelaus, however, after going to Judaea, was accused before Caesar of obscenity in his conduct and insolence. When the case between the parties had been heard, he was banished to Vienne, and his wealth was added to Caesar’s treasury.

He deservedly paid this price, for he had not restrained his desires even from his own brother’s wife. When Alexander died, delivered to death at his father’s command, his wife Glaphyra, daughter of Archelaus, king of the Cappadocians, as we have mentioned above, was joined in a second marriage to Juba, king of Libya. When Juba died, she returned to her father. On seeing her there, Archelaus—thinking that, as her husband’s brother and her children’s uncle, he could hardly be shunned consistently with family devotion—began to love her so desperately that he cast out his wife Mariamme and put Glaphyra in her place. Not long afterwards, when the woman had returned to Judaea, she saw Alexander in a dream and wished to embrace him. But he seemed to withdraw from her embrace like an indignant man and to say: “Is this, Glaphyra, faithfulness to your promise? Is this how you have preserved my love for you, which you ought to have remembered? But let it be so: as a very young woman you had not refused a second marriage. But even a third? Even your husband’s brother? Did the injury to me so delight you that you were not ashamed to return to my house married to a third husband? But I shall see to it that my dishonour, your pollution, does not last longer. Nor will the incestuous man long rejoice in his brother’s marriage.” The woman rose and told her household the dream. By dying herself two days later, she confirmed that marriages of this kind do not go unpunished either by the laws of the living or by the wishes of the dead.

Archelaus himself also saw in a dream nine large, full ears of grain being devoured by oxen. When he inquired, an interpreter answered that the nine ears signified the nine years in which he had enjoyed the fullest and greatest power. In the ninth year of his rule, therefore, a change would come upon him, since oxen, which were accustomed to turn the fields with the plough, signified a laborious change that would devour and swallow up his former achievements. On the fifth day after he learnt this, a man came from Caesar to take him to Rome for judgement. Condemned there and driven into exile, he fulfilled his dreams also in death.

The dominion over the nation that had belonged to Archelaus was given the name of a province. This was the name the Romans gave to regions situated far away when they brought them under their authority by conquest. Yet the tetrarchs remained as before, Philip and Herod, the latter having changed the name by which he had previously been called, Antipas. For Salome, at her death, had left the places she held and authority over her people to Livia, Caesar’s wife. Such was the state of Judaea when Caesar died, leaving as successor to the rule of Rome his stepson Tiberius, the son of his wife Livia by an earlier husband. In his honour Herod founded Tiberias. Philip too thought that a city should be called Livia after the name of Tiberius’s mother.

And since our purpose is to reveal the causes by which the Jewish people revolted from Roman rule and hastened their own destruction, events show that Pilate, the governor of the province, gave their ruin its beginning: he was the first of all who did not hesitate to bring images of Caesar into the buildings of Jerusalem. The people were stirred to resist, and since he held that the images must be admitted, he drove very many to their deaths.

While these events were taking place in Judaea, Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, came to Rome, wishing to contest his case against Herod the tetrarch in a hearing before Tiberius. But, spurned by Tiberius, he remained at Rome and won very many friends, especially Gaius, Germanicus’s son. Whether he thought Gaius dear to the people through the favour attached to his father’s name, or closest to imperial power through his connection with the royal family, or acted from some foreknowledge, he cultivated him more eagerly than either his age or his rank warranted. Thus one day he raised his hands and prayed that Tiberius might die sooner and that he might see Gaius as emperor. When this was disclosed by his freedman Eutychus, Agrippa was led into chains at Tiberius’s command and cruelly tortured. He was not released before Tiberius ended his days. Yet Tiberius’s reign, foul with outrages, and his retreat on Capri, intolerable in its indolence, roused no man capable of effective action to kill him—because, I think, of reverence for the recently established rule of Rome, or of terror at his most savage cruelty, since harshness is very often safer the more oppressive it is.

During his reign, the notorious outrage against Paulina, a woman of a most distinguished family, became widely known at Rome. She had an outstanding reputation for chastity among everyone, and was of surpassing beauty and eminent charm. Though assailed by the solicitations of Mundus, a commander of cavalry, she did not yield; but through the fault of excessive superstition she laid herself open to deception. The priests of Isis were suborned to bring her what purported to be a message from Anubis: he invited her to the temple, and, delighted by her devotion and chastity, asked for a night, having something he wished to entrust to her in secret. On receiving this, she joyfully reported to her husband that the god favoured her prayers, that the god asked for her presence, and that she could not refuse obedience. So, with both her own and her husband’s approval, she went to the temple of Isis and spent the night there. With witnesses removed far away, she lay down on her bed as though about to receive knowledge of a sacred mystery, thinking that her god would come to her in sleep and reveal himself to her in a vision. But when some of the night had passed, so that the woman could more easily be deceived while sound asleep, Mundus came in the face and dress of Anubis, lifted her clothes and rushed to kiss her. When she awoke, he told her that he was Anubis and displayed the face of Anubis. She believed him to be the god and declared herself blessed because her lord and god had deigned to visit her. She did not refuse when he sought her embrace, but asked whether a god could mate with a human being. He brought out examples: Alcmena had received Jupiter, the highest of the gods; Leda had enjoyed intercourse with him, as had very many other women who had given birth to gods. He also persuaded the woman that a god would be born of himself and her, and had intercourse with her. She returned to her husband happier still, saying that she, a woman, had mated with a god and, according to his promise, would bear a god. Her husband felt immense joy at the woman’s violation. Afterwards Mundus met the woman and said: “Paulina, blessed in your intercourse with a god! Great is the god Anubis, whose mysteries you have received. But learn not to refuse human beings any more than gods: the gods grant them what you have denied, since they do not disdain to give us either their forms or their names. See, the god Anubis called Mundus too to his rites, to join him to you. What good did your harshness do you, except to cheat you of the gain of the twenty thousand I had offered? Imitate the more indulgent gods, who grant us without payment what we could not obtain from you at a great price. But if human names offend you, it pleased me to be called Anubis, and the favour attached to this name helped to bring about the result.” Stunned by his words, the woman understood that she had been deceived. Grieving at the injury to her chastity, she confessed the deceit to her husband. He had no grounds for anger against his wife, to whom he had himself given permission to sleep in the temple, and, knowing her marital chastity, he brought a complaint before the emperor. Moved by the dishonour done to a powerful man and by the contrivance of an atrocious crime, the emperor dragged the priests from the temple, subjected them to torture and, after they confessed, killed them. He sank the statue of Isis in the Tiber. Mundus was allowed to flee, because, overcome by the force of love and the charm of beauty, he was thought deserving of a lighter penalty for his deeds.

I therefore thought that I should not pass over the outrage that occurred while Tiberius ruled, so that the emperor’s depravity might be inferred from it. For just as a good ruler’s life is a kind of rule of probity and a pattern of living for everyone, so an emperor’s filth is a law of crimes. Pilate, sent by him to Judaea, a wicked man who made little of lying, deceived the Samaritans into going to the mountain named Gadir, which was sacred to them, on the claim that he wished to learn their mysteries. Going up, he forestalled the people with cavalry and infantry and struck them down on the fabricated charge that they had prepared to revolt from the Romans and seek a meeting place of their own.

For what would he not dare, who had even nailed to a cross Christ the Lord, coming for the salvation of the human race, pouring out upon human beings the grace of his mercy through many divine works, and teaching nothing except what would make peoples obedient first to God and then to emperors? Madman, to be the minister of sacrilegious fury and kill the author of salvation! From that time, therefore, the fortunes of the Jews were ruined; from that time destruction was hastened for the nation and ruin for the temple. For if Herod, who delivered John to death, paid the price of his faithlessness and cruelty by being cast down from his kingdom and given over to exile, how much more must we understand the man who killed Christ to have been driven by headlong furies?

I shall briefly explain the cause of John’s death. We have shown above that Philip and Herod, who was previously called Antipas, were brothers; Philip’s wife was Herodias, whom Herod joined to himself by an unlawful and unspeakable bond of marriage. John did not tolerate this and said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” Then Herod, angered, thrust John into prison. Not long afterwards he killed this just man, a steadfast enforcer of divine law. For John had rebuked the incest of a brother’s bed not only as a preacher of the gospel, but also, as an enforcer of the law, had condemned the transgressor of the law who had taken away his living brother’s wife, especially when she had offspring by that same brother. Hence arose the hatred of almost all the Jews against Herod, and his punishment was hastened.

Herodias brought this about. Seeing that Agrippa had become very influential with Caesar, she compelled Herod to go to Rome to win the emperor’s favour, taunting him with the disgrace of idleness: by shunning exertion and lingering at home, he allowed men unworthy of comparison with himself to be preferred to him. Since Agrippa had been made king from private station, how much less would Caesar hesitate to confer kingship upon him, who had long been a tetrarch! Unable to bear the woman’s reproaches, he therefore set out for Rome. While seeking Gaius’s friendship, he was accused by Agrippa and lost even the tetrarchy he had received from Julius Augustus. Fleeing to Spain with his wife Herodias, he was consumed by grief of mind.

On Tiberius’s death, Gaius succeeded him. Wishing to be regarded and called lord and god, he gave the Jews grounds for most grievous sedition; had his rule not come to an early end, he would have brought the Jewish nation to an earlier end. For not only did he fail to restrain his own men from unlawful acts, but he even threatened those sent to Judaea with the ultimate punishment unless they carried out by arms every act against the law and sanctity of religion. Agrippa was very powerful during his rule, but, wishing to enclose Jerusalem with a very great wall so that the Romans could not take it—for he foresaw the impending ruin—he was overtaken by death and left the work unfinished.

He exercised no less power under Claudius, since he had also taken part in the beginnings of his rule. When Gaius had been killed and Claudius himself had been raised to imperial power by the soldiers, the senate resisted him out of weariness with kingship. He sent Agrippa as an envoy, through whose mediation a pledge of moderation was given, goodwill established and peace agreed. In place of Agrippa the father, his son Agrippa was appointed king by Claudius Caesar.

Won over by the persuasions of his wife Agrippina, Claudius himself too, as he was dying after thirteen years, appointed Nero emperor over the Roman dominion. Her deceit proved so powerful that she deprived the emperor’s son Britannicus, designated successor by the very right of nature, of any share in imperial power. She soon repented of this cunning: in providing for her own son, she had denied the emperor his, unaware that, exalted by power, her son would not even acknowledge his mother and would turn the reward for her benefit into her destruction. Yet he was married to Claudius’s daughter Octavia, a son-in-law preferred to a son in a reversal of the proper order, because the evils of the commonwealth weighed more heavily. It deserved a murderer of kin, a sacrilegious, incestuous man, so that crimes, not the merits of any good pursuit, should reign in him.

Under such an emperor, whether in view of his conduct and in contempt for his indolence, or because the protection of the most high God had been withdrawn from the Jews for their grave sacrileges and ultimate destruction was being prepared for them, their insolence erupted into grave seditions, brigandage and dissensions. Eleazar, the chief of the brigands, had ravaged them most grievously for twenty years. At last, however, he was captured by Felix, who governed Judaea, and sent to Rome, where he paid a heavy penalty.

Not even so was the people inhabiting Judaea broken by the great number of the slain. In Jerusalem itself another kind of brigand sprang up, called Sicarii. No longer hidden in secluded places or lying in wait in the darkness of night for travellers without protection, they struck in daylight, in the middle of the city and the press of the crowd, at anyone whom they approached. Carrying short swords in their hands and mingling with the crowded people, they stabbed someone beside them, and the unsuspecting victim fell with an unseen wound, death forestalling his cry. The corpse was in plain sight, but the killer was hidden. Anyone moved by another’s wound was brought nearer to his own and became one of the slain. Thus, whether through fear of danger or concealment of the crime, the Sicarius was not caught: such was the speed of those lying in wait and their skill in concealment. The priest Jonathan was killed; many were added each day. The fear of the living was heavier than the misery of the slain. Each day everyone went out as though to battle, but under a harsher condition: an enemy can be seen beforehand, whereas the Sicarius lurked unseen. Death was before their eyes, fear in their minds. No one believed that he would return, and not even friends were trusted while the Sicarius was feared.

Terrified by this, many made for the desert. They were indeed innocent of the crime of brigandage or association with the Sicarii; their hands were innocent, but their judgement was weaker. Yet, while looking to their own interests, they aroused a fear of revolt, from which first suspicion of war against the Romans, and then odium, flared up. Moved by this, the ruler of the province sent cavalry and infantry and slaughtered a very great multitude.

An Egyptian false prophet also arrived, versed in the magical arts, and boasted that he proclaimed heavenly oracles through a prophetic spirit. He attached about thirty thousand Jews to himself and gathered them at the Mount of Olives. In repeated assaults he penetrated Jerusalem, even attacking the Roman guards who were stationed there to prevent any disturbance by the people.

When this insolence too was suppressed, another part became more grievously inflamed, as in a sick body. Very many openly cried that they must revolt from the Romans and prefer freedom to slavery, and those who lacked food went out into the countryside and sought it by force.

Finally, in the city of Caesarea, grave sedition arose between Jews and gentiles. The Jews claimed possession of the whole city on the grounds that it had been founded by Herod, a Jew. The gentiles resisted: its founder had indeed been a Jew, but he had given it Caesar’s name; moreover, he had built temples within it and set up statues, and so it seemed to have been assigned rather to gentile uses. The sedition arising from these disputes turned to blows, because the leaders of the Jews could not restrain their own people who were bent on sedition, and the gentiles thought it a disgrace to concede that they must yield to the Jews. They therefore roused Felix; as he sought to suppress the unyielding crowds on both sides, recourse was had chiefly to arms, since no other remedy was possible.

Festus succeeded him and, after capturing very many brigands, delivered no small number to death. Albinus too, entrusted by the Romans with the same power, left no kind of wickedness untried. He was a wicked plunderer: anyone who had not given money was dragged into chains, though innocent; anyone who had given it was acquitted, even if guilty. Greed bred pride, so that he showed himself a tyrant to the poorer and a slave to the richer.

Yet, just as he had surpassed his predecessors in wickedness, so he was surpassed and left behind by his successor Florus, as though idle and slow in crimes: next behind him, but at a great distance, he could be thought blameless in comparison with a worse man. Those who had at first complained of their affliction afterwards longed for Festus as a good judge. He had stripped individuals; Florus plundered cities, most polluted in his obscenities and most cruel in his savagery, disturbing everything with arms and sowing battles from battles. He neither forgave when begged nor spared when sated.

In the sight of Berenice, King Agrippa’s sister, who had come to the temple for religious observance, he raged against the people in a most bitter slaughter. He did not think he should yield to her entreaties, though he saw her devoted to religious observance, standing barefoot, and treated her prayers with disdain. Hence she too wrote to King Agrippa, and the Jewish people sent to beg assistance for their freedom.

As he returned from Egypt, many came to meet him, going out more than sixty stades from Jerusalem. They led him around the city, proved the truth of their complaints, and began to insist that they should send envoys to Nero. He himself pitied their grief as that of fellow citizens. Yet, discerning with deep prudence that attempts at war against the Romans were being set in motion, he gathered the people together to prevent odium from falling upon himself and the utmost danger upon the people. At the place called the Xystus, near the temple and separated by a bridge, he gave the following speech.

“Although in many cases heedless grief, intolerant of counsel and restraint, makes some seethe with bitter complaints, when counsel is taken the feeling of grief is set aside. For if I had found all this people ready to avenge their injuries and make war upon the Roman dominion, and had not found the better and calmer part minded to choose peace and prefer quiet, I would not have dared either to come to you or to offer counsel. It is pointless to advise what ought to be done when the listeners favour the worse course. But some have no experience of the evils of war; others have a superficial hope of freedom, very sweet to seek but often unreasonable to expect to obtain—for many, in seeking freedom, heap up slavery, and everything is often snatched away from those who had at least the name of freedom left. Others, dissatisfied with their present circumstances because of their low standing, are attracted by change, and disturbance is reckoned a gain. I therefore thought I should deliberate with you, so that the sobriety of the more prudent should not be overborne by the audacity of the more insolent, or so that those who do not know how to judge rightly might at least learn from my admonition that they must yield to wiser counsellors. I therefore think you should grant me silence, so that I may set out what I believe is to your advantage, and that none of you should raise a disturbance if he hears anything against his wishes. For no one can judge the nature of what is said unless he has first heard it. Since he himself will decide whether to approve or reject it, he pointlessly raises a disturbance to avoid hearing it. Even after deliberation, each is free to hold the opinion he holds and, if he chooses to dissent, to maintain his ill-considered resolve even after sober warnings. But someone asks why I should wish to be heard in vain if those who hear me will not agree. Because, if they refuse to agree when they have heard, only part of my audience, not the whole people, will be endangered; but if they refuse to hear, even when only part of the audience raises a disturbance, the whole people is deprived of the benefit of hearing. My speech will therefore die even for those who wish to hear, if silence is denied me in any part of the assembly. For the whole speech is cut off and falls, as it were, lifeless, when the uproar of the assembly and its restless noise obstruct and kill it. There are therefore two things to which I think I must first reply, which carry the greatest weight in the complaints: that many cry out about the injuries inflicted by governors, and that many lament the loss of their freedom. These propositions seem to me to have been joined together and need to be separated. For if the governors are wicked, what need is there to raise the cry of freedom? You must not seem to accuse the governors as agents of domination out of loathing for slavery, rather than because they deserve it. Or, if slavery is intolerable, the complaint about the governors is needless. For even if they show restraint, slavery is still shameful. Let us therefore consider whether each of these provides substantial grounds for war. What is more foolish than to complain of injuries and weave a war out of them, exchanging insults for dangers, fleeing a judge and bringing in an enemy, when an unjust judge is often an interpreter of the law, whereas even a just enemy always seeks your life? A judge should therefore be soothed, not exasperated; an enemy should be avoided. Do not embitter the one and summon the other, since the one becomes gentler through soothing, while the other must be avoided so that he cannot harm you. In dealing with judges, then, take care that the complaint is not greater than the injury, and the odium of the charges heavier than the price of the offences. For often those who at first offended with some restraint become more insolent when accused, and those who previously stole in secret afterwards practise brigandage openly. Nothing so aggravates the heat of a wound as impatience in bearing it. Indeed, even with wild beasts, the tightest bonds press into them if they struggle and loosen if they remain still; and the severe force of fevers is lessened by endurance and increased by restlessness. If wild creatures know how to look to their own interests, forgetting their nature to relieve their pain, how much more has repeated experience taught human beings that the endurance of the injured has put those who injured them to shame, so that without an accuser they corrected what they would not have amended under accusation! But let it be granted that the insolence of Roman judges has been intolerable: which, then, is more tolerable, to endure them all or one? And what justice is there in making war upon all when one has injured you? Are all the Romans responsible for the injury? Is Caesar himself? Or was a wicked man deliberately chosen to be sent to you? They cannot keep watch across the seas and direct their eyes from west to east, to see there what is being done here, nor can they readily hear it: even if their concern demands it, distance denies it through the difficulty of obtaining evidence. Will one man’s guilt, then, tear the Roman world apart, when redress is swift even without your complaints, with none of the odium of an accusation and none of the toil of a journey? For Roman magistrates are changed in annual rotation, so that an insolent man does not remain long and a more restrained one soon succeeds him. Remaining quiet will therefore do no harm, since a remedy is brought even to those who remain quiet. But to weave together causes of war is ruinous, because war against anyone is a harsh condition; against the Romans it is fatal. If you wish to flee them because you cannot overcome them, you must leave the world. But you put forward your desire for freedom. That deliberation comes late. You should have fought to avoid losing freedom, rather than to demand it back once lost. The experience of slavery is harsh; therefore either it should not have been accepted at the outset, or, once accepted, it must be borne calmly. The proper time to resist was when you were being summoned to servitude. That was the more just struggle. But anyone who has once given himself into slavery, even if he later wishes to withdraw, is not defended as a lover of freedom but condemned as a disobedient slave. Where was this defence of freedom when Pompey invaded your regions and entered the city as its lord? Where were the arms for freedom? Why were they laid down by our fathers? They were certainly stronger than we are. They were vigorous in spirit, abundant in resources, eager to resist, but they could not withstand a small portion of the Roman army. They were conquered but spared. They acknowledged the yoke of slavery so as not to endure the punishment of captivity. Why do you, their heirs, refuse what you owe by right of succession? Your fathers’ dealings bind you. How do you shun obedience when you are so much inferior to those who obeyed? Or what will remain for you when you rouse Caesar and all Roman strength against yourselves? How can you withstand those who have triumphed over all and are now helped by all who serve in their armies? The Athenians, for the freedom of all Greece, gave their homeland to the flames, exchanging their homes for exile so that Xerxes should not rule them. He sailed on land and walked upon the waves; neither the seas could contain him nor the land bear him, since his march encompassed the whole expanse of Europe, and the bounds of the lands were narrower than the passage of his army. Yet they pursued him in his flight so closely that, fleeing in a single ship and in need of help, he barely escaped captivity. But those very men who crushed all Asia for tiny Salamis, and in a most glorious battle drove Xerxes to flight in the very element he thought subject to him, though he ruled the waves and subdued the seas, now serve the Romans. The Athenians, leaders of all Greece, obey Italian commands, and Athens, which gave laws to others, now serves under foreign laws. The Lacedaemonians too, after Thermopylae and the triumphs of the dead Leonidas, after Agesilaus the explorer of Asia, now love their masters. Macedonia and Africa, which through two most powerful commanders had brought dominion over the whole world into their own right and possession, do not resent its transfer from them. Content with so great a change in their circumstances, they desire the favour of those whom they sought to enslave. The Macedonians are stirred neither by Philip’s riches nor by Alexander’s triumphs. They think these commanders not undeserving of being called the wisest of all, because the one kept within Greece, while the other, fleeing Roman arms, came victorious as far as the Caspian kingdoms, the limits of conquered Persia and the hidden places of the Indians. He won the name ‘Great’ because he did not challenge the greatest of all. Although an early death withdrew him from a Roman triumph, he too serves in his descendants. For them the spoils of the East were acquired not as a support for dominion but as the price of slavery, so that the nobility of those who served might pass into the victor’s wealth. Great was Alexander’s valour; yet what wonder is there in that? He extended victory to the Ocean; the Romans extended it beyond the Ocean. Britain bears witness: situated outside the world, it was brought into the world by Roman valour. Those unknown to an earlier age became known through Roman victory. Even those who did not know what slavery was now serve: born for themselves alone and always free in their own right, separated by the intervening Ocean from greater powers, they could not fear those whom they did not know. It was therefore a greater thing to cross over to the Britons than to triumph over the Britons. For what could they do when the elements were already subject to Roman rule? The Ocean taught them to endure slavery after it too, as Roman ships crossed it, had acknowledged a slavery to which it was unaccustomed. For what need is there to recount Hannibal’s story? Victorious over so many regions, he too served the Romans by the triumphs with which he opened the Alps, paved the way and subdued cities to be acquired by his conquerors. Though often victorious, he never cut off the hope of the defeated; defeated once, he could not recover. He yielded of his own accord to his conquerors, whom he could not withstand even as victor, and, casting away his victorious arms, withdrew to King Prusias: from commander to mercenary, from triumphant general to fugitive. I shall come to the peoples inhabiting Gaul, fierce by nature and fiercer because of their natural walls. To the east they are protected by Alpine ridges, not masonry walls; to the west the Ocean encloses them. To the south the precipices of the Pyrenees, and to the north the streams of the Rhine and vast Germany, were thought to have made them unconquerable and inaccessible through the benefit of these barriers. Yet nothing was impassable to the Romans, travelling above the clouds and extending their dominion beyond the Pillars of Hercules: so easily was the hidden enemy found and the resisting enemy conquered. At their unexpected arrival Germany believed that the mountains had subsided and the Rhine dried up. Stronger than others in the size of their bodies and their contempt for death, the Germans had previously thought the Rhine a restraint upon themselves; now they thought it a defender of their safety. Thus it is now filled not with German skiffs but with Roman Liburnian galleys. Ranging through the whole course of the two-horned river as far as the sea, they press once free nations into slavery, so that those who formerly presumed that dominion over the whole world would be theirs now pay the price of their own slavery. What benefit did the Illyrians gain from the gold dug from the veins of their lands, when it was not enough for their battle for freedom? How much more precious is Roman iron, which Pannonian gold serves! The Pannonian therefore pays a tribute of gold and willingly transfers his wealth to the Roman treasury, to be safer in slavery. Nor has the water of Pactolus, turbid with gold, lifted its inhabitant into pride: he willingly serves those whom he sees kingdoms serving. Nor does the Indian marvel at his gem, or the Seres at their wool: these things are produced for their masters’ use, not as proceeds of trade but as dues of tribute. We hear of the proud dominions of the Persians, but we also see their hostages. Although they rule very many nations, they nevertheless offer their children and rejoice that their nobility serves the Romans as a pledge of peace, and also so that by serving they may learn to rule their own people. They offer garments, necklaces, even elephants. One thing has been granted to the Romans: to impose kings. Let us add Egypt, abundant in its own resources and needing no rain from heaven, since it generates its own rains and creates the abundance of showers. Although hotter than all other regions, it alone does not complain of drought, and, with a resource that no other place possesses, it nourishes its crops by irrigation. Ships sail through the sands, ships sail through sown fields where rain is unknown. Yet its extraordinary endowment and natural fertility serve the Romans, so that it feeds its masters for four months. What shall I say of the city itself, bearing the name of a most valiant king? Enclosed by a river as its wall, it knows no siege. The greatest of all rivers, spreading its bed through the expanses of the land, both removes the hindrances of a siege and supplies relief by carrying in what is needed for use. What land could have been more readily stirred to rebellion than Egypt? It counts seven million five hundred thousand people, apart from the inhabitants of Alexandria, enrolled under the Roman fasces. Yet, though it has so great a multitude, it prefers to labour under the tributes of Roman rule rather than to wage war at its own expense. I shall not pass over the Cyrenaeans, of Lacedaemonian stock. They once contended with the Carthaginians over boundaries and dominion, proposing death as the end of the contest. Defeated by this offer, though they had nevertheless avenged the injury, they conceded victory to the Philaeni brothers. Nor shall I pass over the Syrtes, terrible even to hear of, since they draw everything towards themselves and whatever approaches sticks fast in the shallow sea. Those versed in such matters have declared that a third part of the whole world is bounded by the Atlantic sea and the Pillars of Hercules on one side, and the Red Sea and the Ethiopians on the other. Who could number the peoples of so many nations? Supported by them, Carthage could not withstand Scipio’s hand, and preferred to feed Rome against itself for two-thirds of the year rather than rely on others’ resources to rebel against the Romans. Crete too, renowned for its hundred cities, displaying most fertile kingdoms, surrounded on every side by sea and accustomed to repel an enemy with its waves as with mountains, fears one man of consular rank; and very many peoples bow in fear before the rods of six fasces. Asia, Pontus, the Heniochi, the nomadic Scythians, the Tauroscythians, the Maeotian kingdoms and all the Bosporans are subject to Roman rule, and forty ships keep that formerly unnavigable sea at peace. For what shall I say of Armenia? It not only preserves the peace of its own frontier but also, intent on guarding the Gates, watches diligently lest anyone creep in to disturb the peace. All, then, are eager to serve the Romans. Do you alone disdain to be subject to those to whom everyone is subject? What arms do you trust in? What troops make you proud? Where is your fleet of ships to blockade the straits and range through the Romans’ seas? For even the elements have come under their name, as the world too has passed to them. It is enclosed and bounded by the Roman dominion; indeed, many call it the Roman world. For if we seek the truth, as I said above, the earth itself lies within the Roman dominion. Roman valour has advanced beyond it, seeking another world for itself beyond the Ocean, and has found in Britain a new possession remote from the confines of the lands. Indeed, those denied the right not only of Roman citizenship but almost of human fellowship itself are sent there, to live there as exiles from the world. The Ocean has yielded its borders; the Roman knows how to seek its inner secrets. Your war will be against the very men against whom even nature cannot maintain its own right. That Euphrates, formerly inaccessible to all but its own inhabitants, is now Roman on both banks, and shows that the whole East is under Roman rule. In the northern regions the Ister, flowing among savage and innumerable nations, receives hostages and restrains enemies. The southern tract, as far as it can be inhabited, ploughs for the Romans and gathers its harvest for them. In the west the coast of Gades, once the limit of the lands, receives new guests to bring their tribute to the Roman dominion, and has somewhere to send its own merchandise too. Where it formerly imagined only shipwreck, it now conducts trade. Since everything belongs to the Romans, where will you seek support against the Romans? From what uninhabitable region will you call for allies? For all who are in the world are Romans. Or will you send an embassy beyond the Euphrates to the Adiabenes? But they have no leisure to abandon their own affairs, nor does the Parthian allow the peace he sought for himself to be broken, lest he himself be held guilty of rebellion in his neighbours. Do not think this war like battles you might wage against Arabs and Egyptians: Roman arms are different, their resources are different, acquired throughout the world. Nor let the protection of Jerusalem’s walls flatter you: they have broken the stronger wall of the Ocean. But do you presume upon the aid of religion, when Jesus’ disciples have already filled the Roman world? Or do we think that without God’s will that religion grows and the city of Rome extends its dominion over all regions? Indeed, our religion abandoned us long ago, because we abandoned faith and often sought things forbidden by heavenly commands. How did the Egyptian come against us? How did we become captives of the Assyrians? Did Scripture not say that these things would happen? Was it not written that all the sacred mysteries of the temple would be profaned? Now repeatedly profaned, they no longer manifest their power and the full grace of the mysteries. The temple has been defiled with human blood, the shrines filled with corpses, the altars drenched with gore. Battle has been fought on the Sabbath; transgression has been committed, since the temple is defended not by its own observance and the solemn keeping of holy days, but by bloody battle. And this, indeed, it says again. How, then, can we merit divine aid as though against enemies hostile to religion, when we ourselves transgress against our own religion? What remedy is there, then, when neither human resources support us nor divine grace comes to our aid? One or the other of these commonly invites people to war; you lack both. What therefore remains but manifest destruction? If you do not turn aside from it while there is still time to take care, you yourselves will do nothing but burn your homeland, set fire to the temple, and give your wives and children over to death. You will be responsible for their utter loss, when the inconsolable addition to all evils is that what we suffer should be ascribed to our own fault. Moreover, other cities’ wars end with the destruction of their own inhabitants; your rebellion will destroy the whole religion, which, spread throughout the world, has scattered its people everywhere, and in every city there is a portion of us. All Jews will therefore be involved in your battle, and there will be no region free of our blood. Or, if the Romans are such that they do not persecute Jews even when provoked by war, how unjust it is to make war upon those whose humanity you may hope for! It is good, dearest friends, it is good, while the ship is still in harbour, to foresee the coming storm. Let no one expose himself to imminent dangers, lest, once you have put out into the deep, you can no longer avoid shipwreck. Often, indeed, a storm arises suddenly, and war is encountered even if it is not begun; but there is a difference between provoking an enemy and receiving his attack. He spares more readily when unprovoked, and necessity excuses insolence; but when someone plunges into sheer danger, he is also burdened with reproach. This is not an enemy you can avoid by flight. Wherever you go, danger will follow you; indeed, you will find it there. For all are friends of the Romans, and whoever is outside Roman friendship is the enemy of all. Let love of your homeland enter your minds. If regard for your children and your wives does not restrain you, let the sight of the most sacred temple restrain you. Spare religion at least; spare the most holy priests, whom the Romans will no longer spare, nor the temple itself. They regret having spared them, since all nations have long wished to extinguish our religion; yet Pompey, though he could have extinguished it, spared it. I have omitted nothing; I have given every warning that concerns your safety. I advise you to take the course I choose for myself; consider what is to your advantage. I desire peace with the Roman people for you and for myself. If you refuse, you yourselves deprive yourselves of my alliance. Either we shall share favour, or you shall face danger without me.”

As he said these things he wept, and so did his sister Berenice, for she too was in the upper part of the Xystus. Agrippa had moved them greatly with his tears, so that the Jews said: “We are not rebelling against the Romans, but think that war must be waged against Florus, who has done things that deserve war.” Agrippa answered: “But this is to make war upon the Romans; your deeds aim at injuring the Romans. Tribute is being withheld from the Romans, not Florus; from Caesar, not Florus. The soldier in the fortress called Antonia belongs to the Romans, not Florus. You have separated the temple from that fortress by demolishing and cutting off the porticoes, so that the guard should be kept apart. Restore the former state. Let the tribute owed to Caesar be paid to Caesar, lest Florus report that you have repudiated Caesar’s rule, not himself.”

The people had agreed to these words: they went up to the temple with Agrippa, began to rebuild the porticoes as they had been, and collected the tribute. Industrious agents were sent for this task, and in a short time the forty talents lacking from the tribute payment were gathered. All the tumult of war had been suppressed, but Agrippa wished to add that they should obey Florus until a successor came to him from Caesar. He so exasperated the people that they did not refrain even from insulting him; when he was driven from the city, it is uncertain whether some struck him with stones they threw. Moved by this injury, the king had those responsible among them arrested and sent them to Florus. He himself withdrew to his kingdom.

On his departure, the instigators of war laid an ambush and occupied the fortress of Masada, killing the Roman guards and installing their own. Eleazar too, the son of the chief priest, a man of reckless audacity, urged that no gift or sacrifice from any foreigner should be accepted. This was the trumpet of war against the Romans and roused everyone to tumult.

All the leading men, therefore, seeing that this would cause a reckless revolt, argued with the people that not only was war being brought upon Caesar, but the institutions of religion were also being violated and reverence for the temple diminished. The traditions of the fathers, who had adorned the temple with foreigners’ gifts, were being arraigned and condemned. Its wealth had increased far more through the contributions of the nations and the gifts of diverse and innumerable nations. The ancestors’ sacred practices were being obliterated, the sacred rites changed. What would become of the things already given, if gifts from the nations were forbidden to be offered in the same way in future? Or, if the Romans alone were forbidden what everyone else was allowed, what an incitement to war this would be! Lastly, it was impious if only among the Jews were foreigners permitted neither to sacrifice nor to bring gifts. They ought to consider that Caesar’s peace would be broken. Offended by such a disturbance, he would undoubtedly deprive the Jews of all practice of sacrifice, so that those who had rejected Caesar’s sacrifice would not even sacrifice for themselves. This must be forestalled promptly: if such decisions reached Florus, and thence undoubtedly Caesar, they would bring ruin upon the Jewish nation.

At the same time, wishing to support these points with the testimony of the priests, they asked whether a sacrifice of the gentiles had ever been rejected by their ancestors. Those bent on sedition raised an uproar to prevent this; not even the attendants dared to intervene in so great a dispute among the contending parties. Only one remedy seemed to remain: that Florus and King Agrippa should come with a military force, so that at least fear might make those desist whom counsel could by no means dissuade. But Florus wished the sedition to increase, so that there would be no room for pardoning the Jews: if they were caught up in war, all opportunity for them to press charges over his plunder and grave offences would be extinguished. He allowed the frenzy of war to grow and gave the envoys no reply. Agrippa, whom the embassy of his kinsmen Cylus, Antipas and Costobarus entreated most earnestly, was benevolent towards all. To preserve the Jews for the Romans, religion for the Jews, the temple for his homeland, the city for its citizens, and for himself the honour of rule and the tranquillity of his kingdom, he sent three thousand cavalry, with Darius and Philip as commanders of the squadrons, so that the advocates of the good cause, relying on this assistance, might exert themselves more readily.

From this confidence arose among the good and indignation among the wicked. War grew: one side was stirred by a juster cause, which nevertheless gave no help in armed conflict, the other by frenzy and the size of its multitude. The fighters’ battle lines were divided. The chief priests and the portion of the people that desired peace, together with the royal cavalry, occupied the upper part of the city; the others, stationed in the lower parts, claimed for themselves the temple and the places near the sacred precincts. At first they provoked war on both sides with stones, rocks and volleys of missiles, and fought with arrows; afterwards, when the need for combat happened to arise, they came to grips. The royal troops excelled in skill and experience and wished to keep the instigators of war from approaching, lest they defile the temple. Eleazar and his men, by contrast, were intent on invading even the upper city, which was called Zion. Battle was fought for seven days without any interruption.

The eighth day of the festival, at which everyone was accustomed to lay wood on the altars so that the fire should never fail—it had to remain unextinguished—increased their frenzy, so that all the attendants were excluded from the temple. As the Sicarii rushed forward more boldly than usual, the royal troops yielded and did not dare to hold their ground even in the upper parts. The houses of Agrippa and Berenice were burned and all the royal furnishings plundered. Fire was carried around, so that even the debt notes stored in the public archives were burned, so that the poor might rise more insolently against their moneylenders. Thinking themselves released from every bond, they set fire to the city with their own hands. The sinews of the city were burned away. The fortress called Antonia was stormed, all the guards found there were killed, and it was afterwards burned.

Menahem, son of Judas the Galilean, also hastened to Masada. An acute sophist, practised in unsettling affairs, he seized the armouries and armed the unarmed. Returning to Jerusalem with bodyguards attending him in royal fashion, he had become so immensely insolent that, rising above private station, he thought he need not refrain even from unlawful acts that free peoples could not endure. Many rose against him, denouncing him as a tyrant and master who, supported by royal attire, had weighed upon the citizens’ freedom. He paid a heavy penalty: tortured first, he died under his torments. Yet war was not removed, for a much graver disturbance arose.

Finally, Metilius and the Roman soldiers begged leave to depart. A pledge of faith was given and oaths were sworn. When they had laid down their arms according to the agreement and were departing without fear, Eleazar and the members of his faction slaughtered them unavenged. The Roman soldiers thought they should neither resist force nor beg, but cried out only against the violation of faith and the perjury of the faithless. All were therefore killed; Metilius himself, the prefect of the soldiers, alone was spared by pleading and supplication, at the same time promising to become a Jew even to the point of circumcision.

All Judaea was in flames, and the whole province of Syria too was roused to war. The people of Caesarea killed all the Jews they had among them. Roused by this grief, the Jews attacked very many cities of Syria and rose in revolt. Nowhere was there law, nowhere religion; the man who had plundered more was more highly honoured, as though piling up rewards of valour. It was a pitiable spectacle: unburied bodies lay everywhere in the cities, old men mingled with children, women too, without even coverings left to hide their private parts out of regard for the onlookers’ sense of shame. Everything was foul and full of pitiable sights. Although these grievous and wicked cruelties went beyond ghastly horror, they nevertheless threatened one another with still worse. There was monstrous brigandage between Jews and Syrians, since there was no hope of safety unless they forestalled one another. For what city did not contain Jews and Syrians mingled together? Days were passed in blood, nights in fear; neither hatred nor greed had any limit. For besides the differences of sect and worship, which had erupted into a public calamity so that each side wished the other destroyed, greed for possessions and the desire to plunder had seized their minds. They thought that no one should be spared whom they had assigned to death in their pursuit of plunder.

Why speak of smaller numbers of the slain? For, apart from the people of Antioch, Sidon and Apamea, scarcely any people failed to persecute the Jews living among them. The people of Gerasa, however, even escorted those who wished to leave as far as their own borders, so that they might depart without any treachery.

At Alexandria, however, a dispute arose between gentiles and Jews. When the Hebrews demanded vengeance and, seizing torches, threatened to burn the gentile people gathered in the amphitheatre, they drew the attention of Alexander Tiberius, the prefect of the place, who was occupied with other concerns, towards themselves. At first, indeed, he tried to restore public concord with peaceful words.

But when he perceived that they mocked his earnest warnings and that so great a sedition could not be removed in any other way, he gave the soldiers permission to attack them. Attacking those crowded around, they made a very great slaughter throughout the city, killing some as they resisted, others as they hid in their houses. No pity for small children, no reverence for the aged, no regard for women came over them. Fifty thousand Jews were therefore killed. The streets swam in blood; everything was filled with corpses. Flames crackled in a savage fire throughout the city: kindled in the Jews’ houses, they also devoured the neighbouring buildings. At last Alexander relented and ordered the soldiers to desist and sound the retreat, but the mob’s anger, once it had gained the power to kill, was by no means assuaged.

For they were paying the penalties for their own crimes: after crucifying Jesus, the arbiter of divine things, they went on to persecute his disciples. Yet many Jews and very many gentiles believed in him, drawn by his moral precepts and by an outpouring of works beyond human capacity. For them not even his death put an end to faith or grace; rather, it increased their devotion. They therefore laid murderous hands on their own kin and led the author of life to Pilate to be killed, and began to press the reluctant judge. Yet Pilate is not excused by this; the Jews’ madness is compounded, since he ought not to have condemned a man against whom he had found no guilt, nor ought they to have doubled their sacrilege with the murder of kin, so that the one who had offered himself to redeem and heal them was slaughtered by them. On this the Jews themselves also bear witness, since Josephus, the writer of histories, says that at that time there had been a wise man—“if indeed,” he says, “the creator of marvellous works ought to be called a man”—who had appeared alive to his disciples three days after his death, according to the writings of the prophets, who foretold both these and countless other things about him full of wonder. From him arose the congregation of Christians, and it spread into every race of humankind; no nation of the Roman world remained that had no share in his worship. If the Jews do not believe us, let them at least believe their own. Josephus said this, whom they themselves esteem the greatest; yet even in the very thing in which he spoke the truth, he was so errant in mind that he did not believe even his own words. He spoke for the sake of the faithfulness of his history, because he thought deception impious; he did not believe because of hardness of heart and obstinacy in faithlessness. Yet his failure to believe does not prejudice the truth; rather, it added more to the testimony, because, even unbelieving and unwilling, he did not deny it. In this the eternal power of Christ Jesus shone forth: even the leaders of the synagogue acknowledged as God the one they had seized for death. And indeed he spoke as God, making no exceptions for anyone and fearing no death, and announced that the temple too would be destroyed. Yet they were moved not by the injury to the temple but by his rebukes for their outrages and sacrileges. Hence their anger blazed up, so that they killed one such as no age had possessed. For while others had won by prayer the ability to do what they did, he had the power to command whatever he wished to be done.

Before Jesus’ death, John the Baptist had been killed, a holy man who never held that true salvation lay in prosperity. Indeed, in addition to all the things full of righteousness that he taught, by which he invited the Jews to worship God, he had also instituted baptism for the purification of soul and body. His freedom of speech caused his death, because he could not endure Herod’s violation of his brother’s marriage rights and his taking his own brother’s wife away. For when this same Herod was going to Rome, he entered his brother’s house as a guest. His brother’s wife was Herodias, daughter of Aristobulus and sister of King Agrippa. Forgetful of nature, he dared to solicit her to leave his brother and marry him when he returned from the city of Rome; with the woman’s consent an incestuous compact was made. News of this affair reached King Aretas’s daughter, who was still married to Herod. Indignant at a rival, she conveyed to her husband on his return her wish to be sent to the town of Machaerus, on the frontier between the Petraean king and Herod. He suspected nothing. Moreover, since all his affection for her had already waned, he agreed to her departure, so that he might more easily keep faith with Herodias in their compact if he sent his wife away. But when she approached her father’s kingdom, she disclosed what she had learnt to her father Aretas. By an ambush he destroyed Herod’s whole army, which had been drawn into battle, through betrayal by those who had joined Herod from the people of Philip the tetrarch. Herod therefore brought his complaint to Caesar, but God’s indignation prevented the vengeance ordered by Caesar, for in the midst of the preparations for war Caesar’s death was reported. We find that the Jews judged and believed this, with Josephus as a competent authority against himself: Herod had lost his army not through human deceit but through God’s anger, and justly indeed, in vengeance for John the Baptist, a righteous man who had said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have that woman as your wife.”

Yet we are weaving this account as though the Jews had kept lawful usages even among their own, when among them the right of the high priesthood had perished, destroyed either by greed or by the insolence of the more powerful, who thought that whatever they wished to do was lawful. For at the beginning Aaron was high priest, and in accordance with God’s will he transmitted the prerogative of the priesthood to his sons by lawful anointing. From them, in order of succession, were appointed those who held the primacy of the priesthood. Hence it became established by ancestral custom that no one should become chief priest unless he was of Aaron’s blood, since the right to this kind of priesthood had first been conferred upon him; a man of another lineage, even a king, could not lawfully succeed. Thus Uzziah, because he usurped the priestly office, was covered with leprosy and cast out of the temple, and spent the rest of his life without rule. He was certainly an excellent king, but he was not permitted to usurp religious office.

From the fathers’ departure from Egypt to the building of the temple founded by Solomon there were therefore thirteen chief priests, amounting to six hundred and twelve years, since at first the man who was chief priest remained so until death and no one was substituted in the place of the living. Later men were appointed in their place even while they lived. These thirteen, then, obtained the priesthood by succession; in their times there were aristocracy, the monarchy of judges and the power of kings. Again, from Solomon to the time of the captivity, when the people migrated into Syria after the city was captured and the temple burned, there were eighteen chief priests over four hundred and sixty years, six months and ten days. The people were in captivity for seventy years. Afterwards Cyrus, when he released the people from the region of the Assyrians and gave them permission to build the temple, also allowed the chief priest Josedec, who had been carried away with them, to return, so that the observance of the old rite might be restored through an experienced priest’s knowledge. He himself and his successors, fifteen men in number, fulfilled the office in order of succession from the people’s return to Antiochus Eupator, and held the primacy of the priesthood for four hundred and fourteen years. Antiochus, whom we mentioned above, and his commander Lysias first appointed Jacimus to the priesthood in place of the chief priest Onias, whom they had killed. Although he was of Aaron’s line, he was not of that same house. Ananias, the brother of Onias, therefore went to Egypt and petitioned Ptolemy Philometor—who had introduced rites of observance modelled on the solemn worship at Jerusalem into the religious practices of the city of Alexandria—and Cleopatra, Philometor’s wife, to be appointed chief priest there, since Jacimus did not have the lawful succession to the priesthood. Yet this same man died after three years; he who had abolished the observance of lawful succession did not deserve to have a successor. The city was therefore without a chief priest for seven years. Up to this point in the period of the fathers’ return from the land of the Assyrians, it had maintained democracy, because the Jewish people recognised that it had been led into captivity through the wickedness of kings. Afterwards the Hasmoneans obtained the power to govern the people and appointed Jonathan chief priest. Having discharged the office he had received for seven years, he met his end through Tryphon’s treachery. His own brother Simon succeeded in his place, as though by hereditary right, yet by election. We have learnt that he was killed at a banquet through his son-in-law’s treachery. From him the prerogative of the priesthood passed to his son Hyrcanus, whom flight had rescued from danger. Hyrcanus was succeeded by Aristobulus, who also added kingship to the office just mentioned so that he shared in both; Aristobulus was succeeded by Alexander. Both kingship and priesthood remained with Alexander until the last day of his life, for twenty-seven years, though often in an uncertain state: victory hung in the balance between him and Demetrius, and the citizens’ hatred was immense.

As he was dying, Alexander saw that the hatred he had incurred would be a dangerous inheritance for his sons. He wished his wife Alexandra to take the helm of the kingdom: she was trained by experience of rule and the habit of shared counsel, yet more favoured by the people, because she had often protected those endangered by her husband’s cruelty and restrained her husband. At the same time he appointed her to decide which of his sons in particular should be entrusted with the high priesthood. She put Hyrcanus in his father’s place in the priesthood, either because of the prerogative of his greater age or because, being of a gentler disposition than his brother, he seemed unlikely to cause his mother any trouble over the affairs of the kingdom. She entrusted no public office to Aristobulus, but even while his mother lived he took advantage of her illness to play the king in remote and more strongly fortified places. Offended by this and anxious over Hyrcanus’s complaints, his mother aggravated her illness. Her rule lasted no more than nine years, and she left Hyrcanus heir to everything, not because she expected him to keep it, but so as not to help an unworthy man or encourage a usurper’s insolence by a more favourable judgement.

But Alexandra’s death also took the priesthood and kingship from Hyrcanus. Defeated in war, he withdrew to more strongly fortified places and detained Aristobulus’s wife and children, whom he had found in the fortress. He welcomed a change of status: all power and the priesthood were to pass to Aristobulus, while he himself, as a private citizen, was to withdraw to Aristobulus’s house.

Yet he did not long remain content to have exchanged the royal palace for a private house. Stirred by Antipater, he first made for Arabia, as though protesting the injustice of the agreement. Then, when he saw that the Arab king’s assistance was weak against the Romans, whom Aristobulus had enticed into his alliance through Scaurus, he brought his complaint to Pompey as he approached.

Aristobulus, now in the third year of his rule, was evading Pompey. Pompey assailed him in war, seized him by his authority and placed him under guard before victory. After overcoming his people and taking the city, he ordered Aristobulus himself to be sent captive to Rome with his sons, restored the dignity of the priesthood to Hyrcanus, and appointed him to preside over the citizens, but without a diadem or the insignia of kingship. He was generous in honour but concerned for quiet, lest peace be disturbed by the spirit of Aristobulus’s insolence. Thus Aristobulus, though captive, stripped Hyrcanus of kingship; Hyrcanus afterwards spent twenty-four years in power, greater in practice than in name.

Yet the end of Hyrcanus’s power was not the end of his life. The rest of his life was spent in dishonour, as we mentioned above. Defeated in battle as the Parthians crossed the Euphrates, he was captured and put into the power of Antigonus, Aristobulus’s son. Even with his ears cut off, he had not yet endured the full bitterness of his pitiable suffering. For after these events he was also carried into exile in Parthia, a feeble old man who became a laughing-stock for the barbarians. Later, on learning that Herod ruled, to whom his granddaughter Mariamme was married, he returned to Judaea. There he was at first received with the greatest show of honour, so that a veil might be drawn over the plots; not long afterwards he was killed on the fabricated charge that he wished to regain power.

Herod had thus obtained the kingdom, which he had received from the Romans as the reward for attacking or betraying his homeland. In the place of Antigonus, who had held power for three years and three months, he appointed successors to the priesthood, not men of the Hasmonean lineage, whom we have learnt to have been of more illustrious ancestry, but any obscure men whom his whim or chance offered. Yet, worn down by the entreaties of his mother-in-law Alexandra, or frightened by her accusations, he appointed Jonathan, his wife’s brother, a young man of seventeen, as priest. Soon he himself put him to death, suspecting him of seeking rule, because each day he saw immense favour for him growing among the whole people. Passing over Anhelus, whom he had already appointed to the priesthood from among the obscure before Jonathan, he then chose the rest in succession, men of such a kind that he had nothing to suspect of them. For how would he not guard against in strangers what he had been unable to endure in a relative by marriage? Archelaus followed similar practices in such appointments: under the guise of his father’s custom he maintained the outlook of a narrower mind, following a sort of habit innate in mortals, among whom the sluggishness of duller men arouses less suspicion than the favour enjoyed by good men. Yet a weak mind is more insolent in prosperity, while a wiser one knows how to repay benefits.

Thus from Herod’s reign to Roman rule, which had added Judaea to the other provinces after Archelaus was deposed, and thence to the destruction of the temple and the triumph of Titus, there were twenty-eight chief priests over a hundred and seventy years. Most of them, indeed, only discharged the duties of the dignity; a few also held the right to exercise power. It is therefore clear that succession from the lawful lineage did not continue among the chief priests, for not all were descended from Aaron or from his sons, who were put in his place and left for the others the pattern of the prescribed succession. Thus, when the ancestors’ institutions had been corrupted by the greed or faithlessness of their own people, the laws of religion violated and the safeguards of antiquity torn apart, divine aid abandoned them not undeservedly. They were consequently assailed with every kind of injury as a people left defenceless: in domestic seditions they turned their hands against themselves, were afflicted by grievous brigandage, and received the vilest judges as their lot, so that men worse still succeeded the wicked.

Albinus, indeed, was regarded as the worst of the earlier governors, but with Florus as his successor he was ranked among the good. Florus raised the torch of war and kindled battle between the Romans and the Jews, which caused the final destruction of the temple and the city.

For when Cestius, who had received supreme military command in the regions of Syria from the Romans, learnt that the Jews were ablaze with the fury of war, he took up arms in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign to avenge the killing of the Roman soldiers who had been entrusted with the duty of restraining insolence and preserving peace. Having gathered the allies’ auxiliaries too, he entered Judaea. The inhabitants of the city named Zabulon had scattered in fear, leaving it full of riches which their owners had been unable to carry with them when they fled to the higher parts of the mountains. He allowed his army to plunder it. He also admired the beauty of its public works and ordered it to be burned.

As though this were too little for vengeance, he sent his army ahead to prevent anyone from escaping destruction by flight and seized Joppa, the men he had sent breaking in by land and sea. Eight thousand men and nearly four hundred more were killed; once its spoils had been plundered, the city was burned. He also laid waste the country near Caesarea, plundered what he found and burned the villages.

Sepphoris checked his onslaught, for all its inhabitants came out to meet Cestius. Soothed by their favour and goodwill, he left the city free from disaster. A band of brigands was active in these parts, but on the army’s arrival they had withdrawn to the mountains. They boldly attacked and harried Gallus, commander of the twelfth unit, as he advanced to battle, killing about two hundred Romans. But when the Romans occupied the higher ground, the brigands could not withstand the infantry at close quarters; as they fled, the cavalry easily surrounded and killed them. More than two thousand were therefore slain, and a few were put to flight who managed to hide in the steep parts of the mountains. The whole region was cleared of brigandage.

Gallus returned to Caesarea; Cestius marched to Antipatris with his whole force. There the Jews had massed no small multitude. But before they joined battle, they scattered in different directions, leaving the countryside and villages to plunder and fire.

Lydda too was found empty of inhabitants and burned. Gabao, which lay fifty stades from Jerusalem and was plainly visible, roused the Jews to arms when it received the Roman army. Disregarding the celebration of the Sabbath, which they solemnised with ancient worship and customary observance, they sprang upon the Romans with such force that they would have routed the whole army had the cavalry not come to the aid of the hard-pressed infantry. Five hundred and fifteen Romans were killed, but all had been in grave danger; twenty-two of the Jews were lost in battle. Here the valour of Monobazus and Cenedaeus shone forth. On learning that the Jews were rising against the Roman battle lines, they attacked from the front, drove back many and forced them to return to the city.

Simon too stripped the Romans of their baggage as they advanced up towards the city. For this reason Cestius remained in the district for three days. During this delay the enemy surrounded them and, stationed on higher ground, watched every approach so that no one could break in with impunity.

King Agrippa, seeing that this could not be attempted without great slaughter on both sides, sent his men Borcius and Phoebus to tell the people that whatever outrage they had committed against the Romans could be pardoned, if only they would lay down their arms and take thought for their safety in future. He judged that he should either persuade them all to renounce battle or detach a portion from the rest. The rebels, by contrast, fearing that one or other of these aims might succeed, attacked the envoys and killed Phoebus; Borcius was wounded and barely managed to escape.

Seeing disputes of this kind in the city, in which some rose against the envoys while others urged that the Romans should be received into the city, Cestius tried to force his way in. He drove those who resisted back as far as Jerusalem, and himself approached with his army to within three stades of the city. He spent three days there; on the fourth he attacked, entered Bethesda and immediately burned it, along with Caenopolis. As he pressed on towards the upper parts of the city and the rebels fled further inside, had he decided to force his way into the city, the whole war would undoubtedly have been ended.

Indeed, Ananus son of Jonathan had stationed many men to call out invitations to the Romans as though they were about to open the gates. But while Cestius was either being held back by Priscus and many centurions, who had been bribed by Florus and wanted the war to grow, or placed too little trust in the invitation, Ananus and his men were driven from the wall. When they fled to their homes, the rebels occupied their position. For five days the Romans tried different approaches. When they saw that they could not force an entry, they selected the strongest men and the archers and attacked the temple from the northern side. The Jews were not idle either: they fought bravely and grew prouder as they repeatedly drove back the enemy. At last, however, some were wounded by the multitude of arrows, others struck and terrified, and they yielded to the Romans, who had begun to undermine the wall and set fire to the temple gate.

Great fear had come upon the rebels, and a kind of bewilderment of mind. Many fled as though escaping the city’s imminent destruction. By not daring to stand their ground, they had given confidence to the people: with the departure of those whose multitude had hemmed them in, they now felt free and released from a sort of siege by the wicked. They poured around the gates to open them and receive Cestius as though he had come to defend the city, not to attack it. But Cestius himself was also suddenly seized by a kind of stupor, so that he noticed neither the desperation of the wicked nor the eagerness of the common people. Had he persisted a little longer in what he had begun, he would have put an end to the war and captured the city. But, as far as we are allowed to understand, God’s will, hostile to the Jews, postponed the imminent end of the war until ruin should engulf very many, indeed almost all, of the Jewish nation. The wait, I think, was for the enormity of their crimes to grow into every kind of wickedness and, with the increase of impiety, to reach the full measure of the worst outrages.

How was it that, when he ought to have pressed hard, Cestius suddenly recalled his army and raised the siege? This sudden change of circumstances, contrary to expectation, broke the spirits of the good, while the brigands took heart and gained confidence. Turning from flight to pursuit, they attacked the rear of the column and slaughtered many cavalry and infantry there as they rushed about in confusion. The day was already declining.
