Will I not also be asked, ‘Where are you, who have come without a command, whom I have not released from the bonds of nature? Take him into the outer darkness: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ We have learned that these acts are forbidden not only by human custom but also by laws. For some order those who have plunged iron into themselves to be cast out unburied. It is fitting that those who have not awaited their Father’s command should be deprived of burial in the earth, as though of a mother’s lap. Others cut off the right hand of the dead, so that the hand which fought against its own body in mad fury is separated from that body’s limbs. But this is the end suffered by the sacrilegious, or traitors, or killers of their parents. Those who have not acknowledged their true Father do not recognise themselves either. Thus they are either forbidden burial altogether or are not buried whole. Nor does paradise receive their souls, but the darkness of the underworld and savage torments. As I consider these things, although everything has been taken away, these alone terrify and frighten me: that I might inflict on myself what not even the enemy can inflict, and rob myself of those things of paradise which the Roman has not yet been able to take away—he can certainly hasten them, he cannot remove them—which alone I impatiently desire. For no desire for this life holds me, in which I have found nothing to delight me either among my fellow citizens or among my enemies. The former denied me peace, the latter robbed me of my country. Amid so many evils, what sweetness can remain in this life? Only you, almighty Father, author and arbiter of nature, grant me an honourable end. Break this bond of nature, restore my soul to its secluded places. Though the people be destroyed, their right taken away, their freedom broken, I shall not transgress your law by dying unbidden. I await your command; I await the release I desire from you. You have many to carry out your will: from you I await the command, from its executor the service. It is good to die, but if I die as a Hebrew, not as a brigand, not as an executioner, not as an enemy. Though I be defeated in war, I shall remain what I was born, so that I do not abandon the inheritance of Abraham our father. I shall not cross over into the number of the enemy to become my own slayer. I can offer myself to the enemy to be struck without loss of devotion; I cannot turn my hands against myself as an enemy without crime. Or is the fear that we may not be allowed to live according to the law? Truly, great is the freedom we now enjoy, when we are not allowed to die according to the law.”

Josephus put forward these arguments to undermine the defence of voluntary death. But those who had once devoted themselves to death, unable to resist his words, surrounded him with swords as though ready to strike him at once unless he thought fit to consent. Surrounded, he called one man back with a commander’s authority and addressed another with a stern gaze and the consciousness of his own valour. He restrained one man’s right hand, bent another’s anger, soothed them with wholesome counsel. In different ways he wrested unreasoning fury from each man. For although the final turn of fortune had stripped the defeated man of his dignity, it had not wholly abolished their reverence for him. Little by little, therefore, hands were lowered and swords put away, but their resolve persisted.

When he saw that he alone was held besieged by many, whether by some chance or by design he devised a way to reduce the number of those opposing him. “Let us entrust the order of dying to the lot,” he said, “so that no one may withdraw, since the lot embraces all. Let the condition of this lot be that whoever is drawn is killed by the man who follows.” Thus it would be the lot, not each man’s own will, that condemned him to death. “Let each therefore stand with the lot as judge, free from crime and free from captivity, so that he neither hastens the death to come at another’s will nor evades it at his own. No one will be able to refuse an outcome which either chance has brought about or God’s will has marked out.” The offer inspired confidence, and all agreed to the lot. Each man designated by lot offered himself to the next, ready to be killed. So it happened that when the rest had been killed, Josephus and one other survived the slaughter. It necessarily remained that either he would be condemned by lot, or, if he survived the destruction, he would be stained with his companion’s blood.

He persuaded his companion that they should renounce the lot. Thus he escaped the battle within and was conducted by Nicanor to Vespasian. A crowd gathered to see him arrive, with almost all the Romans flocking together. Some wished to see cast down the man whom a little earlier they had seen in the highest honour, in command of the whole enterprise; others strove to mock the captive; others marvelled at the changes in human affairs, so varied and shifting. Many, with greater wisdom, groaned, reflecting in another’s fall that the same could happen to themselves. Titus was moved more than the rest by his innate gentleness of spirit: this man, lately a proud warrior, suddenly subjected to the enemy’s power, awaited his fate at another’s nod, shipwrecked in life, an exile from hope, uncertain of safety. So much could a moment in battle accomplish, that a brief turn of fortune made men unlike themselves, when either the powerful were cast down or the afflicted raised up. Thus the better part of them, namely those who held honour, offered gentler counsels. Yet Titus played the greatest part in securing Josephus’s safety with his father. Vespasian ordered him to be kept under guard, lest he slip away.

A few days later Vespasian returned from there to Ptolemais and then hastened to Caesarea, the largest city of Judaea, but inhabited more by gentiles. They therefore welcomed the Roman army with applause and joy, not only because they desired the favour of Roman alliance, but also from an ingrained hatred of the Jewish people. With the loudest cries they shouted that Josephus, its leader, ought to be punished. Vespasian let this anger subside in silence, as the unreasoning anger of the crowd. Since both the season and the city were suitable for winter quarters, he stationed two legions in Caesarea, and the tenth and fifth legions in the city of Scythopolis, lest Caesarea be worn down by the burden of the whole army. The aforesaid city was therefore consecrated to Scythian Diana as a foundation of the Scythians, and was called the city of the Scythians, as Massilia was of the Greeks. The situation of the place shows that its founders, in their innate hardiness, chose open plains rather than ground suited to habitation. For open places bring more hardship than pleasure both in the harshness of winter and in the burning season of summer: in winter they lie more exposed to the cold, and summer’s heat is fiercer in places which receive the full sun without the delight of any green field. Thus the flat and coastal region of the aforesaid city was heated still further by the heat of the sea.

Yet Vespasian was not free from the business of war. He learnt that very many people had gathered from different places at the city of Joppa and had restored it as a convenient base for piratical raids, repairing the buildings which Cestius had destroyed. Since the countryside had been devastated, they sought their means of subsistence at sea. He carefully investigated everything. They fitted out vessels suitable for brigands’ use and watched the passage of travellers, plundering almost all the trade of Phoenicia and Egypt. Their frequent raids spread such terror that they closed that entire sea, and fear of certain danger interrupted navigation. On learning this, he ordered a force of infantry and many cavalry to set out and enter Joppa by night. This was easily done, since no guard protected the city: it was thought that the Roman commander would give no attention to a city reported to be destroyed. The inhabitants were there, but did not dare resist the arriving Romans or deny them entry. They boarded their vessels, went beyond arrow-shot and spent the night at sea.

The subject seems to require a brief account of the shore along Joppa, so that it may be clearly shown how the aforesaid city suffered a second disaster without any battle. The city has no natural harbour. Its seashore is rough and straight, but bends slightly into promontories at either end. There are deep-rooted cliffs and immense rocks projecting from the sea; although they rise from the sea’s depths, they also jut out into it. Hence the shapes of the places and the very appearance of the landscape seem to reveal that Andromeda was there when she was exposed to the sea monster, lending no small credibility to the ancient tales. When the opposing blasts of Boreas strike the shore, the waves rise to an immense height. Dashed against the rocks, they raise a mighty crash and, falling back into the waters, make that inlet so restless that there is more danger in harbour than in the open sea. While the boats which, as we said above, had put out from Joppa were tossing there, a violent wind, which those sailing in that region call Melamborium, swept down towards morning. At once, with the waves driving them, it threw the boats against one another and engulfed them. Some, their anchor cables broken, it drove against the rock. Others were heaved violently upwards against the oncoming sea as the sailors sought to escape the danger of the rocky shore or slaughter by the Romans, who had spread along it. A wave met them, towering above them in a lofty mass, overwhelmed them and sank them. There was nowhere to flee and no hope of remaining, since the wind drove them from the sea and the Romans shut them out of the city. The sound of the vessels colliding was grievous; the groaning of the men as they were crushed was unbearable. When they saw the sea breaking into their unsteady hulls, some, skilled in swimming, threw themselves overboard. Others, leaping towards boats drawing near, fell into the sea and were crushed by the collision of hulls. Many sank into the depths with their light vessels, having lost confidence in swimming clear. Yet death came with less torment to those who lacked the skill or any hope in trying. Those who attempted to swim were struck repeatedly by broken fragments of the ships, which crashed into their sides and hideously battered their wretched limbs. Or death overtook them as they were driven against the rocks, amid their very prayers to embrace the shore; yet they had what consolation they could in dying on land. The sight was therefore pitiable: the rocks were spattered with the brains dashed out of the unfortunate men, the shores wet with blood. You could have seen the sea stained with gore, everything filled with corpses. If any had escaped, they were killed as they approached the shore. For the Romans judged that the storm raged there not from the roughness of the place and the customary winds, but that divine indignation had stirred the sea, with the winds conspiring beyond their usual manner to prevent the Jews from escaping. They therefore feared to spare those whom God had not spared. Some killed themselves with the sword, thinking it more bearable to perish by the sword than by shipwreck. Others, trying to push boats away with poles, pierced them. Some drove back with oars or struck with a weapon those who had fallen into the sea, if they begged to be taken aboard by those in the boats. I have not passed over this, so that it may be clear that the Jewish people faced greater danger from themselves than from the enemy: they killed one another, as though all the things hostile to them together—sky, enemy, sea and rocks—were too little for their destruction. Four thousand five hundred dead bodies, which the sea had spat out, were therefore counted; the city was captured without battle and razed to its foundations.

Thus, within a short time, Roman hands destroyed Joppa for the second time. Vespasian thought this order just, lest pirate dwellings be established there again. Hence, although he was leaving, he left cavalry there with a smaller number of infantry. The infantry were to remain in the place, to prevent a band of brigands accustomed to brigandage from making any attempt; the cavalry were to range through the neighbouring countryside, villages and small towns, so that everything might be utterly destroyed and the inhabitants prevented from combining in any enterprise.

While these events took place at Joppa, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, distant though they were, were not even so free from sharing the disaster. They heard what the Romans had done in Judaea, and especially that Josephus had been killed. They did not believe it, first because no informant had come to them from those places, and secondly because they thought that so great a commander could not readily have fallen into the enemy’s hands. Indeed, no messenger had survived so great a disaster. This very fact, that no informant survived, confirmed the report of utter destruction: everything had perished, nothing remained even to tell what had happened. An impression spread that exceeded any report. As the very silence terrified them in their uncertainty, everything they feared was believed. Far from anything going unreported, even things that had not happened were added. For rumour had also insisted that Josephus had been killed, and this brought the greatest grief to everyone.

But when they learnt that he was living among the Romans, they pursued him with such hatred that they detested the life of the very man whose death they had first lamented, as a sign of either cowardice or treachery. Hence their agitation against the Romans grew greater, to avenge themselves on Josephus; and the more their fortunes declined, the more they were inflamed for war. Where there ought to have been an end, they took up a new beginning of evils. For the wise find in adverse outcomes a lesson in greater caution, so that the same things which have already gone badly may not happen again; but for the foolish they are an incentive to misery. Their allies’ danger ought therefore to have brought the people of Jerusalem to their senses, but because they refused to understand so that they might act well, it turned to their destruction.

Vespasian, however, yielded to Agrippa’s request to spend about twenty days in Caesarea Philippi, a city of his kingdom, so that the very delay might allow the Jews to take better counsel for themselves and the army to rest a little from its toil. At the same time the troubled parts of Agrippa’s territory might recover their senses from the frenzy of agitation and discord. Their inhabitants ought to understand that, if they changed their course, they could be received through the king’s intervention, when such diligent exchanges of services bound the king and the Romans together. Indeed, Tiberias, near Caesarea, did not reject the remedy and found health. For it too seethed with a grievous disease: its people were divided against one another. Vespasian therefore decided to summon three stronger legions and send them to Scythopolis, dispatching his son on the business. This was the greatest of the ten cities, near Tiberias. From there he ordered Valerian to approach the walls with fifty cavalry, to urge peace and call those shut within to faithful alliance. The terror of the assembled army was to strike the unwilling, while the messenger of peace invited the willing. Valerian dismounted near the walls, and those who had approached more closely with him did the same. Jesus, the leader of a band of brigands, and his companions, who dared to advance with him, thought them contemptible for their small number. In a sudden sortie they drove them from their position and seized the horses which Valerian had brought, as his men withdrew together. Fools, they did not see that Valerian showed better judgement in yielding to their insolence than they did in taking spoils from those who offered peace.

The elders, offended by the enormity of the deed, therefore left the city and came to beg Vespasian not to attribute the insolence of a few to the whole people. Vespasian immediately sent Trajan to the city to discover whether the people rejected the attackers’ rashness. By reporting that the people’s wishes agreed with the elders’ entreaties, he added credibility to the embassy. Thus pardon was granted to those who asked for it, especially since Vespasian saw the king’s concern for the condition of the whole city. On the king’s pledge that they would dare nothing of the kind thereafter, he willingly granted pardon for the offence.

From there he made for Taricheae with an alert and well-equipped army, since a very great multitude had gathered at that city because of the strength of its position. Josephus had enclosed it with a wall, except where, inaccessible on foot, it was washed by the waves of Lake Gennesar. They therefore gathered vessels and clamoured for war on two fronts: if the battle on land turned against them, they would flee to their ships; if they gave way in a naval contest, they would return to the city and defend themselves with its surrounding walls. The defences of Tiberias and Taricheae were similar, but the characters at Taricheae were more desperate. The wall of Tiberias was stronger, but the fury of the Taricheans readier, so that, if necessary, they would throw everything together, naval contests with those on land, those on land with naval. At last, surrounded by the opposing army, they dared more than their strength allowed. Their rashness made no headway against the order of the Roman deployment and the valour of the veteran army. Before they suffered any destruction, they turned in flight and rushed to their vessels. They packed these together and fought as though in a close battle line, as if the contest were being fought hand to hand on land. An innumerable multitude was also awaiting the enemy on the plain. On learning this, Vespasian sent his son with chosen cavalry.

When he saw himself surrounded by immense forces, he reported to his father that the enemy’s multitude was greater than had been supposed. But he called together those whom he had led out with him and fired them for battle with this address.

“Men of Rome,” he said, “as you go into battle, you ought to remember your name and race. No one in the Roman world has escaped your hands. For how did you give this name to all lands except by conquering? You must also remember the place where you now are and those against whom you Romans wage war. For we stand at the furthest part of the world. In crossing so great an expanse of lands, you have therefore seen nothing belonging to others. For what belongs to others when the whole world is in your possession? Whatever exists anywhere is yours by right; whatever all peoples inhabit is your possession. You were running well. Who has halted your triumphs as they ran throughout the world? Those triumphs which Hasdrubal the Carthaginian could not halt, nor Pyrrhus the Aeacid, nor Brennus pressing upon the approaches to the Capitol, nor the Persian hordes, nor the Egyptian phalanxes—rebellious Judaea has halted them, displaying an unskilled rashness in warfare, fitter for a brawl than a battle. Yet this is not what I fear. I consider it full of shame that you grow weary of conquering while those who are conquered so often have taken courage; that you are wearied by prosperity while they grow harder in adversity. Raise your spirits, then, men of Rome, and rise against the enemy hordes in confidence in your native valour. Do not let the numbers of the Jewish people disturb you, when they are not deterred by so many proofs of our valour, which are far stronger than numbers. For the Hebrews have neither knowledge of military affairs nor experience in fighting nor a gift for command, no practice of discipline, no patience to endure. They bring to battle only contempt for death; but no one has ever conquered an enemy by dying, only by killing. They know weapons only in war; we train with weapons in peace, so that in war we do not feel war’s uncertain chances. For the inexperienced, the outcome is doubtful; for veterans, triumph is customary. What else do we do every day but ensure that battles are never new to us? Each man trains at home as though in battle, so that in battle there is a kind of rehearsal of the contest. Indeed, no one would be mistaken in saying that our rehearsals are wars without blood, our wars rehearsals. We advance into war protected on every side: the head is covered by a helmet, the chest by a breastplate, and the whole body by a shield. The enemy can find nowhere to strike the Roman soldier, whom he sees enclosed in iron. Such arms are a burden to others, a covering for us, since practice makes them light. Thus our battle is against men unarmed and naked. Or do we fear being surrounded by their numbers? First, cavalry have freedom of movement in battle, making a game of war by retreating and pursuing; they ride round battle lines however great, and withdraw over whatever distances they please. Then, even in infantry combat, it is not so much the numbers of the many that decide the battle as the valour of the few. A multitude unused to discipline is its own hindrance: in prosperity, to victory; in adversity, to flight. But steadfast valour grows stronger in prosperity and does not collapse altogether in adversity. There is also this: our habit of victory is an incentive to fight. Even if they fight for their country and children, they ought not therefore to be readier than we are. For it is no less—indeed, I do not know whether it is not even more—to fight for ourselves than for our own people. We fight for ourselves when we fight for glory, so that we may not become less than we are. Who, then, could doubt that it is greater to fight for glory than for safety? But for us this war concerns the danger to our reputation, lest the right we have won be lost. We also risk appearing equal to the Jews, though we are conquerors of nations and rulers of the world: we set them up as opponents equal to ourselves if we engage them only with equal numbers. Our ancestors often routed great enemy forces with a small band. And what benefit do our daily exercises bring us, what our daily toil, if we come to battle with equal numbers? We have indeed reported their numbers to my father, because we were not permitted to do otherwise; but let him see that we have not feared the danger, but preserved our reverence for the arbiter of the war. We may taste the battle first, hold the enemy, seize victory while reinforcements are coming, lest those who arrive boast less that our common strength overcame the adversaries than that their valour protected us. With what face, then, shall we come before my father if we have feared to begin the battle? With what shame shall I, a degenerate son, meet the eyes of so great a man, who does not know what it is to see his soldier as anything but a victor? How shall I prove myself his son, when he is always triumphant but I am defeated even in my own judgement—which is worse—having yielded to a Jewish enemy? What will become of you when your commander is condemned, the man whom my father confidently entrusted to you? But I would rather you had to plead your case over your commander’s valour than over his cowardice. Let us therefore rush upon our adversaries, hasten, forestall the enemy. I shall run first into danger; follow, so that you may guard my father’s deposit and preserve what my father has entrusted to you. I ask for companions not in danger but in victory. Yet take care not to seem to have reserved for others the palm of triumph offered to you, and snatched it from yourselves. Certainly, if things turn out otherwise, I would rather my father recognised his son in my wounds, if he has not recognised him in his soldiers. But let us suppose that my father is offended by our beginning the battle. Which, then, is more bearable: to have seized victory too soon, or to have abandoned it? In seizing it too soon there is the haste of courage; in abandoning it, the fault of cowardice. Let my father condemn us as victors: I do not shrink from guilt of this kind. I would rather be guilty with the commonwealth triumphant than innocent with it injured. If only I might imitate the son of Manlius Torquatus, even in the danger alone, whom his father ordered to be struck with the axe because he had led the army against the enemy contrary to his father’s command! The young man stood with the enemy slain, clothed in triumphal glory, untroubled by death beneath the executioner, since he thought it the greatest happiness to die in victory. For what is more illustrious than to close one’s life with a triumph and not be kept for the uncertainty of events after a certain victory? O charge of victory, which the wise should seek! If only we too were accused of having conquered! Certainly, on that example, I alone shall be in danger; you will triumph. Yet my father has not forbidden us to fight, but commanded it by sending us into battle. Hence I think he will be angrier that we yielded to the Jews when we could conquer them than that we fought.”

With these words he was the first to drive his horse against the enemy, and the others followed with a great shout, spreading across the whole plain, which made them seem more numerous. Trajan too arrived with three hundred cavalry, sent by Vespasian when Titus was already advancing. The Jews could not resist much longer, thrown into confusion by the men’s lances and the horses’ snorting. They therefore turned in different directions, many making for the city. Titus sprang forward, overwhelmed some as they fled with their backs turned and cut down others as they strayed. By forestalling their route he drove them all away from the walls and, meeting those who ran back, cut off their flight. Nevertheless, while some were struck down, others escaped and found refuge in the city.

But there too the battle was fiercer. Those who had come from the neighbouring places at the beginning preferred peace, but the people who arrived later had forced them into support for the war against their will. Hence there was dissension and a grievous tumult within the city. Roused by the noise, Titus turned to his soldiers. “This, most faithful fellow soldiers,” he said, “is the moment I was seeking. The enemy stir up disturbances among themselves within the city: outside they are cut down, inside they fight with swords. Let us hasten while they are still divided, lest fear of danger bring them to reconciliation.”

He therefore mounted the horse from which he had dismounted near the walls and, turning towards the lake, made for the city through the waves. He was the first to burst into the city, and the others followed him. At once all those within scattered in flight. Some were struck down, others boarded vessels and sank into the lake; many people were killed inside. Those from the countryside, however, offered themselves to the Romans, declaring that they had no part in the guilt. Titus, with merciful restraint, thought they should be spared, pressing only those responsible for the rebellion.

He also sent a horseman to his father to announce the victory. Vespasian rejoiced at it, especially at his son’s triumph, for he had completed the greatest part of the whole war being waged against Judaea. He hastened there and ordered the city to be guarded more carefully so that no one could slip away, because all were liable to punishment. On another day, however, he ordered rafts to be made because of those who had taken to the boats. They were made without delay, since the neighbouring woods and the many workmen made it possible to hasten the task.

For the lake itself, with a very broad expanse like a sea’s circuit, stretches a hundred and forty stades in length and spreads forty in breadth. Its rippling waters raise a breeze for it from itself, whence it is called Gennesar, a Greek word signifying, as it were, that it generates a breeze for itself. Its water is fresh and fit for drinking, receiving none of the thickness or turbidity of marshy moisture, since it is surrounded on every side by a sandy shore. It is more temperate than the chill of a river or spring, yet colder than the surface of a still marsh, precisely because the water does not lie flat like a pond but is stirred more often by blowing breezes across the lake’s wider spaces. Hence a draught of it is purer and softer for drinking. If anyone wishes to add care to its natural excellence and prepare it for drinking by hanging it out in the air on summer nights, as the inhabitants do, he would think it scarcely different from snow. Its kinds of fish too are superior in taste and appearance to those of another lake. The subject seems to require that we explain the source of the Jordan, as we promised elsewhere. For when men of an earlier age were uncertain whether the Jordan arose from the lake named Gennesar, Philip, tetrarch of the region of Trachonitis, refuted the false opinion and dispelled the error by throwing straw into Phiala, which the river threw up at Panium. It is therefore clear that Panium is not the Jordan’s source but a place where it flows. Its spring is not there, as though it began there in the manner of other rivers: it is brought there from Phiala by underground passages. There it wells up again like a spring and is revealed as it emerges. Phiala is in the land of Trachonitis, a hundred and twenty stades from the city of Caesarea. Its appearance gave Phiala its name, as though expressing the shape of a wheel, for it is so constantly full of water that the water neither overflows nor is perceived to be drawn away by any decrease. The water therefore flows below in a certain measure and wells up again at Panium, as the reappearance of the straw made plain. Thus the Jordan was shown to have risen again where men of an earlier time had thought it was born. Yet Panium did not have the same splendour from the beginning, only its natural beauty. Through Agrippa’s royal munificence a richer and more splendid adornment was added to the place; by it, we are told, the cave through which the Jordan rises was built up and beautified with admirable decoration. From there it begins to spread, no longer by a hidden course concealed in the earth’s hollows, but in a visible and open stream over the land. It cuts through Lake Semechonitis and its marshes. Then, directing its course, it proceeds a hundred and twenty stades without any mingling as far as the city named Julias. Afterwards it passes through the middle of the lake called Gennesar. From there, after wandering through many deserts, it is received by Lake Asphaltites and buried in it. Thus, after emerging victorious from two lakes, it remains caught in the third.

The region of Gennesar stretches along the lake of the same name, from which it too took its name, with a marvellous natural grace and appearance of beauty. The fertility of the soil supplies spontaneous fruits; rich in groves, it raises itself of its own accord into every kind of fruit-bearing tree. The ingenuity of cultivation, imitating nature, has turned the gift of abundant fertility to whatever uses it wished, so that there is nothing there which nature has denied, nothing which cultivation has passed over. The air is suited to all fruits and never unfavourable to any, so temperate that it accommodates the diversity of everything that grows. There both what is nourished by cold and what is fostered by heat spread in abundance. There you may see summer growth mixed with winter growth, northern nuts together with dates which know no birth except in hotter places. Why speak of figs or olives, nourished by a milder stretch of sky? Yet they do not equal those mentioned before. For the former are the principal fruits of Palestine and, in a sense, native to it, and therefore more abundant; the latter are their near equals and, though separated by a long distance, nevertheless come next. You might call it a pleasing contest between nature and the seasons: nature, like a fruitful mother, creates everything; the temperateness of the seasons, like a good nurse, rears everything with gentle nurture. Thus not only are diverse fruits produced abundantly, but they are also preserved, so that some kinds do not fail for the greater part of the year, while all the rest last through the entire year to its end. For grapes and figs, which among cultivated fruits possess a certain royal grace, abound for ten months without any failure. The other fruits of the branches, whether the willing fields have produced them spontaneously or human industry has brought them into being, do not know how to abandon their service until new ones succeed them, following as it were the practice of attendants. To this fertility of nature and temperateness of the air is added the benefit of a spring, which irrigates the aforesaid region with a life-giving flow. Its name is Capharnaum. Some have thought, not without reason, that it is a vein of the river Nile, not only because its richness makes the fields fertile, but also because it produces a fish of such a kind that you would take it for the coracinus found in the lake at Alexandria through the Nile’s inflow. The district too, named after the lake, stretches thirty stades in length and twenty in breadth. Since we have spoken of the nature of the place, let us return to the conclusion of the battle.

When the rafts had been prepared according to his command, Vespasian put a force of soldiers aboard to pursue those who had escaped destruction by fleeing in vessels. They could find no course to take. There was no place of safety on land, with the enemy surrounding everything; no possibility of flight on the water, since the lake was enclosed and surrounded on every side by Romans; no confidence even in resisting in their small light vessels. For what could a few do against so many as the rafts drew near? The rafts’ approach was indeed slower and the vessels’ sorties more effective, but the Romans suffered no wound: only the rattle of shields was heard as the missiles bounced off them. The Jews did not dare approach, and no one brought a boat nearer with impunity, since at close quarters it was easy to be struck by missiles or sunk by the rafts. If anyone tried to swim clear or rise to the surface, he was pierced by an arrow and gave up his wretched life in the waves. They could not resist much longer, as their numbers were reduced in different ways. Little by little, as more rafts converged, the Romans drove the greatest number of vessels towards the shores. Hemmed in there, they either leapt ashore and were killed there by the Romans, or were cut down by those pressing them from the rafts, or were crushed by the collision of rafts, or threw themselves into the lake when the enemy leapt into their boats. You could have seen the waters mingled with blood, the lake full of corpses. No one encountered was spared. The smell was grievous, the stench of the place utterly foul. Six thousand seven hundred Jews were killed in that battle, including, however, those killed earlier.

Vespasian returned victorious to Taricheae. There he prepared to separate the people of the region from the townspeople, so that those who had not been responsible for the sedition might be spared. But many advised that allowing so great a multitude to survive, capable of renewing the fighting, was contrary to peace and harmful to the district. Where would they settle, driven from their homeland? On what food would they sustain themselves, deprived of everything, unless they lived by plunder? He changed his decision and, having inspired hope of being spared death, ordered them to leave by the gate facing Tiberias and make for that city. They readily believed what they desired. They began to leave, but the whole route had been occupied beforehand: the passing columns of Jews were hemmed in and led into the city’s stadium. Vespasian too entered and inspected the age and strength of all those whom he had ordered to be set before him. He selected six thousand of the stronger young men and sent them to Nero at the Isthmus. He ordered twelve hundred old and infirm men to be killed, and sold thirty thousand four hundred of the rest. All who were found to come from the territories of Agrippa’s kingdom he gave to the king, who likewise accepted payment and transferred them into the service of slavery. In addition, other people of the regions of Trachonitis and Gaulanitis, and the Hippeni and Gadarenes, paid just and deserved penalties for their crimes as instigators of war and disturbers of concord: they had abandoned their own lands and invaded those of others, taking up arms and violating the peace.

With Taricheae destroyed, the Romans held most of the cities and territories of Galilee, except that Gamala, a city in the region of Gaulanitis, sustained the spirit of a stubborn people, relying on its rugged position. For it stands on a mountain. Cut off on the right and left by sheer cliffs, it narrows towards the top; at the front it is severed by a deep chasm, while at the rear it spreads out somewhat. On that side too the approach is narrow and difficult, so that you would judge the road taken by those making for the city to resemble a tail. From its highest point it stretches out a neck to an immense distance, so that it presents its citadel like a head and raises it to a lofty height. Narrow at the beginning, with the ground, as it were, curving through winding slopes and sinking into the depths, it then raises a sort of tendon in the middle of its neck; the rest is steep and impassable. Hence many think that earlier generations called it Camela because it presents the form of a camel, but that the name Gamala became attached to the city through a corruption in the inhabitants’ usage. If you look at its closely joined buildings, you would judge it a city suspended in the air, and think especially that its northern parts hang down, while the southern parts bend back a little.

Josephus had added fortifications to this city too. Relying on these and on the numbers of people flocking there, they had made a mockery of King Agrippa’s siege for seven months. For it, Sotanis and Seleucia were all parts of his kingdom. Seleucia lay beside that most pleasant grove of Daphne, renowned throughout Syria, interwoven with cypress trees and abounding in springs. Through these it pours nourishment, as from milky breasts, into the local river flowing past, which they call the Lesser Jordan. This city and Sotanis, however, form the upper part of Gaulanitis, Gamalis the lower. Hence, with their inclinations differing, those cities had chosen alliance with Rome,

while this one was rebelling so stubbornly that, when the king wished to approach the walls and address them, he was wounded by a missile from a sling. Inflamed by the injury done to him, the Romans pressed the siege more fiercely, and battle was joined with the greatest eagerness on both sides. For the Jews too fought with all their strength: having injured their own king while he was offering useful advice, they reckoned that they would receive no pardon if defeated.

Agrippa, then, struck by a stone on his right elbow, withdrew from the fighting, and the Romans burst into the city. For the enemy yielded to missiles, the wall to rams. Those who had been obstructing the engines could no longer resist, and the wall, shaken by three rams, gave the besiegers an open route to the besieged. But impatience in their haste brought no slight disaster upon the victors. For when they poured into the houses, searching them or striving to seize the plunder first, the cramped dwellings gave way under the weight. Their foundations swayed and brought on a collapse, and each neighbouring building, crashing against the next, caused destruction. Many Romans, caught in these falls, met destruction in victory. Many, throwing themselves forward, were overwhelmed by fallen buildings; others were dragged out, their bodies mangled, scarcely half alive; dust killed many. Crowded into narrow spaces, they were cut down, while from above women, feeble old men and the younger men who had fled hurled stones upon those beneath them, or whatever kinds of missiles came to hand. Darkness had poured over everything, taken away sight and confounded the mind. In their ignorance they could find no way out.

Thus, barely extricating themselves from danger, they left the city. Meanwhile Vespasian, pressing the enemy, had advanced into the interior of the city and kept the battle raging amid the hostile ranks surrounding him. For it did not befit so great a man to turn his back to the enemy, nor did he consider it safe. He had sent his son Titus to Syria. He roused his confidence in his well-known valour and gathered himself under arms. With shields locked together, he stood undaunted with the few men he had at hand, as though considering whom he should hurl himself upon. Dreading his onslaught, the Jews began to press him less vigorously, and each, fearing for himself, loosened the battle line. Thus Vespasian, facing the enemy, gradually drew back, more like a man fighting than one retreating. There fell Butius, a decurion, a man proven in many earlier wars and of known experience against the Jews and robust courage. A centurion too, with ten other Syrians, performed an outstanding and memorable deed. In the midst of the tumult, seeing the Romans hard pressed, he withdrew into the hidden parts of a house. There, while the Jews were talking over supper about what they had contrived against the Romans, he killed them all in the dead of night and presented himself again to the Roman army with his soldiers.

When Vespasian saw that the army was dejected at the loss of so many men, and above all ashamed of having abandoned its commander, because they had left him alone inside the enemy’s city, he consoled them with the greatest goodwill, saying: “If the danger that fell to my lot causes you shame, I too had advanced to war to face dangers, not to avoid them. If, rather, it is because many of our men have been killed, there is nothing to wonder at: when is any victory won without bloodshed? Battles have their own outcomes. Although proven valour usually excels in war, something is commonly left to chance. But it belongs to the prudent man to correct a fall in adversity and to maintain moderation in prosperity. It belongs, on the contrary, to a rough and untrained mind always to presume upon success, as though the contest were not against men; it belongs to a weak man to lose confidence in the whole undertaking because of some fall, when all that happens in war may suddenly turn on the slightest impulses. Thus the best man is he who, sober amid adversity, wrestles with chance, trips up the stronger opponent and seeks to recover himself and correct his own falls. The less careful man, however, often falls through his own movements: rushing in heedlessly, he is thrown down by his own onslaught and lies prostrate. If this often happens where valour stands alone, how much more in war, where forces of different kinds meet in combat, with no single plan or shared judgement, where the ground is unfavourable and rugged, and the conditions of fighting in a confined space are unequal for many against few, since the very multitude is a burden to itself, while the few are less likely to miss among so many. But these things often steal upon us for a moment; they do not arise from valour, but happen by chance. There is therefore nothing that should distress you, fellow soldiers. It was not any weakness of your force, nor the courage of the Jews, that turned the course of events: the difficulty of the ground hindered our victory and gave them time to delay it. Nor is there anything to blame except an ill-considered and disorderly onslaught. For in following them to the higher parts of the city and rushing into their houses, you entangled yourselves in danger. You entered their dwellings; you took on their dangers. You held the city: who compelled you to go further inside? The enemy ought to have come down to you; you ought not to have striven recklessly for victory, forgetful of life and safety. Recover your spirits, then, and expect from your valour not merely consolation but, what is more, vengeance. You will certainly have me leading the way into battle. Be ready in spirit; may these dangers have made you stronger, not more timid. It is easy to redress an injury if valour recognises itself.”

With these words he kindled the soldiers’ courage. While they were repairing the rampart, many of the besieged slipped away from the siege by the steep places. For shortage of food was already assailing them, and they thought that the damaged stretches of wall would give way to the engines. Moreover, there was only one spring within the city, and that too was close to the walls. This put them in the greatest fear, so that very many slipped away. Those who thought they should remain, however, fought stubbornly.

Meanwhile the Romans undermined a very high tower and brought it down with tremendous force. Its fall shook the city; all were thrown into confusion, fearing the collapse of the whole city. Chares too, ill in body, was overcome by terror at so great a crash and met his death.

Yet the Romans refrained from entering the city when it lay open, until Titus returned and, stirred by distress at his father’s danger, burst into the city with a few men and inflicted very great slaughter upon the Jews. Those on the heights, however, rolled down stones and prevented the Romans from approaching; they hurled javelins and shot arrows. Stones pushed by the Jews rolled easily downhill, missiles reached their mark and arrows descended, not without danger to those they struck. For the Romans, hurling missiles towards the higher parts of the mountain was ineffectual, their effort fruitless and dangerous to themselves. Suddenly a storm of wind arose, turning back the Jews’ arrows and driving back their javelins, while carrying against the enemy whatever the Roman army hurled. Thus, overwhelmed by the barriers raised by the very elements and by whirling winds, all who were found there perished in the final destruction of the captured city. We have learnt, however, that four thousand were killed by the Romans and five thousand perished by falling from the heights; no age was spared.

Gischala alone among the districts of Galilee had not yet drawn the enemy against itself, since the quieter dispositions of its inhabitants, a rural people content with their own produce, had no taste for war. But through the gathering of many men who made brigandage their way of life, even the inclinations of the milder people were corrupted by wicked habits. There was also a man named John, son of Levi, a native-born plague upon his people, second to none of the cunning in deceit, knowing no equal in wickedness. His desire to do harm had never failed him, though for a time poverty had prevented him from practising iniquity—yet I do not clearly know how to decide whether poverty had concealed him or restrained him. He was cunning in deceit, an artist in deception, skilled at winning belief through lies and securing credulity through fabrications. He regarded deceit as a virtue and thought it a mark of refinement to cheat those dearest to him. He was ready to conspire, vehement in daring, keen in carrying things out; a troublemaker in times of quiet, a deserter in danger; accustomed to brigandage, inexperienced in war. Though he could not conduct wars, he nevertheless sowed them to prepare the way for his own rule. His mind, then, was restless, his audacity ready and nourished by successes, and he had wealth with which to gather a band of reprobates.

When Vespasian learnt that the people of the aforesaid city were being roused to war by John’s faction, he sent his son Titus with a thousand horsemen, so as not to weary the entire army. Accompanied by them, Titus approached the city. But when he saw the walls crowded with people, he said that he was amazed that they followed in rebellion the example of those whose destruction ought to have brought them to their senses. “Granted, however, that their first attempts offered some ground for confidence, what hope could the destruction of them all hold out? Their hopes of freedom may certainly have been pardonable at the beginning, but perseverance when all is lost and beyond hope is unforgivable. For against those who are moved neither by an example of humanity nor by earnest verbal admonition, words are not needed, but arms. You trust in walls, as though they had protected anyone against Roman valour. What else can men shut in display, men besieged put forward, except their boldness in captivity?”

No one had the freedom to speak; the band of brigands had occupied the entire circuit of the walls. John was taking care that no one should invite the Romans in through friendly conversation. He therefore forestalled any reply, saying that he willingly accepted discussion of their common affairs and did not refuse to try it: he himself might perhaps offer useful advice, or have to assent to what was proposed. But he was forbidden by ancestral law to discuss conditions of peace, since the day of the sacred week had not yet passed. Just as taking up arms was forbidden, so it was also unlawful to deliberate on peace on holy days. For to decide on business even in words was sacrilege for those compelled to do so, and would not go unpunished for those who compelled them. He asked the indulgence of a single day; so small a delay would be no hindrance. For, with the enemy surrounding them, those shut in had no free means of escape. Was he being offered a choice of peace? With so fair a choice, there was no fear. Meanwhile he ought not to be pressed into deliberations on peace, when he and his people held it a religious scruple to transgress their ancestral law. Moreover, it was fitting, with so generous an offer of peace, that the man who freely offered peace beyond expectation, so that no one should face danger, should also preserve their own laws for those who would escape it. Titus thought these arguments had been put forward without deceit, sounded the retreat and recalled from the walls those he had brought with him.

Thus John obtained the opportunity to flee and departed in the dead of night with many others. Women too followed him as he went. But the further the men advanced, the more women and little children were left behind. Abandoned by their own people, the frightened women watched the road. When their husbands were already passing out of sight, they thought the enemy was at hand and trembled at every sound. If anyone ran, the wretched women turned round, afraid that they were being attacked and chains were being put upon them, as though those they feared were already present.

In accordance with the agreement, Titus made for the city with his army once the sun had shed its light. The gates were opened; the people came out in exultation and welcomed the Romans with joy and eagerness, glad that the pestilent man had gone. He had fled during the night, they said, and they had been given the freedom to decide for themselves. They begged pardon, asking that the flight of a man whom they could not have held without their own destruction should not count against them. Consoling himself for the postponement of vengeance with the speed at which the business had been completed, Titus immediately sent many men to seize John, in case they might catch up with him. He himself entered the city and, content to have dealt with the disturbers of peace by threats rather than punishment, pardoned everyone. He did so lest anyone, stirred by hatred or private disputes, should bring odium upon innocent men and assail them with a charge of the gravest crime, since it is far more tolerable to leave an uncertain matter to the fear of a complicit conscience than to condemn an innocent man. For fear often corrects a guilty man, but there is no remedy for the punishment of an innocent man. Those whom Titus had sent did not find John, but they did find the little children and women who were following him. About two thousand were killed; three thousand of vulnerable age and sex were assigned to captivity once the appetite for killing had been sated. He gave the city a military garrison. Thus all Galilee was brought under Roman power.

For Mount Tabyrius too, whose height is thirty stades and whose level summit extends for thirty-three stades, had been abandoned by some for want of water and handed over to the Romans by others who asked for pardon. Yet through the valour and skill of Placidus, to whom Vespasian had entrusted the task, the whole crowd of newcomers, while following him as he yielded and pressing upon him as he artfully drew back, had been surrounded in the middle of the plain and had lost its refuge and found destruction.

Thus far we may be allowed our digression, as we have kept our pen occupied with other cities, shrinking from the defilements of the holy temple founded by our ancestors and of the sacred law. But now it is time to undertake the account of what happened at Jerusalem, not trusting in our ability, but lest we seem to have denied our ancestral law and ancient worship the service of our grief. Though there may have been in them shadow, not truth, yet shadow marks the traces of truth. For a shadow has the outlines of a picture, but lacks its brilliance; it has not received the finishing touch, yet to those who look closely it portrays what is to come. Thus the figure gives less delight; grace attracts more. Hence it pleased the arbiter of all things to abolish the old and establish the new, so that those who, through the narrowness of faithlessness, did not follow the images might follow the truth.

Fleeing from the regions of Galilee, as we said above, John made his way to the city of Jerusalem and, like a kind of plague, infected the minds of many who, foremost in outrage, had flowed there from various regions as into a cesspool. For this was a cause of greater destruction for that city: the service the reprobates rendered to their crimes—many gathering there where they believed they would either be safer or more unrestrained in heaping up their outrages—was thought to be service rendered to faith. They were therefore received everywhere as though they had come to defend the temple out of devoted love for it. This was the first blight of these evils.

Hence the gentleness of the few was overwhelmed by the insolence of the many. Hence they proceeded to killings, since an outsider was less inclined to spare anyone. Hence they conspired to neglect the observances of the law and transfer priesthoods from good men to wicked ones, because men who were strangers not only to devoted worship but to the very knowledge of the law did not know what was holy. First, men of royal stock who resisted were bound, so that the rest would yield through fear; then they were killed. To conceal the outrage, they falsely claimed that the men whom they had killed without trial by sending assassins into the prison had been put to death on a fabricated charge of treason. Fear therefore struck them all. Since powerful and innocent men—Antipas, Levias and Foras—had been so easily overwhelmed, they no longer dared to resist.

From this they went so far as to install obscure and unworthy men as chief priests. Men whom no claim of merit commended for the honour obtained priesthoods contrary to their deserts and were made subject, in every wicked deed, to the will of those who bestowed them.

But when the men of the priesthood opposed them, and above all Ananus, senior to the others, the rebels called for the chief priest to be chosen by lot, so that the prerogative of the highest title should not be bestowed through favour. In this way the outcome of the lot would be regarded as entrusted not to favour but to divine judgement. They did indeed invoke an ancient custom, by which those to be appointed to the chief priesthood were ordinarily summoned to the lot; in fact, however, they were plainly working to dissolve the law.

For the law selected for the lot men of priestly succession, but they, for appearances, brought forward a single one of the priestly tribes, named Eniachim, and ordered the choice to be made by lot. Then a certain Phanis, son of Samuel, a villager, was chosen by the lot. He not only lacked any succession traced through the chief priests, but had no knowledge at all of priestly office, since he occupied himself in the country and therefore did not know what a chief priest was. In short, he was dragged unwillingly from the fields and made to assume another’s role, as though on a stage. He was also clothed in the vestments consecrated by ancient custom and taught on the spot what he ought to do. Thus the outcome of the lot exposed the wickedness of the seditious men, when the exercise of so great a priesthood was handed down to an ignorant rustic. But the evasion of the ancient observance was a jest to them and a grief to the priests, who wept and groaned that the law was being mocked by reprobates.
Yet, relying on the authority of devotion itself and on the indignation of good men, they gathered together and rushed upon the disturbers.

But the others, distrusting both their cause and their numbers, fled to the temple as to a citadel and established it as a kind of camp from which to repel the crowd of people rushing upon them. At first they stood before the temple doors and in its very vestibule, fighting against the people. Anyone who had been wounded made for the interior of the temple, pouring his blood upon the inner threshold and wiping his bloodied face upon the pavements. Wounds and the flesh of open wounds were packed with garments they were not permitted to touch. There was war within the city, war among citizens, war before the temple. The brigands showed no reverence even for this: when the people pressed them more fiercely, they withdrew inside the temple itself and immediately closed the doors. This barrier checked Ananus, lest he seem to be bringing war upon the temple and breaking through the temple doors consecrated by ancestral religious observance. He turned back the people’s onslaught and stationed six thousand men in the porticoes, armed to stand guard and keep a vigilant watch. Gradually, however, he softened his resolve and sought peace, chiefly from his concern that the blood of citizens should not defile the temple. He urged that an embassy be sent to mediate peace, so that civil war might be laid aside.

John was enlisted to carry out the embassy, a man of doubtful faithfulness and inflamed with the desire to secure power. An oath was demanded; he did not refuse, lest by refusing he should lose the benefit of perjury. He pretended to favour the people in order to deceive them.

What more? He went, prefaced his words with a little about peace, and wove much more into them to kindle war. He said that war was wrapped in the name of peace, that there were hidden snares, and that Ananus had prepared to hand the city over to the Romans, so that ancient observance would be dissolved and the precepts of the law abolished. He fashioned everything into its opposite and turned against the chief priest the odium of the things he himself was planning. He also cunningly stirred up those whom he knew to be the leaders of the men shut inside and the chiefs of their faction, by fear of the death prepared for them. He asserted that Ananus had devised destruction especially for them; that he himself had come to reveal the deceit; and that they must seek help speedily, before punishment was exacted from them.

What more? The mediator of peace kindled war. Men were chosen to ask the Idumaeans to fight—a fickle, restless, insolent people, ready for discord, rejoicing in upheavals, heedless of danger, headlong in battle.
Thus they were won over and came without delay. Twenty thousand men assembled, intent on no cultivation of the land but ready for brigandage.
The arrival of the Idumaeans could not escape Ananus’s notice. He ordered the gates to be closed, so that they should not enter in tumult but, if possible, learn the truth and renounce war.

The chief priests therefore climbed the wall and addressed the Idumaeans from a tower. They were utterly amazed, they said, that, so swiftly ensnared by lies, the Idumaeans were pursuing by arms causes they had not yet understood. They ought to have been judges of disputes before becoming fighters in wars, and above all to have learnt the merits of the case before taking up arms—arms against men of their own stock, their own worship, their own observance. No greater injury had been inflicted upon anyone than upon the Idumaeans, who were being stirred to share in such grave outrages. For what else was being asked of them but the murder of their own kin—their fellow citizens—and sacrilege against the temple? Different aims and different characters did not ordinarily agree with one another. Similarity of character creates fellowship in purpose and binds kindred aims together. The most wicked men, who maintained their livelihood by brigandage, had presumed to summon the Idumaeans as allies, although the Idumaeans’ purpose differed so greatly from that of those who had called them: “Those men have brought war upon their own country, yet have entreated you to come as though to defend a city not your own. You, who are innocent, have nothing in common with plunderers; you, who are sober, have nothing in common with men who make themselves drunk. If only that drunkenness were of wine and not of fury! Once they have gorged themselves on outrages, squandering their own inheritances, they plunder the property of others; and what they have wickedly gained they squander still more wickedly and pour away still worse. There is no end to their plundering, because there is no limit to their gluttonous consumption. When they have drenched themselves in wine and filled themselves with drunkenness, they belch out a surfeit of public affairs, so that they may become drunk again on our blood and mock holy religion, which has always been an object of veneration and reverence to you. Flee, then, these gatherings for the murder of kin, abandon their sacrilegious ventures, forsake the assemblies of brigands. You have been called to a share in crime: let your coming bring a remedy to your country. We see a most distinguished people, who ought to have come at the request of a public council, to give aid against the enemy to the most eminent city of the Jews, held to be the mother-city of the whole nation. But even if we failed to ask, while hoping for peace and unwilling to weary you hastily—we were offering peace to the stirrers of war—nevertheless, as though you had come by divine judgement, deliberate for the common good and present yourselves as arbiters between both sides. Ask where the disturbance began; who sounded the war trumpet in a peaceful city; who shed the blood of its most eminent citizens; at whose instigation punishment was exacted from men not condemned; who brought destruction upon us before the Romans did. We were preparing war against the Romans, yet were already suffering these men as enemies. Whose favour with the Romans, then, is suspect: that of the men who avenge the Romans, or that of the men who repel them? These things are certainly more grievous to us than battles with the Romans. At their hands we would die for freedom; by these men we are butchered as though for a crime. Charges of treason are invented against the innocent, and the accusation is fabricated after death, although investigation ordinarily precedes punishment, not punishment investigation. For what does it profit a dead man to be acquitted, when he is no longer answerable to judgement? Yet we accept even a fate of this kind, that our innocence should be investigated after our killing; and we willingly plead before you too the case for our own integrity and that of the dead, although you stand armed on behalf of our adversaries. So utterly do our accusers lack arguments that their case is the worse even before you, who believed them so quickly. For a good judge grieves at having been deceived by lies and is therefore more hostile to the deceiver than to the man attacked, because he thinks he must take vengeance for having been rashly induced to believe falsehoods. Preserve, then, an impartial examination for us, and gather the truth from the course of events, not from the weaving of words. First of all, why should we betray our country to the Romans, whom we could have refrained from provoking? Perhaps that was what we ought to have done, so as not to rouse the conquerors of all nations. But deliberation on this is no longer part of our present task. It belonged to an earlier time to choose what course we should follow; now we must fall for freedom. For it is better to die for one’s country. It might have been more advantageous before the war to prefer peace to death; but since war is at our necks, many of our brothers have already been captured, others killed, and there is grief for the dead and groaning for those in chains, a free death must be chosen rather than a life of captivity. Yet it remains open to those about to die to wipe away the disgrace of the false charge of treason. Before you, Idumaeans, we plead our case: let those privy to it, the intermediaries who conveyed the messages, be exposed and brought forward. If they have informers, let them produce them; if they have none, why do they accuse us and charge us on empty suspicions they have themselves devised? They ought not to allege what they cannot prove. But because they do not dare to accuse us openly, they wish to spread it among the crowd, and therefore rush into war to avoid being called to judgement. For in war there is a chorus of fury; in peace, an examination of truth. See, we are here first; we offer ourselves willingly for punishment, if only an accuser comes forward. Or if odium is being turned upon the people, inquire more carefully what the purpose of the public assembly was. Was it not to prepare forces equipped for war, so that each man should help his country in the cause of freedom? Against the brigands themselves, what had been resolved except that peace should be agreed? The grief of individuals, the blood of the innocent, the groaning of women and the violation of ancestral statutes had sharpened public indignation. The groaning of all rang out, because each feared the same things for himself. Priesthoods were being bestowed upon the most unworthy men. They began to be attacked with cries; they struck down the people with stones and killed them with weapons. Public grief blazed up; they established refuges for brigands in the temple. Thus the place of peace, revered even by the nations, and the dwelling of holiness became an assembly-place of plunderers. Where people used to flock from every part of the earth to worship at the festal celebration, there are now dens of wild beasts wet with human blood. You may investigate these things even while armed, but without the law of war. Judgement has often taken place amid arms, and justice has laid aside the instruments of war; the verdict of equity has silenced the trumpets. You can turn to the defence of the city these arms which you took up for its overthrow. You may also enter unarmed, hear everything and inquire into it. If you find any slackness towards the enemy, deem it treason. But if you wish to act neither as our defenders nor as arbiters, why are you surprised that the gates are not opened to armed men? They are closed against arms, not against kinsmen. Lay aside war, and the gates will open.”

When the priests had spoken in this way, especially Jesus, who was senior to the others but came after Ananus and held second place, the Idumaeans were indignant that they had not immediately been received into the city. Simon, one of the Idumaean commanders, said: “It is no wonder that they rage against their fellow citizens and keep them shut in, when they have closed the gates against an allied nation and do not allow their fellows and partners to enter. They speak to us from the wall and repel us with walls as though we were adversaries, when they had us as friends. Who can doubt that they are preparing to receive the Romans and perhaps to crown the gates when they enter? What greater injury could there be? This city is accustomed to lie open to all men for religious observance; to us alone it is barred, as though we were enemies. We alone are disowned, we alone are repelled. They pretend to seek our judgement, though they did not think us worthy even of the city’s threshold. Let what they have done against those men remain hidden: we are witnesses and judges of our own injury. We see what those shut in suffer, when we ourselves are ordered to lay down our arms. Can it be believed that they await the judgement of men whose faithfulness they suspect? Let us hasten, then, to rescue those shut in, for whom the temple has become a prison, lest they be kept until the arrival of the Roman army and handed over as captives to Vespasian. Let us lift the siege from the temple and remove the foulest of guards, who allow no one to go out even to empty his bowels. If anyone wishes to bring food to those shut in, he is prevented; if anyone wishes to go out, he is dragged to death. Religious worship has been made a crime.”

On hearing this, Jesus withdrew, considering it vain to struggle against God’s adverse will, since hostile uproar resounded both within and without, and the city was being assailed from both sides. The Idumaeans raged at being excluded; those stationed in the temple contrived how to join them. Fear troubled the latter, lest the Idumaeans should leave before accomplishing their purpose, while shame deprived the others of the will to return. Distrust had already almost crept over them when suddenly, in the night, an unbearable gale arose, a black storm. The winds roared, the sky grew terrible, torrents of rain poured down; there were dreadful flashes of lightning, monstrous peals of thunder and a bellowing of the earth, so that the world seemed to be dissolving. Who would believe that this did more harm to those inside the city than to those outside, when the former were certainly sheltered by roofs and the latter exposed to the rain? But fear of harm terrified them more than the harm itself. Those who had no shelter of roofs covered themselves with shields, remaining at their duty and not dispersing. Those inside scattered, each about his own house, and gave those within the temple the opportunity to open the gates.

The people’s judgement, however, was uncertain and divided. Some thought that the supreme God, indignant at the Idumaeans because they had come armed against their fellows, had stirred up the storms. Ananus and the more penetrating minds among the elders conjectured that the harm suffered by the Idumaeans was rousing them still more to destroy their allies. Ananus, more watchful on other nights, that night was undone, not by bodily weariness but rather by despair of spirit. He yielded to events flowing against him and to the storms of the world fighting for his destruction. He did not think to inspect the guards again, as though he were authorising them to disperse wherever each pleased. Seizing this opportunity, those who had fled into the temple rose and cut through the bars of the gates. The crash of the sky helped them, so that the sound of the saws and the tumult of those going out were not heard.

Then they came to the wall and opened the gate near the assembled Idumaeans. That would have been the last day of the whole people, had the Idumaeans not thought they should make for the temple before entering the heart of the city. Those kept shut inside the temple feared for themselves: once the Idumaeans’ entry became known, the people surrounding them might rush upon them to exact vengeance before dying. They therefore asked to be saved from slaughter first; then, once they had been freed and their forces joined, they could pour out against the people. The Idumaeans turned aside to those who had sent envoys to beg for help in saving them, also so that the authors of their unexpected entry might be repaid with this benefit above all.

When this had succeeded as intended, they all poured out together from the temple as though from a camp, their battle line extended, and slaughtered throughout the streets whomever they found, some asleep, others terrified. Prayers availed nothing, tears nothing, marks of honour nothing; no services won favour. All were indiscriminately butchered. Seeing the bestial savagery of their pursuers, and that no one was spared, they hanged themselves: an end more pitiable, as it seems to me, than being killed by the enemy, because voluntary death is ascribed to savagery, and the hideous knot of the noose is reckoned a disgrace as well. But what room was there for counsel, where the fear of punishment was so great, when each man feared not death but the torments before death, for which death would be a remedy? Blood overflowed everywhere, and especially around the temple, because those guarding the men shut in had gathered there. That day eight thousand five hundred slain men were found.

Then they turned towards the city and killed whomever they met as though slaughtering a herd of cattle. It was a pitiable spectacle: war waged within a city formerly revered by all, destruction inflicted equally upon the poor and the weak. The young and stronger men, however, were thrust into prison, since they were thought suitable for the faction. But many, with great courage, preferred to undergo every punishment rather than join the reprobates. There was no limit and no shame, so fiercely did the frenzy of savagery rage. Afterwards, when they seemed to have spent their fury, as time passed they began to invent grounds for killing people by bringing the accused to trial, so that cruelty might be stirred up, not justice sought.

There was in the city a man named Zacharias, who hated the wicked and did not mingle with evildoers. He was rich in wealth, whose abundance they thought could either be effective in breaking up their faction or offer them rich plunder. They decided to summon him on a charge of treason. But he, with a conscience clear of any such thing, began to speak freely in his own defence, not only refuting the charges but also establishing that they themselves were guilty of the gravest outrages. The case was heard before seventy men. All acquitted him, because nothing connected with a crime was brought forward. But the others rushed upon him and hurled him into the depths. They drove out the judges, not only insulting them but also putting them in danger, so that their example would warn the rest against presuming in future to show firmness in judgement contrary to their will.

Again, however, so that no one should be acquitted, they themselves became the executors of their anger and killed whomever they pleased without trial. Gorgon, a pleasing and lovable man, was slain. So too was Niger the Peraean, who had been chosen among Judaea’s defenders to safeguard its highest interests. A warrior, who even bore the marks of his valour in the scars of his wounds, he was dragged to death. When he saw that he was being led outside the city, he began to beg, no longer for life, but for burial. Yet not even to this pitiable petition did he receive an answer consistent with mercy. False charges were fabricated: if anyone bought himself free, he was innocent; the man who offered no money was struck down as guilty.

While these things were happening at Jerusalem, Vespasian meanwhile was subduing other parts of the Jewish nation. News reached him of the strife at Jerusalem, the deaths they had inflicted upon themselves in domestic battles, and the punishments citizens had exacted from citizens. Many urged him to proceed there, lest anything be taken away from Rome’s triumph and his own glory. But he was a moderate and far-sighted man, who judged advantageous not what accorded with common practice, but what, on deeper consideration, he thought would benefit the whole undertaking. He began to reply to those giving this advice that the state was not always helped by battles, but often glory was won and the debt to the fatherland paid even by laying down arms. “What difference does it make how the enemy is defeated, by our sword or his own, except that by his own he is overthrown without odium attaching to Rome? For they cannot complain of us when they have wounded one another. At the same time they show how justly they have made war upon us, since they do not spare even themselves. This would seem vengeance from heaven, that those who have provoked the Romans should rage in madness. But if anyone asserts that something is being taken from our glory, let him recognise that a remedy achieved in silence always outweighs a battle fought with danger. Indeed, our Maximus broke Hannibal more by delaying than by fighting. Although the Scipios subdued Africa, victory in war is shared with many; to Maximus alone was it granted to restore the Roman state by delaying. It is therefore a greater thing to have preserved the Roman dominion than to have extended it. Yet let us reckon the merits of these valiant deeds equal. Surely, in war itself, the devices of wisdom are no less than the distinctions of courage. Let them therefore perish by their own arms: nothing is taken from our praise, and a very great deal is added to our victory. Those whom we spare do not know how to preserve their own people. What if, when we begin to threaten them, they perhaps come to their senses and are reconciled with one another? I do not fear this, but put it forward against your view. Or, if the strife persists, should it appear that they have defeated themselves, that the Roman army has done nothing, that our hands have been idle, and that victory has been won not by our valour but by the enemies’ mutual slaughter? The wiser course, then, is for them to rage to their own destruction in our absence, lest anyone think that they have been harassed more by our intrigues than by their own. We shall do better to approach when a victor remains to be added to our triumph. Certainly, let those who flee their own people come to us; let those whom the scourge of their own people has driven out find safety with us.”

Vespasian’s expectation did not deceive him. For those who could buy their release fled to the Romans. Every paved road and every path was filled with fugitives. The rich were let go; the poor, who lacked money for their ransom, were killed. Many also greatly feared ambushes and brigandage outside the city, especially the poor, who had no escort. Thus they faced equal danger outside and at home, deadly in either case; yet to many, in the hope of burial in their native land, death among their own people seemed more tolerable.

When fear, spread among all by the immense slaughter of the people, had made everyone subject to the faction, John, not content to exercise power in common with the leaders of the faction, began to aspire to tyranny and resented an equal.
