He therefore overturned the decrees of others, recognised nothing as valid except what pleased him, and gradually attached bodyguards to himself. Skilled in deceit, he ensnared by fraud those he wished, bound them to himself with money, and terrified them with power; by these arts he had joined very many to himself. Yet there were also men who rejected servitude, even at peril to themselves, especially since, accustomed to rule, they could not endure slavery. Thus three kinds of deadly calamity contended in one city: tyranny, war and strife, each of which could destroy not one city but many. Yet of the three, war was the lighter evil, and an enemy in regular warfare seemed more tolerable than a tyrant or a faction.

To these was added a fourth kind, that of the Sicarii. Seeing the city occupied by the upheavals of tyranny or the tumults of strife, they ravaged all the neighbouring places and carried everything away. They put to death women and children who, through the weakness of their sex or age, could not endure the hardship of the journey. Seven hundred in number were thus killed. Grain was conveyed into the strongholds. They rushed upon fields, cities and temples, carried off plunder, and let no opportunity for killing pass. In the guise of an army they practised brigandage, in greater numbers than the practice of brigandage required. They made war more bitter with the savagery of brigandage, allowing no pardon for surrender or mercy in receiving those who submitted.

Thus Vespasian, from whom destruction had been feared, was asked to come as a remedy. He hastened to Gadara, where there were very many wealthy men who, on account of their estates, were increasingly afraid of the brigands’ ambushes and raids. They had therefore secretly sent to Vespasian to ask him to approach them, so that the city might be rescued from the brigands. The Roman army arrived. On seeing it, the Gadarenes wished to flee to it, but could find no way to do so without destruction to themselves, lest the faction rise against them as they departed and destroy them all. Yet it did not escape the faction that Vespasian had been invited by an embassy of the Gadarenes and that Dolesus, a leading man of the city, was privy to that embassy. The faction seized and killed him; having avenged the affront, they left the city and withdrew to hidden and more strongly fortified places. Gadara was handed over to the Romans, and Vespasian was received with great applause. He at once sent Placidus to pursue those who had fled, and himself returned to Caesarea.

Placidus sent five hundred horsemen ahead and pursued the fugitives, forcing them into the nearest village. Finding there a picked body of young men, they took courage to rise against the Romans. This brought them very great disaster. For the cavalry surrounded them and cut them off from the village, and they were killed without any hindrance; while others withdrew in a mass, they were slaughtered before the thresholds of the gates. A mound heaped up from the bodies of the slain had reached the height of the walls.

The Romans pierced some with arrows and wounded others with various missiles; at last they stormed the stronghold, and all within were killed except those who had the opportunity to escape. Others, as they fled, magnified by their words the great fame of Roman valour: the bodies they had seen were larger than human bodies, and no one had any confidence of resisting the unconquered. Hence all were terrified and fled at once. Not only neighbouring and adjoining places were abandoned, but even the city of Jericho, which, because of the throngs of its inhabitants, had sustained the hopes of the rest. With events going as he wished, Placidus pursued these too with his horsemen, striking down some in masses and others as they strayed, as far as the river Jordan. At the riverbank too he found a very great number whose passage was blocked, because the aforesaid river happened then to have swollen with rain or melting snow. When they saw the Romans at hand, they made ready and crowded along the edge of the river. With the refuge of flight cut off, necessity put the remedy into their hands, and the many charged and hurled themselves upon the fewer horsemen. These, with familiar skill and in the old manner of soldiering, began to ride between them, break up the enemy’s wedge, disperse their masses, press the weary and pursue those who yielded. Thus some were killed by the enemy’s weapons, others by their own, upon which they fell as they were crowded together and dashed against one another. Others rushed into the river, where their very fall and their entanglement with one another submerged them. Many also entrusted themselves to the river, thinking they could cross it; when they had advanced a little, the force of the eddies swallowed them or the rush of the river swept them away. Even those who, practised in swimming, had made progress over the water and kept themselves afloat above the current flowing beneath, lost their lives in the river, caught in the branches of trees carried down by it or crushed by the trunks themselves. Often too a man unskilled in swimming, on grasping a swimmer, held fast so that he too might escape, and wore him out, locked in his arms, until both sank, each bringing destruction upon the other. And if someone, carried down by a favourable current, seemed likely to escape, he was sewn through with arrows and suddenly perished face upwards, the oars of his arms ceasing to move. There were also men who, unable to swim and seeking a painless death, flung themselves willingly from a raised bank into the river; others entered from a sandy shore, their feet sank, and they were drawn down. Many too slipped on rounded stones or stumbled in the shallows, swayed with unsteady footing and were overwhelmed by the currents following them. Thirteen thousand were killed by the sword, while an innumerable multitude was consumed by the river. Immense plunder was gained from flocks of sheep and herds of camels, asses and cattle.

Although this slaughter of men was very great, it was nevertheless reckoned greater than it really was. For not only was the whole region filled with human bodies, since the scattered and straying were killed wherever they were caught, but the Jordan itself was so obstructed by the bodies of the dead that it could not maintain its own course. Lake Asphaltites too, into which everything the Jordan had drawn along was carried, changed its natural appearance through the blood and entrails of the dead. Indeed, it was reckoned that ninety-two thousand two hundred Jews had perished that day at the hands of only five hundred horsemen and three thousand foot soldiers. Advancing further, Placidus also restored Abila, Julias, Bethesmon and all the villages of that district as far as Lake Asphaltites to the Roman dominion. He also put soldiers into boats to kill all who had fled into the aforesaid lake.

Thus these places too, and everything as far as Machaerus, were recovered. Vespasian, however, was awaiting the time for battle, when he would attack the chief city of all Judaea with the Roman army. Meanwhile, as he was occupied with the affairs entrusted to him, news reached him of fresh disturbances in the regions of Gaul: certain powerful men of the Roman army had deserted Nero. On learning this, he wished to bring the turmoil of wars in the East to an end and bring relief from the civil wars and the danger to the whole state and the entire Roman dominion, so as either to suppress or forestall all disturbances in Italy with news of successes. As soon as the rigours of winter had been tempered by the beginning of spring, he set out from Caesarea with the greater part of the army. The city called Antipatris received him. Advancing from there, he burned villages and killed those he found hostile; above all, he ravaged whatever places he encountered near the Idumaeans, because they were a restless race of men, friendly to wars rather than leisure or quiet. He also seized two villages of Idumaea, Legaris and Caphartor, and shattered their inhabitants by immense slaughter. More than ten thousand men were killed; he carried off a thousand captives and drove out the rest of the populace, to station a force of his own men there, since the mountainous places of that region were infested with brigandage. He himself returned with the army to Amathus, which took its name from hot waters, since the vapour of water is said to be called amathus in the language of Syria. It is therefore called Thermae in Greek, because it has a hot spring within its walls. Then, through Samaria near Neapolis, he hastened to Jericho. There Trajan met him, leading a large force drawn from those peoples of the region of Peraea beyond the Jordan who, defeated, had returned to Roman rule.

At the news of the Roman army’s approach, many had left the city of Jericho for the mountains of the region of Jerusalem, since they saw that it was unsafe. The whole multitude of those who remained was destroyed. For it was not difficult to capture the city quickly: it was supported by no natural defence and had been deserted and abandoned by its own people as they slipped away. The city is built on a plain, above which rises a broad mountain bare of vegetation. For it extends northwards as far as the territory of the city of Scythopolis, while to the south it stretches as far as the region of Sodom and the boundaries of Asphaltites. The soil is poor and barren, and therefore deserted by inhabitants, since its natural sterility makes it of no use to cultivators. Opposite it is a mountain beyond the Jordan, which begins to rise from Julias and the northern quarter. It extends southwards as far as Sobaros in Arabia, bordering on Petra, where there is also a mountain called Iron by ancient usage. Between these two mountains lies a plain which the inhabitants, by ancient usage, have called Great because of its size, since it extends over a vast space. Its length is two hundred and thirty stades, its breadth a hundred and twenty; it begins at the village of Genuabari and ends at Lake Asphaltites. The Jordan cuts through the middle of this plain, not merely leaving its beauty unimpaired but adding to it: the banks grow green through the river’s flooding, and the lakes Asphaltites and Tiberias follow in succession, sharing one source but differing in character. For the water of the one tastes salt and is barren in its use, while that of Tiberias is sweet and life-giving. In the days of summer, however, excessive heat burns over the expanse of the plain. Hence, as the blight of excessive drought combines with the dryness of the ground, the air grows more corrupt and causes pitiable illnesses among the inhabitants. For everything is dry except the edge of the river. Indeed, in the more distant places even the fruit of trees grows sickly, since the yield of palms growing on the banks of the river Jordan is both more abundant and richer, while elsewhere it is far poorer.

There is also beside the city of Jericho an abundant spring, rich in water for drinking and nourishing for irrigation, which Joshua son of Nun, a Hebrew by nation and mighty in hand, first wrested from the nation of the Canaanites. At first it was considered corrupt, barren in generation and of little wholesome use to those who drank it. Hence the prophet Elisha, Elijah’s disciple and a successor by no means unworthy of so great a master, was asked by the inhabitants of the places he had visited to leave them a reward for their hospitality and relieve the corruption of the waters. He gave a remedy, as the ancient Scripture of Kings teaches, ordering an earthen vessel with salt to be brought to him. Taking it, he threw the salt into the spring and said: “I have healed these waters, and no one will die in them or be made barren by them.” “And the waters were healed,” it says, “according to the word of the prophet Elisha.” From that time, then, the waters were tempered by the infusion of blessed salt, the mouth of the spring was opened, and the courses of its waters were sanctified, so that the gushing of its veins poured forth sweeter draughts and all that bitterness of the waters grew sweet. The earth gave richer fruits, and a fruitful succession of children born supplied an abundance of posterity. Nor did the life-giving water fail, upon which divine grace had breathed through the blessings of so great a prophet, in response to the faithful zeal of the righteous. Thus, at the prophet’s prayers, the answering voice of the heavenly oracle changed the nature of the waters and at once drove out sterility and poured in fertility. Generations of men and the fruits of the earth began to multiply there. The water, formerly barren and bitter, accustomed to kill the crops and twist the mouths of drinkers with its harshness, began to pour fertility into the soil and sweetness into those who drank, so that, if it touched cultivated ground there only briefly, it did more good than where it had watered for longer. For this is a new grace: the increase is more abundant where the use is less, and where anyone has used more, the yield is less. It therefore irrigates more than other springs, because even a little of it is more than enough for fertility. Indeed, a plain surrounds it, extending seventy stades in length and twenty in breadth. In it you may see the wonderful grace of gardens, various kinds of palms, and dates of such sweetness that you may watch honey flowing from them, by no means inferior to other honey. There are also excellent broods of bees there; nor is this surprising, where gardens breathe upon such varied flowers and pour forth sweet scents. Opobalsam is produced there. We use the name with this addition because farmers cut through the bark of the twigs in which balsam is produced, so that the liquid dripping gradually through those openings may collect. An opening is called opē in Greek. They report that henna grows there, and myrobalan, and other things of this kind that are nowhere found in other places. The water is like other spring water. Yet here it is superior: cold in summer, warm in winter; the air is milder, so that in the depth of winter the inhabitants wear linen clothing.

Let us now consider the character of Lake Asphaltites. For it is better to occupy the pen with descriptions of ancient places or the marvel of the other elements than with the strife of the Jews, since the latter exasperates the mind by its wickedness, while the former soothe the spirit as they are recounted and recall it to knowledge of ancient history. But we, whose talent is uncultivated, are eager to retrace the footsteps of the fathers as they went out of Egypt as far as the land of resurrection, so that, if our writings should happen to come into anyone’s hands, he may read not our words but reread those of the fathers. For it is sweeter to dwell among the habitations of our ancestors, recall to memory the words and deeds of the ancients, and cling to their grace. But now let us describe the nature or character of the waters, lest our pen too be cast out of that lake, from which, it is believed, all living things you might think could be submerged nevertheless rebound and, however violently dashed into it, are at once cast out. The water itself is bitter and barren, admitting no kind of living creature. Indeed, it tolerates neither fish nor birds accustomed to water and delighting in diving. They say that a lighted lamp floats upon it and, without being overturned, sinks when its light is extinguished, and that whatever is alive, submerged by any contrivance, can scarcely remain in the depths. Indeed, they say that Vespasian ordered men who could not swim to be thrown into the depths with their hands bound, and that all at once floated, as though lifted by a breath of wind, and sprang back, driven upwards with great force. Many have thought much of what is told of this lake fabulous; as we have not tested these things, we have had no intention of declaring the truth of the matter. Nor have we chosen to set down as true that the water changes colour three times a day and gleams variously in the sun’s rays, since the water of the lake itself is darker than other waters and has the appearance of being scorched. Certainly, if it too shines in a ray of sunlight, there is nothing new or to be put forward as a marvel, since this is common to all waters. It is certain that lumps of bitumen, a black liquid, drift over the water; those whose task this is approach in boats and collect them. Bitumen is said to cling together so firmly that it cannot be cut by iron or any other sharply pointed metal implement. Yet it yields to women’s blood, by the discharge of which during menstruation they are said to gain relief. It is reported to be broken apart by contact with this blood or with urine, as those who have had experience of testing it assert. It is said to be useful for joining ships’ timbers and wholesome for human bodies when mixed with medicines. The lake’s length extends five hundred and eighty stades as far as Zoaros in Arabia, its breadth a hundred and fifty stades as far as the neighbourhood of the people of Sodom, who once inhabited a very fertile region, abounding in fruits and distinguished by splendid cities. Now, however, those places are deserted and burnt out by fire. For although God had bestowed everything upon them as his gift—fields bearing abundant crops and countryside planted with vines and other fruit-bearing trees—they were ungrateful and did not keep before their eyes the power of God most high, as though he did not discern all things and behold every outrage, and as though anything could be hidden from him or escape his notice. Thus they began to confound and pollute everything with the shameful acts of their intemperance, by which they drew upon themselves divine displeasure. As the price of their crimes, fire descended from heaven to burn that region. Five cities were thus consumed, a certain shadow and semblance of which is visible in the ashes. The lands burned; the waters burn, and in them the remnants of heavenly fire are recognised. There still remain fruit green to the eye and a formed cluster of grapes, such as to arouse in onlookers the desire to eat. If you pluck them, they crumble and dissolve into ash and give off smoke as though still burning. These things learnt about the territory of Sodom ought not to have been veiled in silence, because of the punishments of the impious. For after surveying them, there can be no doubt that there will be a reward for the pious.

Vespasian therefore filled all the strongholds or city fortifications nearest Jerusalem with detachments of the Roman army or allied forces, so that they might recognise as hostile to them all the places which they had previously thought would join them in making war against the Romans. He also sent Lucius Annius to Gerasa and captured the city by stratagem. He killed a thousand young men too, who, taken by surprise, had been deprived of escape. Very many captives were carried off, and everyone’s property was seized by the soldiers at their commander’s order. The estates they found were burned, and they exercised their licence to plunder. They ravaged everything in the mountains and on the plains, and the city of Jerusalem, surrounded by these places, blazed with war on every side. Nor were the people of Jerusalem free from awareness of their dangers: all exits had been blocked against them, so that no one might escape danger by flight. Within was the domestic evil; outside, everything was closed. There was neither the wish to remain nor the means to flee. Even anyone who had hoped for pardon from the Romans by deserting was prevented by his own people from leaving.

Vespasian had returned to the city of Caesarea, so that, having gathered all his forces there, he might undertake the siege of Jerusalem. News arrived that Nero had been killed after completing the thirteenth year of his reign, when he was already passing the eighth day of the following year. He deserved that punishment, for he had violated not only faith by sacrilege, family devotion by the murder of kin, and chastity by incest, but also the very power of the Roman dominion, whose offices and affairs he had entrusted to the most wicked of freedmen. For since he himself kept faith with no one, he suspected everyone, and therefore thought he should entrust himself above all to the utterly wicked Nymphidius and Gemellinus, whose lowly condition had made them dependent. But even they eventually shuddered at the example of his cruelty; and because he had killed all those dearest to him, they thought they must take precautions for themselves and wished to forestall what they feared. Thus, conspiring with the others, they deserted the murderer of his kin. For whom was he thought likely to spare, when he had not spared his mother? Abandoned therefore by all his people, he fled the city with four of his freedmen. Seeing himself hard pressed by the conspirators drawing near and by a hostile force, he secretly withdrew to an estate outside the city, torn and lacerated by thorns while he feared being seen by anyone, lest he be betrayed. Then, realising that he was surrounded, he prepared a contrivance of wood and put it together with his own hands to kill himself, so that severe punishments might not be exacted from him. Turning to his freedmen, he said: “What an artist is dying!” Thus the most cruel murderer of his kin met an end to his life worthy of his deserts: he who had killed his mother and his own people did not spare even himself. Truly he was a fine artist of his own death, who devised a way of perishing such that not even his death was free from crime.

Thus the report that Nero had been killed had arrived first, in keeping with the human disposition, which is content, on hearing what it desires, to inquire no further, but at once to spread abroad and send out among the people, still incomplete, what has pleased it. Not long afterwards, however, it became known that Galba was at the head of the Roman dominion. Vespasian therefore decided to ascertain the new emperor’s judgement on the Jewish war, and sent his son Titus and King Agrippa. Titus returned from Achaea on learning that Galba too, on the seventh day of the seventh month after taking power, had been stripped of his insignia and suffered punishment in the very heart of the city, that is, the Roman Forum, and that Otho enjoyed success and the imperial succession. Agrippa hastened to Rome to establish his favour with the new emperor. To Titus, the reverence owed to his father in family devotion seemed of greater worth than that owed to imperial power, since he thought that, if he went on without consulting his father, he would not please even the emperor himself. Certainly the outcome showed that he had returned to his father at an opportune time, amid new events whose direction was uncertain. Indeed, Vespasian too, anxious about the condition of the whole Roman dominion and his fatherland, suspended the war and restrained his own onslaught, setting what was happening in Judaea below his care for the whole state and his devoted concern for his fatherland.

But Judaea was not at rest: it was waging a more grievous war among its own people than against outsiders. For while John’s faction was intolerable, Simon also rose up. He was inferior in wickedness of character, but relied more on his bodily frame to dare every impious deed, and was accustomed through brigandage to practising and attempting outrages. He was a citizen of Gerasa, vigorous in youth, whom Ananus, the chief priest, had brought low for his wicked schemes and driven from the place where he lived, compelling him to withdraw to other regions. But he, who had no place among the quiet and moderate, joined the company of brigands. At first they too suspected him, lest he ensnare them by intrigue; afterwards he easily insinuated himself among them through their common character. With them he ravaged the places adjoining their strongholds, because they did not dare to seek more distant places. Hiding as though in burrows, they lay in wait for passers-by without making any expedition, content, as it were, with brigandage at home. Simon, unrestrained in spirit, could not endure this for long, and soon gathered a large force for himself, promising freedom to slaves, rewards to the free, and recompense to the reprobate.

As very many flocked to him for licence to plunder, he dared to storm strongholds and seize the peoples of cities, and was a terror to all. He prepared walls as a refuge for himself in the village called Aiacis.

He was already advancing surrounded by twenty thousand armed men when the people of Jerusalem suddenly grew afraid of his daily progress. Thinking that, if it continued to grow for longer, it would turn against them, they decided it must be cut short, and in a sudden armed sortie attacked Simon. He did not lie open to their ambush heedless and unprepared, but met them as they approached, routed many, and compelled others, driven from the battle, to withdraw into the city.

He also fought the Idumaeans and withdrew on equal terms, yet was distressed as though defeated because he had not won. When they were to fight again, he thought it more advantageous to try deceit and found a willing servant of fraud. For when it was understood what he sought, Jacob, one of the leaders of the Idumaeans, cunning and crafty in such affairs, came secretly to Simon and offered to betray his fatherland, giving assurance that he would ensnare all the Idumaeans. Having demanded, as the reward of their future association, that he should be the most powerful and trusted man with him, he promised to betray them all. Their friendship was sealed by a banquet, and Simon’s immense promises confirmed the agreement between them. On returning to his own people, Jacob began by telling a few that he had gone out to reconnoitre the enemy’s strength and had seen a powerful force, men experienced in war, a very great multitude invincible in battle. Gradually he introduced such talk among the leaders, and finally spread it among them all: Simon himself was exceedingly energetic; he had organised his army in the manner of a king, maintained its ranks, distributed its units and appointed capable commanders. The Idumaeans ought to look to their own interests, so as to experience such a man as a friend rather than an enemy. Certainly, if they saw him superior in an encounter, they should yield without danger and avoid battle. When Jacob learnt that the inclinations of very many had bent to his view, he instructed Simon to take the field. Confident that the Idumaeans would scatter, Simon did not delay. Jacob, as though leading the advance with his own men and readier for battle, turned his horse and took to flight once the light-armed troops had tested the fighting, before they came to close quarters. His men did the same. Thus he turned and scattered all the battle lines and handed victory to Simon without a contest of war.

Having gained a triumph over so great a nation, he became more insolent towards the rest. He captured sooner than expected Hebron, an ancient city, thronged with people and rich in wealth, found much plunder in it and carried off its abundant produce. For it is said to be the most ancient city, not only among the cities of Palestine but also among all those founded by the ancients in Egypt, so that many think even Memphis, which is considered the most ancient, later than it. There were also those who said that father Abraham had lived in it after setting out from Mesopotamia and making for Egypt, and that his sons had a tomb there, most beautifully built of marble and of exquisite workmanship. Seven stades from the city, a great terebinth tree is asserted to have stood there since the foundation of the world; whether it still remains now, however, is unknown to us. Advancing from there, he ravaged territories, stormed cities and gathered peoples. Surrounded by forty thousand armed men, he emptied everything wherever he went, even as though a friend and ally. For what place could supply food for so many? By the mere tread of the foot soldiers, every place in which he stationed such numbers of fighting men was trampled like pavement. Not only was every crop carried away, as though eaten by locusts, but the ground, beaten into pavement, refused to bear fruit even in the future.

The growth of Simon’s power terrified John, and all the associates of his faction were shaken. They wanted Simon destroyed but did not dare to provoke him to war. Again they prepared an ambush and, lying in wait along the roads, seized his wife with her entire female retinue and a few men escorting her. They boasted as though they had achieved a complete victory and, as though holding Simon himself captive, thought that he would supplicate them. But he was harsh and merciless, could be reached by affection for no one, and held nothing dear or sacred. He was inflamed as though by an affront received rather than a love taken away, and tortured those he found with far greater savagery and grievous torments. He cut off the hands of very many and sent them, their bodies mutilated, to the enemy, to announce his cruelty and make known his threat to overthrow the walls and destroy the city unless his own wife was restored to him at once. He would likewise mutilate the hands and entrails of all who dwelt within the city unless they took thought in time. Thus, terrified, they sent his wife to him. His fury was thereby softened, and he gave those shut in some opportunity for rest, ceasing to press the siege.

Not only had Galba been killed, but Otho too had perished in conflict with the commanders of Vitellius, whom the army in Gaul had made emperor. In the first encounter Otho appeared the stronger. When battle was renewed a day later, Otho learnt that victory had fallen to Valens and Caecina, the companions of Vitellius, and that very many of his own men had been killed. At Brixia he rescued himself from humiliation by a voluntary death, after holding power for only three months and two days. Victorious, then, Vitellius hastened to Rome with the army that had survived on both sides.

At that time Vespasian set out from the city of Caesarea. He ravaged Judaea and subdued all the neighbouring mountains and strongholds. He killed those who resisted, granted those who begged for mercy a pardon that spared their lives, drove his adversaries to flight and stationed his own men in their places. Cerealis too, a commander of the Roman army, ranged everywhere with the cavalry, destroying some, subduing others and driving along columns of captives. Everything around Jerusalem was burned, so that the Jews might have no refuge. Thus every way out had been blocked against the Jews before the siege.

But they not only failed to look to their own interests; they also fought out a domestic contest among themselves. John was the tyrant within, Simon the enemy outside the walls. After receiving his wife back, Simon went on a brief expedition, ravaged Idumaea, and returned stronger, making his arms resound around the walls of Jerusalem. John, stationed within, trained his men for war through vice, giving them licence for crimes. Zeal for plunder, desires for shameful acts, outpourings of luxury and the scents of ointments seethed. They curled their hair with curling irons, painted their eyes with antimony and put on women’s clothing. They sought not only women’s adornment but also feminine softness and the passions of unlawful lusts. Men practised women’s ways, made their voices effeminate and undid their sex by the languor of their bodies; they grew their hair, whitened their faces, smoothed their cheeks with pumice, plucked their beards, and in this dissolution practised an intolerable savagery of cruelty. Indeed, they walked with a mincing gait, yet in a moment became warriors: suddenly drawing the swords they kept concealed beneath their purple cloaks, they slashed apart whoever they found. Whoever had escaped Simon was killed by John if he withdrew within the city; whoever had fled John was captured by Simon and sacrificed before the walls.

The dissension was grievous. The Idumaeans sought to extinguish John’s tyranny: they envied his power and hated his cruelty. They fought against the attendants of the tyranny, drove them back and pursued them as far as the royal palace, which a close female relative of the king of Adiabene had founded. They rushed in, drove out its defenders, occupied the temple and plundered the spoils of the tyranny, since John had established a storehouse for his wealth there. A grave fear arose that the Idumaeans would enter the city from the temple by night, kill the populace with the sword and destroy the city by fire. Terrified by this fear, after deliberation they brought in another tyrant, since they could not endure the one. John had crept into tyranny by fraud; this man, invited as though he would provide a remedy for their safety, brought domination upon the citizens and a tyrant upon the city. Matthias, the chief priest, was sent to beg him to enter. With great arrogance he consented to rule, and, as though it were a burden, yielded to their entreaties and poured into the city with his whole force. They opened the gates with their own hands to admit a more destructive man, while cursing the one within. Thus Simon, having entered as he wished, showed himself equally an enemy to all. With a common hatred of everyone he persecuted both those who had called him in and those against whom his help had been sought. John was hard pressed by his own deceits; the city tossed upon the waves. The contest between John and Simon was who could do more harm to his own people.

Reports of civil wars gained strength in the Roman army. The deaths of Galba and Otho became known, and the rule of Vitellius, who, more wicked than his predecessors, had settled like dregs. Veteran soldiers began to confer among themselves and resent the presumption of the praetorian legions at Rome: although they had long ceased to experience the dangers of war and did not know the names of the nations that made war, they nevertheless appointed an emperor for wars and claimed that the choice of the arbiter of Roman affairs lay in their hands. Then, following this example, the soldiers stationed in Gaul had aspired to give Vitellius imperial power without consulting the senate and Roman people. They themselves meanwhile were treated as mercenaries, following the decisions of others, first in danger and last in honour. For so long they had waged war, with their triumphs increasing daily, yet received masters from their inferiors—not even useful ones, but men utterly idle or devoted to their bellies and to disgrace. They must confront and remove this injury. They had an energetic man in Vespasian, whom everyone ought to have chosen as emperor, mature in years for counsel and stronger than younger men in battle. They must hasten before he was chosen by others and became an object of disregard to those with whom he had grown old in military service and triumphs. When was there a more opportune time to repay his labours with a worthy reward? Vitellius’s voracity was a disgrace to private citizens, to say nothing of emperors. Neither the senate nor the Roman people would endure for long that this disgrace of drunkards should remain at the summit of imperial power, a man for whose expenditure the Roman state could not suffice. “For who could endure a tyrant’s rule when he has in the army a worthy governor of the Roman dominion? What nations would subject themselves to luxury and surrender to vice, when an emperor’s idleness is an incentive to war, whereas the firmness of peace rests on valour in an enemy and sobriety in the ruler of the state? Who would not admire in Vespasian, still a private citizen, the splendour of kingship and the authority of the Roman dominion, when so many military units and the stronger force of the whole Roman army are at his disposal? Why do we wait, so that, supported by our valour, he may owe to others his position as emperor, and we may yield to others what lies within our rightful power? Certainly, if we do not wish to honour him, let us not disparage him or inflict this injury: that by our judgement he should be rejected as unworthy of the imperial power of which Vitellius is held worthy. Finally, since his brother and his son Domitian are in Italy, there is surely reason to fear that a man who should long ago have been a distinction to his family may become a danger to them. Or, if they begin, as we suppose, to press the tyrant, their rebellion as his brother and son may count against him, and we may begin to see as an accused man the one whom we are unwilling to see as emperor.”

Voicing these things among themselves, the soldiers approached Vespasian and asked him to take up the helm of the Roman dominion. He refused, saying that he was unworthy, that an emperor had already been appointed, and that civil war must be avoided. They pressed more readily; he resisted more persistently. At last they surrounded him under arms as he struggled against them, threatening death with their swords. They recognised that guilt and grave danger would remain with them if he refused. Thus he yielded to their pressure rather than willingly accepting what others commonly solicit. The soldiers pressed him, the commanders urged him; he took on the burden before the honour.

He hastened to Egypt, for he knew that the greatest resources of the Roman state were there. Where its sustenance was supplied, he must seek support for himself if he won, or a means of obstructing Vitellius if he thought the war should be prolonged. There were also two military formations there, which he hastened to join to himself, so that a very great city, surrounded by numerous natural defences and highly useful for either outcome of the war, might remain under his own authority rather than another’s. We have therefore thought that something should be said, even briefly, about the situation of the places, and above all about the chief city itself.

The city of Alexandria was founded by Alexander, to whom the name of a great commander was given for his valour. It lies like a barrier between Egypt and the sea, a city with poor harbourage, like most of Egypt, and difficult of access from outside, situated in the more remote parts of Asia. To the west Egypt itself borders on the arid regions of Libya; its southern and upper regions separate Syene and the unnavigable cataracts of the river Nile from the Ethiopians. On the east the Red Sea spreads back as far as Coptos, a place at the furthest edge of the land which opens a passage to the Indians for those about to sail. Enclosed therefore on one side by the burning heat of the sun, on that side by the Indian sea and on this by the Egyptian sea, it adjoins land only along a single northern wall leading into Syria. The rest is shut off on every side and fortified by the aid of nature. Yet the protection of its northern side is divided and opens through a kind of double threshold, through which either foreign supplies are conveyed to it over the Egyptian sea or freer access extends overland. The land stretches to an immeasurable extent. For between Syene and Pelusium lies an immense length of two thousand stades, if the statements are to be believed, and from Plinthine to Pelusium likewise three thousand six hundred stades. The region is unaccustomed to rains, yet has no need of them, since the Nile’s irrigation supplies showers of its own accord. The Nile is both things to it: the abundance of heaven and the fertility of earth. It tempers the fields and enriches the soil, equally useful to sailors and farmers. The former sail, the latter sow; these are carried about their own fields in boats, those cultivate them: sowing without a plough, travelling without a carriage. You may see the land divided by streams and raised, as it were, by ramparts of ships. Dwellings wander across all the lands encircled by the Nile. For it is navigable as far as the city they call the City of Elephants. Beyond it the cataracts we have mentioned do not allow a ship to proceed, not through lack of depth but through the whole river’s steep descent and a kind of collapse of the waters. The city’s harbour, like most approaches along the coast, is difficult to enter, and far more difficult than the others. It resembles the form of a human body: more capacious in the head itself and the anchorage, narrower in the throat, where it receives the passage of the sea and ships, which supply the harbour with a kind of aid to breathing. When one has passed the narrows and mouth of the harbour, the expanse of the sea stretches far and wide like the rest of the body. On the right of the harbour is a small island, and on it a very great tower, which Greeks and Latins alike have called Pharos from its very function: it is seen from afar by sailors, so that, before they approach the harbour, especially at night, the indication of its flames lets them know that land is near. Thus they will not be deceived by darkness and strike the rocks or fail to find the bounds of the entrance. There are attendants there who kindle the fire by placing torches and other piles of wood beneath it. Like a herald of the land and a guide to the harbour’s throat, it shows the narrow approach, the recesses of the waves and the windings of the entrance, lest a frail keel graze the crags and strike rocks hidden beneath the waves at the very entrance. The straight course must therefore be turned aside a little, lest the ship strike unseen rocks and incur danger where escape from dangers is hoped for. For the approach to the harbour is narrower, constricted on the right by the island’s flank and on the left by rocks which obstruct the harbour’s left side. Around the island too, built masses of enormous size are lowered into place, lest the island’s foundations yield to the constant onslaught of the rising sea and be loosened by long-standing damage. Hence, as the waves strike the side of the island and recoil in the opposite direction among the jagged rocks and constructed masses, the channel between is always restless, and the roughened passage makes entry dangerous for ships. The extent of the harbour is thirty stades, its anchorage safe and its calm very great in any storm. For by the narrows of the aforesaid mouth and the barrier of the island it repels the waves of the sea. The harbour within is made utterly safe as a kind of compensation for the dangerous entrance: by those same narrows of the harbour mouth, the whole basin is defended, kept free from storms and calmed from the crashing waves that make the entrance rough. Nor is it without reason that the protection and size of the harbour are such, since things serving the needs of the whole world must be conveyed into it. For the innumerable peoples of those places seek the trade of the whole world for their own use; and the region, fruitful in crops and abounding in the other gifts of the earth and in commerce, feeds the whole world with grain and supplies it with necessary goods.

Having therefore settled affairs in Alexandria in his favour, with the support of all who conducted military affairs united around his rule, he felt secure in his absence and hastened his return to Syria. He had, however, approached Tiberius Alexander, who then governed Egypt, with instructions to attach to him the goodwill of the army in the upper regions, and himself to help bear, with whatever forces he could, the burden of Roman rule that had been laid upon Vespasian. Tiberius made the letter known to the provincials and soldiers. It was received by all with joy; allegiance was promised and favour poured forth. Caesarea received Vespasian, then Berytus, with embassies from the cities flocking to him in the greatest joy.

There Josephus too was ordered to be released from his bonds. Titus approached the emperor to ask that the chains be broken rather than loosened, because, if they were broken, it would be as though he had not been bound. This pleased his father. He ordered an axe to be brought and the chains to be broken, so that the Jews might realise that pardon would not be denied to them either, if they changed their course and asked for peace. At the same time, he did so because he was no longer keeping Josephus for another’s judgement, since authority to decide all matters had now been conferred upon himself.

They came to Antioch. There, after deliberation on where they ought to cross to Italy, speed was the consideration, since he had seen that everything in Egypt and Alexandria was secure. He therefore sent Mucianus ahead with a large part of the cavalry and infantry, to precede the emperor’s arrival in Italy. Deterred by fear of a long voyage, Mucianus directed his route through Cappadocia and Phrygia.

He also ordered Antonius, commander of the third military formation stationed in Moesia, to pour into Italy while it was unprepared, before the Vitellians stirred. For Vitellius, as though surfeited and sunk in sleep, thought he was managing a banquet rather than an empire, and slumbered amid affairs of such importance. Indeed, scarcely roused at last by news of Antonius’s approach, he sent Caecina with part of the army and entrusted the whole issue of his danger to another’s judgement, relying on Caecina’s strength because he had routed Otho’s force. Caecina met Antonius as he approached near the city of Cremona, reconnoitred everything and learnt that a very powerful force was coming against him, energetic in war and practised in triumphs. His own men, by contrast, were equal neither in strength nor in number and could not fight against the stronger force. He summoned the centurions and urged them to desist from war, since they were inferior in number and the other emperor’s glory carried greater weight. The fame of the commander conducting the whole undertaking counted for much in war. Vespasian had shone in the regions of Gaul and in victories in Britain; Vespasian, girded with triumphs in the East, rested on a strong presumption in favour of his name. Vitellius, nothing but a man dissolved in wine and always belching yesterday’s feasts amid his banquets, expected nothing except to perish drunk, without feeling pain, when the enemy arrived. The glory of so great an emperor raised the spirits of the soldiers on the one side; on the other, his disgrace and shameful acts cast them down. They must take care not to lose the fame of the former war. They had defeated Otho, Vitellius’s equal; now they had to deal with a man who had encircled the whole world with his triumphs. They must forestall necessity by goodwill, choosing Vespasian as a fellow citizen rather than experiencing him as an enemy. It was wretched even to win in a civil war. “How much more wretched to be defeated, so that you appear an enemy of your own people! The victor retains his fatherland; the defeated man loses it, or, if it remains, it will remain to the odium of his crime, so that we appear to have made war upon our fellow citizens for a tyrant. For the defeated man is no longer a citizen but a tyrant. Why do we join guilty hands in battle? Let it be enough for our guilt to have won once, so that we were ashamed of the man for whom we won. We thought he would become sober at least through imperial power, or, awakened by the weight of affairs, renounce his perpetual sleep. Why do we wait any longer? Our dangers win no gratitude from any of our fellow soldiers; our judgements are reproved and condemned by all peoples because of the outrages of the man we chose. Consider what kind of man he is, rejected even as a victor. We must certainly deliberate first on the outcome of the war, and then fight. If dangers come first, you will deliberate in vain; once a plan has been approved, you may rightly begin.” He added that, as befitted a vigilant commander, he had reconnoitred everything, and it had become clear that Vespasian’s army was stronger. His allegiance to Vitellius had long since been proved. When he had been confident of the outcome of war, victory had followed; when he lacked confidence, what would happen was plain. He did not fear his own death, but the danger to the Roman army and, what pains men more, the loss of glory already won, so that those accustomed to victory should appear defeated. He must certainly take care lest it be judged that his victory in the former war had been due not to courage but to chance, and his later defeat to cowardice.

By these and similar words he brought the soldiers over to his view, so that they would go with him to Antonius and surrender themselves to him voluntarily. But such is the changeability of the crowd, especially a military one: during the night, in their beds, many were stung by remorse for having deserted Vitellius, lest, if he proved the stronger, no room for pardon should remain for those who had abandoned their own emperor. They rose and began to confer, first with whoever they encountered and then with everyone, on how to amend their error. Drawing their swords, they sprang upon Caecina, wishing to avenge the injury of their own lapse. But when the centurions and chiliarchs intervened, they thought they should indeed refrain from killing him, yet prepared to send him bound to Vitellius. Learning this, Antonius moved the men he had brought with him and rushed under arms upon the deserters. On seeing the column of the opposing side, they prepared for battle. But after daring to resist for a little while, they turned to flee to Cremona. Antonius met them with his horsemen and forestalled every approach, so that the fugitives would not be received, and killed them, shut out before the city.

A very great multitude was killed there; he pursued the rest into the city itself and destroyed them. Everything was plundered. Very many merchants who had come from other places, and very many inhabitants, were killed for the sake of plunder while defending their possessions. Thirty thousand two hundred men of Vitellius’s army who were present were destroyed. Primus too—for that was Antonius’s surname—lost four thousand five hundred of the Moesian soldiers. For when the Vitellians saw themselves surrounded, despairing of safety and wishing to avenge themselves, they too yielded no bloodless victory to Antonius’s men. Caecina was released from his bonds and sent by Antonius to Vespasian. There, not only assurance of safety but also the payment of rewards consoled him for the stain of betrayal.

Elated by the news of this victory, Sabinus wished to win favour for himself too with the emperor by forestalling Antonius’s arrival through the destruction or expulsion of Vitellius; or, if Vitellius resisted, Antonius, who was reported to be on the very point of arriving, would come to his aid. He therefore gathered soldiers for himself, a force drawn from the units stationed at Rome to perform watch duties.

At night he also occupied the Capitol. During the day very many nobles flocked to him, among them Domitian, born to Vespasian’s brother, who feared that the vengeance of Vitellius might be turned upon him as Vespasian’s nephew. Placed between two opponents, Vitellius attacked the nearer, less concerned about the more distant—for dangers close at hand inspire greater fear. In his indignation he sent the Germans against the Capitol. Exceedingly fierce in the savagery of their nation, and also stronger in number, they surrounded Sabinus’s fighting band.

Almost all were killed. Domitian, however, with many of the nobles, found an opportunity to flee while the Germans strove to reach the upper parts of the Capitol and were repelled by Sabinus and his companions with the aid of their position. Or perhaps he himself too was being preserved for the public evil, as a future tyrant. Vitellius tortured Sabinus and killed him; all the gifts offered to the Capitol were plundered and the temple was burned.

A day later Antonius arrived and met them from the opposite side. After three encounters around the city’s walls, all the Vitellians were routed and killed. Meanwhile Vitellius was feasting, lest, about to die, he miss his meal; as men commonly do in their last moments, he stuffed himself with the more abundant dishes of his final table. He overwhelmed himself with more frequent cups of wine, so as to lose awareness of the disgrace or danger to come. He was snatched from the banquet and dragged through the crowd; insults were hurled at the dying man, and injuries inflicted which, drunk, he did not feel. He was killed in the middle of the city, pouring out wine and blood together and belching his drunken excess. Had he lived longer, he would have licked away the wealth of the Roman dominion in expenditure on luxury and the cost of his tables. Indeed, he ruled for eight months and five days, and already Rome had failed to satisfy his appetite. More than fifty thousand others were counted among the slain.

On the following day Mucianus and Antonius entered together with the army and scarcely put an end to the killing by the raging soldiers. For they pursued the Vitellians as men who had presumed to determine who should rule, and searched the houses of private citizens, stirred by such indignation that, when they discovered some of the people hiding in fear, they struck them as Vitellians before an inquiry could reveal the truth. Thus the victors’ fury often forestalled questioning. Since Vespasian was absent, Mucianus put Domitian in charge of public affairs, as though to fill an interregnum, lest prosperity lack any blemish. Yet the lust for outrages had not wholly poured itself into Domitian. He was still unpractised in vices and a novice in crimes as in positions of power.

Vespasian, detained by winter, with the sea closed by winds, returned to Alexandria with his son. There, on receiving news of victory and learning of the Roman populace’s favour towards him, he decided to hasten his departure, lest anything new be attempted in his absence. Yet he did not leave the Jewish war unattended. He thought it should be entrusted to his son as a partner in his works and his successor, so that neither the Romans should lack him in person nor the Jews lack Vespasian, whom his son would represent.

Chosen therefore to carry out his father’s triumph, Titus was sent with a picked force. He set out on foot and made for Nicopolis. That city is twenty-four stades from Alexandria. From there, putting his soldiers aboard a fleet of larger ships, he sailed down the Nile as far as the city of Thmuis. Advancing from there, he stayed in the city called Tanis. The travellers’ second stopping-place was the city of Heraclea, the third Pelusium. After spending two days at Pelusium as a halt, he travelled through the desert and reached the temple of Jupiter Casius. Ostracine was his next stopping-place. It lacked local water, yet by their diligence the inhabitants had provided themselves with a supply by constructing water conduits. The Rhinocori too received the advancing army with welcome refreshment. They came to the city of Raphiul, which marks the beginning of Syria for those travelling from Egypt. They reached Gaza—this was the fifth city for those arriving—then Ascalon, then Jamnia, from which they passed to Joppa and reached Caesarea. There it was necessary to remain for a little while and gather the force of soldiers still in winter quarters. Already the rigour of winter was abating.

In the first year after imperial rule had been conferred on Vespasian, Judaea was being torn apart by bitter wars and domestic seditions. It had enjoyed no respite from its woes even through the winter, when the savagery of wars usually rests.

Indeed, a third tyrant, Eleazar, had joined the others, as though to correct the vices of his predecessors. Judas, Simon son of Ezeron, and Hezekiah, a young man of no low birth, conspired with him, and very many others accompanied them. They occupied the inner parts of the temple and stationed armed men all around above the doors, at the front of the vestibule itself. John, however, had the advantage in the number of his fellow conspirators and the multitude of his faction, but his position was lower. Although he took no rest and fought back against those above him, he was nevertheless hard pressed by having enemies above his head.

Simon, whom the people had brought in as their tyrant, held the upper parts of the city; its lower parts too were filled with his people. The city suffered within itself from a threefold battle. There was no interruption, no rest, no truce; fighting went on at every moment. Many fell, countless men were slaughtered; blood flowed, fouled everything and filled the very thresholds of the temple. Corpses fell everywhere; some were struck by arrows, others by missiles. Of the three, John was in the middle, below Eleazar and above Simon. The advantage Eleazar had over him was the same advantage he himself had over Simon: his position between them meant that the more heavily he was pressed by one, the more he himself harmed the other. Better equipped than the others, however, with the support of engines and various kinds of weapons, he kept the war evenly balanced. Yet, besides those who waged war, many of the priests too were killed and sacrificed among the very victims they had slaughtered. For although a dense crop of missiles fell upon them all and battles raged everywhere, the priests still performed their solemn ministry of sacrifice and did not cease from the duty entrusted to them. The further inside the temple they were, the more severely they were struck down, because missiles driven by an engine delivered more violent blows. Many too who had come from the ends of the earth to pray, hoping for saving remedies, were caught in greater dangers the more closely they clung to the temple. You could see foreigners lying beside citizens, priests beside the profane, men of dignity beside the shameful, the self-indulgent beside the abstinent. The blood of all was mingled indiscriminately and ran like a torrent, pooling in the very innermost recesses of the temple; all around, the blood swelled, so that many champions of the factions, as they attacked one another, slipped on it and plunged into the blood, as though to sate their fury. Yet even then the tyrants’ followers were not frightened by the dangers into abandoning the battle. The greater the danger, the more fiercely the storm of fury raged. If destruction bore down more heavily on one side, the others pressed on more violently, as though towards victory, to destroy their disordered opponents.

Eleazar or Simon could withdraw, so that they were separated by what amounted to truces, even if only for a few hours. John, however, was always under arms, at every moment in combat. If those above rested, those below on Simon’s side pressed him; if he drove these back, Eleazar assailed him. Nor did he himself allow them to remain at rest. When he had repelled one group, he sprang upon the other, ever watchful in combat and tireless in his very cruelty. When they spared their missiles, they hurled fire, which caught the rooftops and devoured the houses. These were filled with grain and other stores of food for enduring a prolonged war; they too were burnt, providing greater fuel for the conflagration. Charred timbers fell; the tops of lofty buildings came crashing down.

Thus bloodshed, fire, ruin and famine severed the sinews of the whole city. No place was free of danger, no time could be found for counsel; there was no hope of a change, no opportunity for escape. Everything was mournful, full of horror, full of savagery: everywhere grief and terror, everywhere the cries of women, the wailing of old men, the groans of the dying, the despair of the living. You would have called those who remained pitiable, those who had died blessed.

How you have been deceived, city, by your peoples, through whom you once seemed blessed! How you have been stormed by your own arms, and your own hands turned against you—you who used to conquer without arms and strike the enemy without any battle, when angels fought for you and the waves of the sea, the chasms of the earth and the crashes of heaven served in your army! Arise now, Moses, and see your nation and the inheritance of the people entrusted to you perishing by their own hands. Look upon that people of God, for whom the sea opened a path as they walked, for whom heaven supplied food when they were hungry: they are shut in without a sea, besieged without a Pharaoh, starving without any barrenness of the land. Arise, Aaron, who once, when death was devouring very many of the people because they had offended almighty God, stood between the living and the dead: death stood still, and the plague was checked by the barrier of your body and could not pass on to infect the living. Awaken, you too, Joshua son of Nun, who levelled the impregnable walls of Jericho as the priests sounded their trumpets, and see the people to whom you subjected foreigners now themselves subjected and oppressed. Awaken, David, who used to drive out the tormenting spirit by the sweetness of the lyre, and see how fury rules and has erased all the sweetness of your psalms from the minds of the lost. Each of their leaders offers the whole people to death to wrest away their freedom—the people for whom you offered yourself to death. Awaken, Elisha, who brought the enemy into Samaria and made him a friend. Through you the crash of four-horse chariots rang out in the camp of Syria, the sound of horsemen and the sound of an army; the enemy fled, the Jew escaped the siege. Where now are those merits, where now those works of the saints? Nor is it surprising that they have lost the works of the prophets, since they denied the master of the prophets. Therefore your own arms are turned against you, Judaea; your prayers avail you nothing, because your faith accomplishes nothing. Therefore your people have turned against you, because your faithlessness has turned back upon you. What remedy can be sought where the author of the remedy is not reconciled? What did you think would happen when with your own hands you crucified your salvation, when with your own hands you extinguished your life, when with your own voices you drove out your advocate, when by your own assaults you killed your helper, except that you would lay your own hands upon yourself as well? You have what you asked for. You deprived yourself of the guardian of peace; you asked that the master of life be killed and that Barabbas be granted to you, who had been sent to prison for sedition committed in the city and for murder. Therefore salvation has departed from you, peace has gone, rest has ceased; sedition has been given to you, destruction has been given. Acknowledge that for you today Barabbas lives, Jesus is dead. Therefore sedition reigns within you, peace lies buried, so that you perish more cruelly at the hands of your own than if you perished at the hands of foreigners. What evil did the Roman bring upon you with his arms, wretched city, that equalled what your own people brought? It was your own people who made you fight the Romans. The Romans wanted peace; you declared war. What reason was there to provoke those stronger than you? It was certainly grievous that a gentile entered the temple contrary to the sacred law; but it was no longer God’s temple. You were not God’s city, nor could you be, because you were the tomb of the dead, and above all of your own people whom you yourself had killed, not those you had lost to the enemy. For how could you be the dwelling of life when you were the habitation of death, a lodging for crimes, a cave of brigands? Ananus and Jesus, chief priests, lay unburied within you. Those who had so recently been clothed in priestly robes and had been held in reverence even by foreigners lay as disfigured corpses, food for birds and a meal for dogs, their limbs torn and scattered throughout the city. The very image of ancient holiness seemed to lament so great an insult to the sacred name and the disfigurement of an office once glorious. But you yourself began this indignity, you who killed the prophets in your very bosom, who stoned the saints of the Lord. Zechariah lay lifeless before the temple; he lay unburied. Thus this blood washes away that blood. And what caused Ananus’s death except that he rebuked your people for not rising in defence of the temple, and protested that freedom had been betrayed, valour abandoned, the remnants of the ancient sacred rites trampled upon and the altars defiled? He declared that the people should be abandoned: like unfeeling images and statues of marble, they no longer felt anything. For dumb animals are accustomed at least to retaliate in vengeance, to feel an injury, to be stirred by a goad, to avoid blows. Whoever, then, is neither stirred nor knows how to avoid what harms him is like things without feeling. And indeed, where is that freedom of yours, from zeal for which you once thought you must yield neither to the Egyptians, nor to the Palestinians, nor to the Assyrians, nor later to the Medes? Where is that faith of the Maccabees which once, with a few men, routed the Babylonians, put the Persians to flight and struck down Demetrius, and at last, in little children and women, overcame Antiochus’s arms, swords and fires, and preferred to die for ancestral observance rather than obey the king’s commands? Where is that devotion of the fathers, the most beautiful of all sufferings, by which they offered themselves to death no more for their children and wives than for God’s temple? Once even the priestly rod blossomed, cut from a wild root; now faith itself is dry, devotion is buried, and all emulation of valour has departed. Nor is it surprising that a people who have withdrawn from God and follow the wicked spirit of contradiction are divided against themselves. For how could they preserve their own peace when they rejected the peace of God? The peace of God is Christ, who made both one. Rightly, then, from one people they became many hostile to one another, because they would not follow Jesus, who unites what is divided, but followed the spirit of fury, who divides what is united. You were therefore paying the price of your faithlessness, Jerusalem, when with your own hands you destroyed your defences, when with your own blades you pierced your entrails, so that the enemy pitied you, so that he spared you while you raged. For he saw that God was fighting against you and taking the Romans’ part, so that you brought voluntary betrayal upon yourself. Therefore the Romans preferred to be spectators rather than killers, lest laying a hand upon your entrails as they raged against one another be judged a matter of contamination rather than courage. To these torments of abominable slaughter was added the enormity of impious cruelty: they denied burial to all who had been killed either in the temple or around the city’s streets. No one had leisure to bury anyone while they were occupied in war against one another, and the concern to strike rather than to bury possessed them all. Thus in a kind of fury they had killed the duties of devotion, while the services of impiety grew savage. In so many calamities nothing had perished more completely than mercy, which alone is accustomed to lighten misery and console suffering. For those who had lost their own people did not dare to bury them out of fear, since grievous terror threatened them from the leaders of the opposing faction; and those who had killed others took care that no one snatched them away for burial. Thus everyone had to fear that what he wished to grant another he would receive himself, or, worse still, that he himself would not obtain the use of a tomb which he had prepared for another. In the temple itself, therefore, instead of sweet-smelling ointments, instead of fragrant censers, instead of the scents of various flowers, there was the heavy stench of unburied corpses, dissolved by rain, scorched by flame, heated by the sun. Every limb of the slaughtered citizens reeked with a dreadful smell. On one side the putrefaction of decaying entrails, on the other the fumes of burnt bodies filled all the senses and mouths of the living, so that they themselves were soon consumed by a more grievous disease. They groaned that they had survived to perish by a harsher punishment, and had been preserved to see the laws of nature dissolved together with their fatherland: justice denied to the living, peace to citizens, burial to the dead; human and divine things alike stained and polluted; everything confounded; mercy made criminal, cruelty counted as religion. A camp in the temple, war on the threshold, a funeral upon the altars: they saw with their own eyes what they had not believed would come when the prophets announced it. Had not David spoken of them: “They polluted your holy temple; they made the mortal remains of your servants food for the birds of heaven; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them”? For at that time the nations came into God’s inheritance to carry everything away, and at the same time the temple was polluted by the deaths of its own people, and the corpses of the slain lay unburied as food for birds, for the voracity of beasts. Blood was poured out until it pooled in the temple; there was no one to bury them, because fury passed from the living to the dead, and from the dead to those who still lived. Someone wished to bury a dead man and was himself killed; the man who had killed the dead man turned his anger upon the one who would bury him, killing the latter to deny the former burial. Again, the man who killed the would-be burier practised greater cruelty upon the dead man, depriving one who now owed nothing to hatred and felt no torments of nature’s final due. What else could happen to those who did not receive the divine oracles? They mocked the prophets’ announcements, trampled upon all sacred law, and did not believe that the things would happen which they themselves hastened to bring about. For there was an ancient and often-repeated saying that the city of Jerusalem would perish and its sacred things be burnt when sedition invaded the law of war and domestic hands defiled God’s temple. They did not understand even this. How often had God’s house been destroyed, how often had there been sedition, how often a siege, how often war! That city never perished except when they truly crucified God’s temple with domestic hands. And let them hear what temple that was: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” For what else was it but sacrilege when they stretched out impious hands against the author of salvation, when they stoned him, when they struck him, when they seized him, when they killed him? Then divine fire truly consumed their sacred things. For those things had been burnt by the Babylonians and afterwards repaired, destroyed by Pompey and restored again; but when Jesus came they were burnt away completely, and, dissolved by the heat of the divine Spirit, vanished.

It was necessary for us, with a somewhat fuller lament, to lead what was, as it were, the funeral of our ancestral observance, to accompany a kind of funeral procession and pay the last duties to the institutions of our forebears. But let us come to the beginnings of the siege of Jerusalem.

Titus had returned to Judaea. After an interval of a few days, to fill the ranks of the military units from which a picked force had been sent to Italy, he fanned the war into flame, hastening to accompany his father so as not to send him alone into danger to fight against the forces of Vitellius. He therefore set out with his army in splendid array, the column alert and ready everywhere, suspecting ambushes because he saw that he had the advantage in valour. He came through the territory of Samaria. Gophna received him, having long since gone over to the Romans. They reached Aulona, from which Jerusalem was thirty stades away and no more. From there he took six hundred horsemen and rode before the city, also to reconnoitre the lie of the land, the nature of the fortifications, the height of the walls and the disposition of the common people. They were said to be oppressed by the brigands’ arms and hemmed in by the mass of the factions, so that they unwillingly submitted to the siege and were prevented from making known their disposition towards the Romans, as they would if given freedom. He therefore rode in conspicuous splendour with a few horsemen along the public road leading to the city walls, and no one was seen to come out.

But when he turned his horse aside to go around the circuit of the walls, with the rest of the troop following their commander, very many suddenly burst out from the place called Opposite Helena’s Tomb and leapt forward to occupy the road, cutting off the greater part of the horsemen following Titus. He himself had passed by with a few men, as the ambushers had deliberately allowed, so that they could more easily overpower him when he was left unsupported by the rest. For it was not easy to return to his men because of the mass of enemies thrust between them, while a ditch or rampart and the other obstacles of the terrain prevented him from going further forward, bringing danger upon him on both sides.

Seeing, therefore, that his only remedy for safety lay in valour, and that a path must be opened by the sword and by no other means—for the others had already turned their horses and withdrawn, hoping that the emperor’s son too would follow—he turned his horse. Shouting to encourage the rest to follow him, he charged upon the enemy. It would seem impossible to explain how he could have escaped, were it not known that boldness has very great power in war and is a wall in itself, even when alone. Moreover, with others following behind him, the worthless rabble thought they should look to their own safety in danger rather than pursue the enemy; and anyone who stretched out a hand to seize his horse was struck down. In the end, only two of Titus’s companions were killed, and the emperor’s son returned to his men with the rest. Nor indeed does there seem to be any doubt why, although his head was uncovered and the rest of him unprotected, he received no wound even when the missiles were being aimed chiefly at him. He had gone out on a ride, not prepared for battle, and had put on neither helmet nor breastplate: so great a man was being preserved for the destruction of that city. The king’s heart is indeed, is indeed in the hand of God.

Therefore, lest the success of their deceit and the progress of their trickery increase the Jews’ boldness, he returned to the city with his army after the night. From a lookout from which the city and the vast expanse of the temple could be seen, he showed his men what sort of city they had to fight. They must be tireless and more cautious, since they had to overcome an innumerable people prepared for deceit. He arranged which ranks should approach the walls; those he knew were still exhausted by the night’s march he stationed at a distance as reserves. They advanced gradually.

When they reached the Mount of Olives, beneath it a valley called Cedron lay between their route and the city. Seeing from the walls that the army had been stationed there, for it was six stades away, the Jews laid aside their zeal for sedition for a time. With external enemies approaching, a domestic compact suspended their civil struggles. For fear often restrains even bitter hatred. Accordingly, the men of the factions encouraged one another to defend their fatherland with a common resolve, lest their discord give the Romans a bloodless victory. Relying on their numbers, they decided to attack the enemy suddenly, and by an unexpected sortie threw the foremost ranks into confusion. But when the Romans, trained by long experience itself and by battles of many kinds, had steadied their spirits, they stood firm in their formation and began to cut down the attackers, repel them with shields and drive them back with volleys of missiles, though by no means without destruction on both sides. The Jews had almost overwhelmed them and the Roman battle line was wavering, when Titus learnt what was happening and arrived. Meeting the adversaries and strengthening his men, he renewed the battle and raised the soldiers’ spirits, rebuking the Roman ranks for yielding victory to a disordered multitude, a thing that could not be done without the reproach of the greatest cowardice. Having repelled the Jews, who were pursuing even those separated from them by the valley, he returned victorious to his men. Confident in the support the higher position afforded against those below, if they tried to engage, he turned to another part of the Roman army.

As Caesar departed, the Jews poured out from the walls and charged upon the enemy in a great column, so that at the onrush of the innumerable multitude the soldiers fled and withdrew to the higher parts of the hills. With their flank exposed, even the others who would have preferred battle fled. Meanwhile Caesar stood in their midst. Very many begged him not to expose himself to danger and, with the army scattered, bear the whole danger alone, since he was master of the world: he should no longer fight as before in the role of a soldier, but in that of an emperor, whose danger meant destruction for all. He did not yield. Placing military honour before safety, and judging a glorious death to outweigh the disgrace of life, he presented his breast to the enemy. When he had terrified those he had advanced against, he turned upon others. By his appearance alone and the renown of his all too well-known and eager courage he drove back the enemy. Those he approached therefore gave way, but from other quarters the Jews poured in more and more. They had almost surrounded Titus when very many soldiers, seeing Caesar in the midst of the battle, cried out to the rest, signalling that the emperor’s son must not be abandoned in danger. Thus shame recalled them all, and fear armed them, lest they be branded with the disgrace of having deserted Caesar. Turning upon the Jews, they drove the disordered multitude into the valley with all their strength and valour; nor was it difficult for those ascending to slip back. Thus Titus twice recalled the fleeing military unit from flight and freed it alike from danger and disgrace. He displayed equal valour on both occasions, and at the last employed shame as well: by shunning cowardice, shame brought valour, first so that Caesar should not be abandoned, and then so that the enemy should be driven back.

When the battle outside had subsided for a little while, the internal battle took its place. For at the arrival of the Passover festival, John enlisted very many men to approach the temple as though for religious observance, and contrived a trap when they were allowed to enter as allies. They entered in civilian guise but armed beneath their clothing; throwing off their garments, they raised their swords, their breasts armoured and themselves girded with protection for battle. Struck with terror, those inside the temple who were attending the festival unarmed rushed out and left the temple empty.
