Simon was therefore the more cruel, since he neither spared a friend nor remitted the punishment of the man who had sponsored his reception. The father was led to execution with three children, for the fourth had escaped by flight. He was placed in sight of the Roman army as an insult, so that those to whom he had wished to go out might see his punishment. “Let your friends free you,” Simon said, “if they can.” His sons too were led out. He was not permitted to give his children a last kiss or receive his sons in a final embrace. Yet he was not deprived of the freedom of a father’s voice, and accompanied his sons with a pitiable address. “I, my sons, brought the enemy upon you; I brought in the executioners when I asked Simon to enter the city. That day was the cause of this death for us, the cause of this spectacle of murder of kin. I deserved it, I confess, and I do not excuse my fault: in my eagerness to restrain one man, I summoned a worse. Simon was sought for help, but turned to the murder of his fatherland and made earnest counsel into a crime. We stand guilty before our fatherland, we who sought a defender. And rightly indeed we pay the penalty for imprudence, but not for faithlessness. Simon himself acquits us as he kills us: he declares that the city was not given to him by me, but that, out of regard for the fatherland, he was asked to come as quickly as possible to help against John’s savagery and bring in the Idumaeans. We thought that, with the two contending against one another, the people would be free. Who would believe me that I offered this to you not out of devotion to you, but because I judged it the more tolerable of the evils, unless you killed me? But why do I speak as though excusing a crime? In my judgement I could certainly have done nothing more grievous than to place you upon our necks. Yet in this I may have been guilty towards my fatherland, not towards you. I may have owed the citizens death, but you owed me gratitude. I may have owed my fatherland the penalty for betrayal because I brought you in: when did I begin to be a traitor to you? If I had thought I should flee, I would have provided for myself, not violated my bond with my fatherland. For who does not flee an enemy, and an enemy within? We thought you a citizen, but found you an enemy. Sought for help, what did you give in return? What did you promise before, and to what did you afterwards turn? You had entered to drive out an enemy, not to act as one; to prevent killings, not to add to them yourself; to repel brigandage, not to practise it yourself; to aid an innocent people. Why did you turn your weapons against that very people? Before, we were attacked by brigandage; you brought war upon us. Before, fewer people were dragged to death; you brought about a slaughter of peoples. Who betrayed his fatherland, who helped Roman arms more, than the man who extinguished his fatherland’s defenders, than the man who deprived it of the defence of so many citizens, than the man who turned his sword from the enemy upon his allies? The enemy outside the walls offered peace; you fought within the walls. He wished to lift the siege; you hastened the city’s storming. He prevented fires in our city; you cast flames upon the very roof of the temple. Out of regard for our sacred rites he granted truces; on the very days of worship you were quenching God’s altars with the city’s final destruction and even with the blood of priests. He had besieged the walls, you the temple. I heap up my crimes: I laid hands upon my fatherland, I armed your fury, I inflicted all these destructions in a kind of old age’s delirium. I acknowledge the imprudence of a deranged age. Let us lighten our shame by confession, since we cannot cast off our sin by denying it. Two of us above the rest hastened our fatherland’s destruction: I through an error of counsel, you through your intent to murder kin. I therefore pay you, fatherland, the penalties I owe, and for this very reason I thank Simon, because I shall not survive your ashes. Would that I did not survive my children either! But, to add to the bitterness of your crime, Simon, I stand as a spectator of my sons’ murder. I deserved it, I confess: I could not bear to see John even in a picture, and I chose you armed. O headlong old age! We feared an image; we sought a tyrant. I was your guarantor, I your petitioner who undertook the embassy. I asked you to be our master; I brought in a killer. Let us therefore watch what we have done: John’s wax image terrified us; Simon’s brigandage delighted us. Let the procession to the funerals therefore be hastened. Let the executioner come and slaughter the sons before their father’s eyes, and the father over his sons’ corpses. Let me, a wretched old man, drink in the sight of the executioner’s stroke as he poises the savage axe above the necks of my children. Nothing is more dreadful than this spectacle except the man who commands it. Cruel, wicked man, I do what you command; I do it, but unwillingly. Yet I have a consolation in so great a calamity. I suffer whatever is most pitiable, provided that you have ordered it. I willingly undergo whatever is most monstrous, with you directing it. You have filled up the measure of the most savage crimes. Let me at least address my children and say a final farewell to my dear ones. Let there be some place for last kisses, which we share even with wild beasts. Do not forbid the pitiable embrace of nature, which chance can bestow even upon the dead. What you have commanded as punishment will therefore serve me as family devotion. I shall fall upon my dead and, while they are still unburied, cover them as though with a turf of my own body, so that birds may not tear them apart or beasts devour them. With a father’s tongue I shall lick up my children’s blood and mingle my own with it, lest beasts lick it. Perhaps devotion and nature’s own compassion will add this too: that as I die I shall clasp my children in so tight an embrace that you cannot separate us when you wish. Certainly, even if you separate our bodies, you will not separate our souls. But enough, now enough provision of tears have we taken for the journey. Go before me, my sons, and prepare the way for the father who will follow. If I can catch up, I shall accompany you; and if old age is an impediment there, so that I cannot keep pace with vigorous young men, go ahead to the resting place, to receive your weary father into an enduring lodging. I wished indeed to go first myself and asked for it, but did not obtain it. Yet because you are innocent, better lodgings will be granted you than if I, who summoned Simon, arrived first. That embassy weighs upon me, though it was commissioned by the citizens and undertaken at the people’s request. Go before me, therefore, my sons, treading the path above with purer footsteps. The Maccabees too went before their mother, but they to a reward, we to punishment. Yet the devoted mother watched her sons dying and rolling upon the blood of their own; she saw the brothers embracing one another in the bond of nature, and rejoiced in the triumph she was winning over the tyrant. The merits of those suffering were indeed different, but the savagery of the two men giving the orders was the same. Antiochus devised this with Persian monstrosity—for among them are the inventions of new tortures—and you followed him. Yet he kept the mother till last to secure compliance with the royal will; you ordered the father to be kept for the torment of a father’s grief. Take comfort, dearest sons: we suffer what the martyrs suffered; Simon has decreed it. What a barbarian persecutor invented, a tyrant has commanded. Let us therefore depart willingly and flee the gatherings of brigands. Indeed, when we have departed to that eternal home, if any come to us and ask how that former people of God fares, what shall we answer them—especially if Jonathan, in the fullness of his age, meets you as younger men, and Saul meets me as a sinner? What, I say, shall we say except that that people—young and beloved Judah, before whom the sea fled, for whom the sun stood still and the Jordan gave way—that people, I say, for whom the wave was passable, the air fruitful, the earth heavenly, which did not take on the form of corruption as this earth of ours does, but assumed the grace of resurrection, now serves the Idumaeans and is subject to Simon, the chief of brigands, and has neither security in slavery itself nor danger with freedom? What do we think those will answer who chose to perish in war rather than survive their fatherland’s freedom? What too will Mattathias, the forefather of the Maccabees, answer, who preferred to die resting on the Sabbath in observance of the law rather than live by fighting, if he hears how Simon not only carried out innumerable killings of citizens on the Sabbath, but also caused the Lord’s own priests to be slaughtered at new moons and on all the holy days of festal celebration? How deeply Jeconiah will groan when he hears that Simon, who first overturned the city with seditions and violated the temple’s ancient religion by slaughtering citizens, though so often called upon to deliver the city from fire by surrendering himself, prefers that everything perish, the city be destroyed, the temple burnt and the whole people killed, rather than lower the height of the dominion he has seized! How deeply, I say, Jeconiah will grieve, though less fortunate in his rule at a time of pressing evils, yet better than his son. For the father preferred to be less fortunate for himself than for his fatherland, miserably indeed, yet dutifully. So he went out of the city and gave himself with his lineage into servitude to the besieging Babylonians, lest he see his fatherland overthrown and God’s people captive. But the son, in equal affliction but with unequal devotion, fearing for himself, brought both himself into exile and the city to destruction. Thus this man was unfortunate for his fatherland and not fortunate for himself, losing both his children and his eyes; the other was more prudent, redeeming the citizens’ captivity with his own. The outcome finally showed it. The former died older in kingship, the latter younger in servitude, although the Babylonian king afterwards set a royal throne for him beside himself and granted him precedence in counsel—consolations for a wretched calamity. Indeed, my lot is now more tolerable if I die after my children’s murder than if I live, so that you may know how cruel is the man who slaughters sons before their father’s eyes. Even his royal gifts are worse than the wounds of family devotion. For either he should not have inflicted such impieties at first, or should not afterwards have put such honours in their place—as though any dignity could be bought by the loss of sons, or the slaughter of one’s offspring compensated by the enjoyment of any honour. No dignity, certainly none, lightens so great a grief. No honour heals this wound except death alone, which takes away feeling and removes remembrance. Make haste, then, killer. Yet wait while I see my children, while I look upon them before they die, lest any, perhaps troubled by the immaturity of his age, fear death when he is escaping a more savage tyrant. It is a benefit, my sons, to die so that we do not see our fatherland’s captivity. Wounds of the body are more tolerable than wounds of the mind. Now I even look more tolerably upon your deaths, from which I recoiled, so that I may not look upon the common deaths of all, may not see my fatherland’s funeral pyre and the whole city the tomb of its own people. Yet he who has died is happier than he who is kept alive. Most high God, may Simon not be laid low with his children among the ranks of the guilty. Let him see in captivity what he has inflicted. Rather, not at all,” he said, “for what he could devise, he can endure. Yet I do not pray for these things. Let him consider how grievous is a crime which its victim cannot turn back upon him even in a prayer: if the vengeance is bitter, how savage is the monstrosity of the crime committed! Let him be what he desires, a captive surviving his fatherland, because life’s humiliations are worse than death’s punishments. But now let there be an end to words. Hasten, executioner, while you bear the sword bloodied with the sons’ blood, to strike the father, so that it may cool his wound. This alone is medicine for one about to die; by this alone the sword’s stroke and the wound’s pain are not felt. Strike in sight of the Roman army, as you have been ordered, so that those who will avenge may watch. Let the enemy have compassion, because an ally has none; let the Romans judge, because Simon kills without judgement. They themselves are witnesses that I was not a traitor to my fatherland but its defender, for they saw me fighting, not deserting. If I could, I would have turned the enemy away from my children, not called the enemy in: would that I had not summoned Simon either!”

Nor was any end put to such cruelty. The children still lay unburied with their father, and sacrilege too was added to the spectacle of murder of kin. Ananias the priest, born of an illustrious family, was killed, though no one is more illustrious through the splendour of his lineage than through an office of religion. Through the former nobility is sought; with the latter it is not lacking. Let ancient lineage keep its fasces of various honours: priesthoods too have their fasces, which are raised not by shoulders but by character, and lifted high not by the length of rods but by perseverance in labours, the height of faith and the summit of devotion. Aristeus the scribe, himself also of illustrious origin, was killed too, and with them fifteen others of the people who stood out above the rest, though it is innocence, not nobility, that makes a killing unjust.

Eleven men were also forestalled. They had conspired together, moved by the atrocity of his crimes and each fearing for himself what they saw inflicted upon others, because Simon was faithless even to friends and hope had been taken away. Hunger ravaged everyone, the Romans were on the very point of breaking in, and Simon was in confusion when it came to providing defence, but raged at his workshop of cruelty. Betrayal was an easy temptation, because Judas, one of them, had been entrusted with guarding a tower. Thus, while he was calling the Romans and promising to hand over the tower, some scorned the offer because the betrayal came so late, while others hesitated because the Jews had often prepared a trick after promising surrender. Simon forestalled them and exacted punishment from all the partners in the conspiracy. Their bodies too were thrown headlong from the wall.

Josephus’s father was kept shut up, and no one was allowed access to him. Josephus therefore urged the Jews to surrender all the more earnestly and had approached the wall all the more rashly, so that he might free his fatherland along with his father. There he was struck on the head by a stone and fell, and would almost have been overwhelmed by missiles thrown from above, had men not been sent at Caesar’s command to protect him with shields and snatch him from death. On learning of her son’s wound, his mother, terrified by the voices of the taunting brigands, took on both fear of his death and belief in it. She began pitiably to lament that she had been kept alive for these fruits of motherhood: neither to enjoy the service of her living son nor to bury him dead. Her wish had indeed been that he should instead give his mother burial, that she should breathe out her last breath amid his hands, that he should warm her cold limbs as she failed, gather her last breaths with his mouth, close her dying eyes and compose her face while it still breathed. But since she had lost her wish, it would have been a consolation if at least she herself could have attended her dying son’s last moments—a pitiable lot indeed, yet a tolerable one—to hold at least the dead body of the man she had wished to survive her. “Yet let me at least look upon my dead from the wall,” she said, “even if I may not touch him. Would that no one barred me! But whom should I fear, bereft of so great a son? What should I dread, when it is a benefit for me to die? Would that all turned their missiles upon me and pierced me with the sword! What I could not do alive, let me at least do dead: cover my son’s body with my garment. One person’s clothing is ample for the burial of two, and perhaps some enemy will take pity and cover the mother’s eyes with her son’s cloak, and join eyes to eyes, hands to hands and face to face.” Thus she rushed to the walls and filled heaven itself with her pitiable lament. Her own people taunted her; the Romans wept. Among allies there was cruelty, among enemies mercy. “Pierce me,” she said, “if there is any compassion: I bore the man whom you think you must persecute. I gave him these ill-fated breasts. Kill me if you seek vengeance upon him.”

While she lamented these things, behold, Josephus came forward at his mother’s voice and began to weep because he had escaped. It would have been sweet for him to die before his fatherland and to fall for his fatherland while urging counsels of safety. He was no longer contending for his parents’ safety: laid low by age, spending the last end of their life in prison, they would be freed if they died. Rather, he was anxious for the altar, for the temple, for the city’s still half-ruined walls. He had offered himself to a wound so that he might not see his fatherland overthrown. Moved by this lament, many thought they should cross over to the Romans and, by whatever path they could, withdrew from the ambushes of the brigands and the watches of those guarding the approaches.

Titus indeed kept his promised mercy towards them, but another, graver affliction befell them. For when a supply of nourishment was given, food which had formerly been useful began to be a burden, and the organs, unaccustomed to the tasks of eating, ceased to perform their service. There was no force in their teeth to chew food, no strength in their air passages; they could not gnaw bread at all. If they swallowed any softer nourishment, they choked, for the passages of their throats were already closed. Their inner parts had grown rigid, the channels for food were blocked, and the veins of the liver which draw in food had dried up. The ability had perished, greed increased; strength had failed, appetite remained. The wretched people rushed upon food and attempted feeble bites like infants. Many failed at the very joy of seeing nourishment, and died amid the food they had longed for, consoled in their misery because they had fulfilled their wish. But it was a tearful procession: more rose from food towards danger than towards health, so that even sustenance harmed them. Their bodies were swollen by unaccustomed food rather than restored, and, distended as though by a kind of dropsy, paid the penalty. If any still had strength to eat, greed, knowing no measure, piled in beyond measure what they could not bear, and, stuffed with sudden food, they burst apart. What was not grievous for people to whom even emotion alone was grievous, so that seeing what they desired harmed them? Unable to bear emotions through prolonged hunger, they were overwhelmed even by natural feeling, and the very movement of joy weighed upon them. It is therefore no wonder if food is dangerous to the exhausted. Indeed, after a two-day fast, if you take anything greedily, it at once remains undigested. Hence many are accustomed to pour liquid milk into their weakened inward parts and, mixing it with honey, temper the imbalance of the humours aggravated by fasting, and nourish the body’s weakness with softer food as though it were a kind of infancy. Thus some of the Jews who fled to the Romans were able to escape death, judging the limits of their food with a certain skill, until the flesh, unaccustomed to eating, returned to its normal functions.

Yet even this did not benefit the wretched, but became the cause of greater destruction. For when many of them emptied their bowels after receiving food, some passed double gold pieces which they had swallowed while preparing their flight, lest their discovery—for the plotters searched everything—expose them not only to loss but also to danger. For anyone except the brigands to possess gold was deemed a crime. Thus afterwards the Jews, in a pitiable spectacle, picked out this gold amid the filth of their bowels. A certain Syrian discovered it, and from one man the report spread to all. This race of men, headlong in avarice and ready for cunning, would recoil from nothing so atrocious, blush at nothing so shameful, in pursuit of money. The rumour spread from the Syrians to the Arabs, whose avarice was no less and whose savagery was closer to barbarous monstrosity: that the Jews were stuffed with gold. They seized and plundered whomever they encountered arriving, against sacred law, against the terms of surrender, against Caesar’s promise. Men whom they were not allowed to kill, they cut open while still alive and with bloody hands disembowelled the hidden parts of the belly. They searched the bowels and sought gold amid their flowing filth, no less shamefully than those whom hunger drove, and with savage cruelty besides. Many bitter things were committed in that war; nothing was more bitter than this one thing. Indeed, in one night nearly two thousand men were cut apart in such wickedness. When the bodies had been divided, Syria counted its gains and Arabia reckoned the profits of its trade, which they had turned to the use of profit and thought merchandise, without the dangers of crossing the sea, by a new invention of cruelty. Even now you may find among this sort of people, and some Egyptians, that they trade in the care of the dead and sell the offices of humanity for commercial gain. The wretched hunger for gold thinks nothing worth pursuing except what is profitable for the present, nothing honourable that is empty of money. A grievous, long since grievous, desire for acquisition has grown into human affections, and human life has become a trade. Life is lived by selling and buying. Thus the vice has crept into everyone, so that the exchange of merchandise is now more tolerable than the exchange of character and souls. The Syrians’ avarice infected even the Roman army. For nothing passes more easily to another than the love of money and the desire to possess, especially riches close at hand with which a neighbour inflames one. Nor is there any passion that more effeminates the soul’s valour than the desire for riches. Indeed, cunning is accounted praise, poverty a disgrace.

This hindered the severity of punishment, because countless men were found implicated in such madness. Thus Titus, who had intended to surround the Syrians and Arabs with the army, revoked his decision in view of their multitude. He pardoned the earlier offence and announced a penalty to prevent its repetition; more severe in the harshness of his words, he rebuked his own men because, girded with gold and glittering with silver and costly weapons, they had no shame even before their own arms, dishonouring themselves with such disgrace. He reproached the Syrians and Arabs because, forgetful of the Roman name, they had devised things horrible even to tell. They had come to share in war, not to practise crimes. In the Roman army valour of mind as well as of body was required; not only courage against the enemy but also the standard of discipline was observed, so that a soldier should not be cruel, impious or insolent, nor intent on booty rather than victory. Such things were regarded as grave offences against military service and punished harshly. Even amid arms the laws held force; wars were better waged with faith, which was to be kept even towards enemies. If therefore it was owed even to armed men, how much more to suppliants! They should accordingly beware of such crimes, lest they lose their share both in victory and in safety. He would no longer allow their wicked deeds to be ascribed to the Romans, to whom they were a burden rather than a help. Thus he restrained the Syrians’ avarice somewhat, but did not cut it out: they avoided a witness instead of cherishing the command. Indeed, after first ascertaining whether a Roman soldier happened to be absent, they drew their accursed profit from the entrails of the wretched. Yet success in obtaining booty did not follow in all cases, but only in a few. Their savagery was therefore the more cruel, because very many were killed not only for wealth but even for the hope of gain, though brigands themselves and pirates, who are more savage than brigands, refrain from robbery where they perceive no booty. For it belongs only to barbarous monstrosity to harm for nothing. Even wild beasts pursue prey when they kill. Thus outside there were bitter punishments; within, John was more monstrous.

Indeed, while the Syrians were doing such things, even if some were turned back when the report became known, others nevertheless did not cease to desert. Among them was Manneus son of Lazarus, who asserted that through the one gate entrusted to him a hundred and fifteen thousand dead had been carried out, with a further eight hundred and eighty corpses, since he had taken charge of this duty. This total counted only those buried at public expense, apart from those whom their own people had buried—and what burial was there except to throw the corpses from the wall? After him, many men of no mean standing fled to Titus and reported that six hundred thousand dead had been counted as they were carried out through the gates. But the number of corpses which could not be carried out because of the countless multitude of the poor, and were packed into very large houses and spaces in various buildings, was beyond reckoning. And the evils still went on growing, though they had already surpassed the limit of all that had gone before. The siege was still savage, the war grievous, though the Jews’ spirit now exceeded their strength. Above all, however, famine was more loathsome still: it lay in wait for beasts of burden as they emptied their bowels and searched through old cattle dung, so that what was horrible to see became food for the hungry.

There was a pitiable mass of unburied bodies, and the ground itself was covered with corpses over a wide circuit. Everything before the walls was filled: a terrible sight, a grievous horror, a pestilential stench which distinguished neither victors nor vanquished, harmful to both alike and a greater hindrance to the Romans, who had to tread upon the fallen remains with bloodstained feet. The land itself lay waste, all the trees having been cut down to be carried away for the necessary use of the soldiers and their engines. For nearly thirteen miles around the city, far and wide the ground was desolate and the soil stripped of growing things. All that tract outside the walls had once offered a pleasing sight, with green groves, gardens breathing the scent of flowers, varied orchards and suburban estates. If anyone saw it afterwards, the stranger groaned, the inhabitant did not recognise it; returning to the place of his birth, though he was there in person, he sought his homeland.

With the siege banks, shelters and other siege engines rebuilt, the fury of war was renewed, and the efforts of both sides converged, as it were, upon putting the final touch to the work. For the whole contest was at stake: the Romans would have to lift the siege if the banks or rams were burnt, since the lack of woodland left them no means of rebuilding; and the destruction of their homeland threatened the Jews if they yielded in battle, as the battered walls would give way under the renewed blows of the rams.

The Jews therefore advanced with torches, so fierce that they meant to scatter fire upon the engines and break the siege, as though the Roman army would yield to them. But strength already exhausted by hunger and shattered fortunes denied them their former successes. Their resources had failed; their boldness remained. The Romans, by contrast, felt all the greater shame at the prospect of having victory snatched from their hands by men drawing their last breath from hunger. Battle was therefore joined, and the leaders of the sedition, unequal to the fighting, were driven back and fled to the protection of the walls. But when John, attentive to his last means of defence, saw that the unstable walls would yield to repeated blows, he built an inner wall in the shape of the letter C. On the next day, therefore, a section of wall was torn apart, and the crash of the falling structure and the Roman army’s shout rang out together, as though the collapse of the wall had accomplished the city’s destruction. But when the sound of the cry over the city’s fall echoed back, the situation was reversed: the unexpected sight of the new wall extinguished the Romans’ joy, and the Jews’ boldness took its place because the danger was postponed.

Then Caesar began to exhort the army to regard that new wall as something to attack without any hesitation: its recent construction showed it to be weak and easily demolished. They need only dare to advance with courage; the fragments of the wall would afford a means of ascent, placing the Roman combatants on a level with the Jews fighting from above. And because he saw them hesitate at the difficulty of the task, he gathered the strongest men around him and fired them for battle with this speech.

“No one is unaware, my bravest fellow soldiers, that the end of every undertaking involves more trouble than its beginning, because completing a task once undertaken demands greater labour. A ship runs freely over the whole sea: even if the winds do not always blow from astern, the helmsman nevertheless sets the curves of the sails at an angle, and the sea is cleft without resistance. But when the harbour is reached, a favourable balance of breezes is necessary, and the ships’ entrance is confined within narrow bounds. Concern over danger is therefore greater where hope is near. For builders too, the beginnings of the foundations lie level, but the work on lofty roofs is arduous. And often, at the very point of finishing the work, the pitiable craftsman is cheated of his reward in wages, either crushed by the fall of the roof or betrayed by an unsteady footing, so that he falls to the ground below. What shall I say of the farmer, for whom preparations for harvest are more laborious than for sowing, and for the vintage than for pruning, and who must always fear greater dangers when the fruits are ripe? It is therefore nothing new if danger still awaits you in the very harbour where your course is to end, because we must climb by narrower paths to Antonia, so that, driving the adversaries from there, occupying the higher ground and stationed above the enemies’ heads, we may in a sense cut off their very breath. But this seems difficult to you, fellow soldiers. As though we had come together for play, not for war, in which men must either conquer or die! You should therefore have made your excuses then, when you were coming to battle to avenge the disaster of the Roman army and wash away the disgrace of a dishonoured soldiery. If in Nero’s time you thought the injury to the Roman name must be avenged, what should you wish to do with Vespasian as emperor? Let us wash away the stain of the previous reign, lest it cling to ours: Nero was expected to remove it through Vespasian, but Vespasian will have transferred it to himself through Titus unless we conquer. My father left us only the completion of victory to accomplish. Where are we retreating, disgraced and unavenged, abandoning victory after so much labour has been poured out in vain, as though deserting military service were not a lesser crime than deserting victory? For the former is an act of fear, the latter of betrayal. But you think it dangerous to descend upon the enemy and make the wall resound with arms, as though nature herself demanded womanly deeds from us, not manly ones—nature who poured the breath of life into us for this very reason, that we might gladly pour it out for glory. To what, then, but the greatest deeds should a warrior be exhorted by his commander? For exhortation to an ordinary task brings shame not only upon those addressed but also upon those addressing them, by demanding what is owed of one’s own accord. That is what a soldier ought to offer of himself. And yet what immoderate demand do I make of you? Is it not better to die through valour than to live for disgrace? A Jew has often charged into the midst of the Roman lines and fearlessly flung himself into the enemy’s formations, not in hope of victory but to give proof of courage and display glory. You, whom no one on land or sea has yet resisted with impunity, for whom it is nothing new to conquer and a crime not to have conquered, with such support from heaven for victory—are you not ashamed that you have not even once rushed forward against the enemy, but waste your leisure under arms and stand ready for battle with idle minds, waiting for hunger to fight for us, so that, laid low by their own starvation rather than our swords, they may turn our triumphs into a reproach at which we must blush? Are you not ashamed, I say, stout fellow soldiers, conquerors of all nations, to hope for nothing from arms, nothing from strength, but only from the siege, and to wait until the enemy wastes away with disease and dies in his own bed? And what victory can there be without war? Everything is filled with corpses; hideous remains lie there, the bloodless relics of the dead, apart from those whom they themselves slaughtered among themselves with their own hands. Why do we fear those whom hunger, fire, brigandage and sedition have already destroyed? Why do we forsake divine benefits? For by whose will but God’s have they been dashed against their own weapons, deprived also of supplies of food, with no end to their domestic fury? I fear that we may now seem rebels against religion too, since we preserve for so long men faithless to both our religion and their own. But let it be so: let the war be savage and fearful. For why should I soothe you with the ease of the war? Let victory be uncertain and danger certain. Am I not speaking to men who know by human understanding that the courage of all living creatures is readier in danger than in less intense struggles? Wild beasts themselves, when they see that armed men have surrounded them, rush at them with greater force to open a way for themselves by violence. And a serpent shaken out of its hiding place pours forth more deadly venom. There are even creatures harmless by nature that are nevertheless strong enough to do harm when they themselves are in danger. Deer have their own weapons if anyone confronts them, and repel death with their horns; little bees, when hurt, have their own bites. But why speak of warriors before Romans, when that Leonidas, born in Sparta, about to fight against the countless army of the Persians, said, ‘Let us dine on earth, for we shall sup in the underworld’? These words had such power among the Greeks that no one withdrew, not only from those three hundred Spartan men whom he himself commanded—apart from one, whom no one afterwards welcomed as a survivor—but also from the others who had gone out to fight with them, except those whom Leonidas rejected as unworthy of so great a battle. What shall I say of entire Roman legions? Cato, champion of Roman eloquence and an honest interpreter of truth, asserted that they went joyfully into a battle from which they did not think they would return, and that all gladly fell rather than change their resolve. Blessed were they, none of whom announced the enemy’s victory to his own people by fleeing. Of the three hundred Spartans, however, at least one escaped, and they fought in a narrow place to avoid being surrounded. Of the Roman legions, no one chose the inheritance of life, but all that of death. You are their descendants, if by contempt for dangers, as glorious offspring, you do not disown your lineage of valour. For what brave man does not know that he is mortal and that an end to life has been appointed for all? How much better, then, to spend for the fatherland what you owe to nature, and exchange necessity for glory, neither living a life subject to the sighs of panting old age nor dreading the hazards of burning disease, when those brought low by age suffer daily weariness, while the souls of those who waste away in illness, their strength and senses failing together, are—as many hold—consigned to the grave along with the body! But no one doubts that the souls of warriors and the stoutest men, who have devoted themselves to death for their fatherland, their children and their religion, released by the sword from the bonds of this body, are received by that pure ethereal element, shining with the light of the stars, into heavenly dwellings, as guests, as it were, in the rest above. On earth too, some mark of favour or injury remains: oblivion hides those wasted by illness, while glory follows those who bear their breast against the enemy, if death meets them. To these rewards I invite you, fellow soldiers: let us go against the enemy whom we hold shut in, and climb onto the wall over the ruins of the stronger wall, which provide us with a kind of siege bank and reach the level of the lower wall. Whoever bears before him the banner of valour and climbs onto the wall first, or second, or third, or as a companion to many, will by no means depart without receiving a rich gift from me, although there is no greater reward than the glory of courage, which is also very often safer. For as soon as any man most confident in spirit and strength has climbed up, those who were resisting will flee, or withdraw to lower ground, or hide in their lurking places. Thus what we now seek at the greatest peril, stationed below, will follow without great labour: the enemy will be cast down and the war brought to an end.”

Titus had scarcely finished speaking when Sabinus, a distinguished warrior among the men of Syria, offered himself. Standing before Caesar, he said that he obeyed his commands and was ready for the ascent. He wished for success so that he might please Caesar. If good fortune deserted him, nothing would happen to him contrary to his expectation, since by his own judgement he had chosen to die for Caesar. Having said this, he extended his left arm and raised his shield above his head; brandishing his sword in his right hand, he rose to arms with such tremendous vigour that anyone would have failed to recognise the man whom, a little before, he had thought contemptible for his slight physique, on suddenly seeing him advance against the enemy and stretch himself up, threatening foes and walls alike, as though already towering above them he fought against men beneath him and shook the wall with his hand. Eleven men followed him, eager to imitate him but unequal to keeping up with him. The Jews resisted from the wall with javelins, stones and arrows, and whatever weapon each man’s hand found was thrown down upon Sabinus. But he, undaunted, ran swiftly up the bank of rubble and, taking his stand on its summit, drove the enemy back, as each man nearest him feared the danger. But as he raised himself and balanced his weight onto the wall, intent upon the enemy and confident of victory, he slipped and fell upon his face with a great crash. At this the Jews turned back and began to press the fallen man with missiles. Resting on his knee and protecting himself with his shield, he defended himself from wounds as long as he could, and did not leave unhurt anyone whom he found nearby. At last, however, pierced with wounds, he gave up his life before he gave up the fight, and was neither driven from his footing nor thrown from the wall until he was dead. Three others were also killed. The remaining eight, though half-dead, were rescued from destruction by the others.

Yet Sabinus’s death did not terrify the rest, but spurred them on. For twenty Roman men serving on watch wished to make up by the achievement of a deed for having been forestalled by Sabinus’s zeal. They formed a great and memorable plan: they would call to them the standard-bearer of the fifth legion, two cavalrymen whom they thought especially ready, and one trumpeter, and at the fifth hour of the night silently climb the banks of ruined wall to the heights, kill the guards and occupy the wall of Antonia. When this was done, the trumpet rang out more terribly than usual, so that the Jews, weary with toil and overcome by sleep, were suddenly thrown into confusion, believing that everything was filled with enemies. They therefore began to flee before the truth of the matter was known. For the hazards of danger and the darkness of the night did not allow their numbers to be ascertained. On hearing the blast of the trumpet, Caesar ordered the army to arm itself; he himself with chosen men was the first to climb onto the wall, to help his own men and hinder the enemy. Day broke, and already Caesar, visible on the wall, was exhorting his men. Some were raised onto the wall by their comrades’ hands; others entered the city through the tunnel which John had dug to undermine the Roman siege banks. The faithless men’s own faithlessness was turned to their destruction. Cut off on every side, they withdrew into the temple. The Romans wished to burst in there too, but were checked by the narrow space and repelled by arms. A fierce battle took place in the vestibule, and the fighting was now hand to hand with swords, no longer with javelins or arrows: hand dealt wounds, sword fell upon sword, blow upon blow. The assailant was drenched in the blood of the slain, so that he rather seemed to have been struck. The fury of war ruled in the temple itself. The pavements swam with blood. The groans of the dying and the shouts of the victors resounded without order or measure. The hope of finishing the contest had fired the Romans; the final destruction of their homeland had stripped the Jews of fear of death. The former fed their valour on the resources of glory; the latter, despairing of safety, poured out their whole provision of valour and kept nothing in reserve.

Julian too attempted a most glorious deed. He was a centurion, a man mighty in arms, who had come from the province of Bithynia but was accustomed to Roman discipline, practised in war and renowned for his honourable military service. As he stood beside Caesar, he saw the Romans turned back, since the Jews were superior in numbers and the Romans present were still fewer. Suddenly he rushed out of Antonia and turned back the pursuers. They did not dare to resist the very appearance of this outstanding man and the proud authority of a valour beyond human form, so that Caesar himself marvelled. O the varied and uncertain game of war, as it were, which, like a throw of dice, so often plays with unforeseen outcomes by chance rather than valour, supplying new endings! For here too there are throws, not indeed of dice but of arrows and many other weapons, and of stones, by which the victor is often laid low by another’s blow; and while he seizes another’s spoils, he is himself despoiled. So it was with this Julian, who pressed upon the enemies’ backs, killing some and penning them within an enclosure. Made less cautious by his very eagerness, he wore shoes studded with nails, as soldiers do, and did not consider that the ground was paved with polished stone and required caution. Instead, as though fighting in an open field, he slipped heedlessly and made a tremendous crash as he fell; nor could he rise, stretched upon the slippery ground. Yet, supporting himself on his knee, he repelled the returning enemy, killing those who approached and avoiding as far as he could those who threw missiles. But wearied and overwhelmed by their very numbers, alone though he was, since no one dared to enter so great a danger, he nevertheless fell fighting stoutly, neither contemptible nor unavenged. Certainly, in my judgement, he did not deserve such an end, that a man’s valour so great should be betrayed in this way. But prudence has very great power in war: ever keen and discerning, it foresees the hazards of uncertainty. Alone he rushed out of Antonia, alone he charged into the enemy’s ranks, alone he plunged into the fighting, alone he compelled the Jews to return into the temple. I fear that this was what harmed him most, because those faithless to God should have been driven out of the temple. Thus, once fallen, he found no remedy. Titus watched him winning with joy, in danger with immense grief; he wished to help him, but was far away. His men held him back, because in a soldier one man’s fate is at stake, in a commander everyone’s. The example showed the danger and taught Caesar what to avoid rather than imitate. Indeed, his comrades were so dismayed and his adversaries so elated that even Julian’s body came into the enemies’ possession, as though they still feared him even dead if he were returned to the Romans. Once Julian was killed, the rest yielded easily. For the troops had not yet come up, and the occasion of his death had increased the Jews’ valour. Most ready in that battle to repel the Romans were Alexas and Gyptheus, John’s fellow conspirators, who were champions of his faction, and from Simon’s side Melchius and Jacob, the commander of the Idumaeans, distinguished warriors. Simon and Judas, sons of Ari, men of the third faction, likewise exerted themselves. With their forces joined, they drove the Romans back and shut them within Antonia.

Titus, on the other hand, considered the narrow confines of Antonia a hindrance rather than a defence, and ordered its fortification to be demolished to the foundations, so that a path to the enemy might be opened for those about to engage. Learning that the celebration of the Jews’ festival days was approaching, he ordered Josephus to interpret in Hebrew what he himself would say. He asked what cursed reasoning could persuade John to provoke the Romans to destroy the temple. If he was confident in his valour, he should choose another place to fight and advance there, provided he spared the city, did not defile the temple and did not prevent the sacrifices of the festival days. He should leave behind those whom he judged fit for the sacrificial ministries and give proof of his courage wherever he wished outside the city and temple: Caesar’s soldiers would not fail to meet him. Against his will, Caesar was being forced to overthrow the whole city, whose remains he wished to preserve, if John would allow it. Torches threatened the temple, not because the Romans were hurrying to burn it, but to draw the instigators of war out of it. If they believed themselves defeated, they should surrender; or, if they hoped to be victorious, they should not withdraw within the enclosures but defend themselves in the open field, so that the temple might be rescued from the flames already licking it and be free for rites of purification.

As Josephus interpreted this to the Jews, the silent crowd approved what they heard in silence, but feared to disclose their opinion. John replied that there was no more excellent sacrifice to God than for men consecrated to God to lay down their lives for their altars, their hearths and their temple. Therefore, if need be, he would gladly fall for freedom; nevertheless, he hoped that the city of God could not suffer destruction. At this Titus said: “Rightly, then, do you keep the city pure for God and the sanctuary undefiled by killing citizens, slaying the innocent and destroying priests! The divine is not appeased by such outrages, but offended. You have deprived your God of the worship of his sacrifices. If someone denied you food, John, you would seek him out; your God’s victims are not sacrificed to him, his gifts are not rendered, men are slaughtered, and do you still think that God assists you? Indeed, so the deeds teach, so the mass of the slain and the heaps of your calamities bear witness. Who could see these things without groaning? Nor would I blame you for fighting for your homeland if I did not wish to spare it, if I did not wish to preserve your homeland or your temple. For Carthage was not worthy of restoration—there is no Hebrew Hannibal to fear, such as the one who had subdued half the Roman world—and yet even Carthage was restored, though it had sustained its citizens’ rebellious spirits until its own destruction. On my faith I pledge to you that all these things will be safe; I promise you pardon and survival, not as a reward for crime but as a ransom for the city, that I may buy from you the preservation of buildings about to perish. Cease, I warn you, to disturb the purpose of Roman devotion by your brigandage. Jerusalem will not be feared so greatly as to be destroyed, when Antioch, stronger in resources, was preserved. Certainly your Jeconiah trusted even the Persians and left the city, entrusting himself and his closest kin to barbarian fury lest the city be overthrown on his account. You celebrate his memory, as your own people affirm; Josephus is here to speak for him and to witness the celebration with which you honour the man who offered himself to captivity for his homeland. Even the barbarian Persian preserved him; I, however, pledge you impunity. Certainly Josephus too took up arms against the Romans: trust the promise of which we have already given an example. We give you Josephus as surety for our pledge—or rather, we have already given him, since we preserved him. Let him speak in your ancestral tongue and bind himself by the rite you customarily use. I am not ashamed to seek a surety and give a guarantor, lest I show myself a destroyer when I wish to spare.” At this Josephus wept, entreated John, lamented the condition of his homeland, implored him in tearful speech and appealed to him as a fellow citizen, though more obstinate than the rest. He testified that by the grace of almighty God John would be safe with his people, if only he ceased to rouse the Roman soldiery to overthrow the city. When he could not bend him, he said: “It is no wonder, John, that you persist until your homeland’s destruction, since divine protection has already abandoned it. But it is a wonder that you do not believe it will perish, when you have read the prophetic books in which the destruction of our homeland was announced to us and its rebuilt edifices foretold to be destroyed again by the Roman army. For what else does Daniel cry out? He prophesied not what had already happened, but what was to come. What is the abomination of desolation which he proclaimed would come with the arrival of the Romans, if not this which now threatens us? What is that oracle, often recalled by our people and pronounced by the highest God, that the city would perish to its foundations when a fellow tribesman was killed by the hands of citizens, if not what we now see fulfilled? And perhaps, because it is no longer pleasing that the temple should be defended, stained as it is with forbidden blood, it is pleasing that it should be cleansed by fire.”

Josephus finished speaking, but John was moved by no tears and bent by no promises. God had long been pressing upon their faithless minds, ever since they had stained themselves with the impious murder of kin by crucifying Christ Jesus. This is he whose death is the Jews’ destruction, born of Mary, who came to his own and his own did not receive him. For when did the Jews not kill their own people? Did they not kill the son of their own Saul? Naboth the prophet was certainly stoned by his own people. Jezebel was Jewish, she who gave the command to the Jewish elders who carried it out; Ahab was Jewish, he who became the cause of Naboth’s death. How many other citizens were killed by citizens! And yet the city long remained intact, though destroyed by the Babylonians after countless years, but restored afterwards. This is the final destruction, after which the temple cannot be restored, because by their crimes they have turned away the guardian of the temple, the arbiter of its restoration.

Such feeling on Caesar’s part and his repeated address changed the minds of some, who were able to slip away and join the Romans. The rest were held back by fear of the danger threatened by the brigands; perhaps there was also a certain inclination of their minds that prevented more from being rescued from the coming destruction. Caesar welcomed those who fled to him with goodwill, since among them were priestly men with their sons and others of more distinguished families. Promising them safety for their lives and the right to their possessions, he sent them to the city called Gophna, lest any offence arise from differing rites and diversity of worship. Those who remained in the city resisting turned this into evidence of murder, alleging that they had been killed, either because such a suspicion had arisen or because someone had fabricated it deceitfully to prevent more from slipping away.

On learning this, Titus recalled them and ordered them to go round near the walls with Josephus, so that they might be recognised by their own people. With tears and great groaning they lamented not their own misfortunes but the destruction of their homeland and temple, and begged their fellow citizens to trust Caesar’s faith and rescue the temple from the fire prepared for it. Nothing contrary to the law had been commanded of them, nothing had been taken from their freedom. The others should yield and themselves experience the clemency of the Romans, whose unconquerable valour they had experienced.

While they were making these pitiable lamentations, they were driven away by their own people, and war blazed up. The Jews rushed forward and rashly burst into the very inner sanctuaries; they occupied every recess, every place inaccessible to men who had no share in the sacred rites. The Romans too prepared for battle. The prohibitions of the fathers were violated through the necessity of war, yet with greater reverence on the Romans’ part than on that of their own people. The Gentiles looked upon the temple with fear; the Jews approached it with fury and recklessness, and, with their hands wet with human blood, touched the very altars.

Titus, however, still holding to his purpose, addressed John and declared that he was being drawn against his will to the destruction of the city and temple. He said to him: “What do those letters engraved before the temple doors mean, John? Do they not signify that no one unless consecrated should approach the temple? Why those barriers before the temple? Are they not there to prevent everyone from looking freely within, so that knowledge of the secrets is open only to the initiated, and the view is free to those whose entry is lawful? You exclude foreigners from the sight, yet force their approach. You write that no stranger is to enter, no foreigner to come within, yet you shed foreign blood inside the temple and stain your altars with the blood of strangers and citizens alike. I testify that your violation of what is yours comes from your own transgression, not our attack. I, a stranger, do not demand it; rather, I solemnly declare that if you are willing to leave, the temple will be safe, no Roman will lay hostile hands upon it, and none of your sacrifices will be violated. I shall preserve the temple for you, even if you are unwilling. For the observance of sacred rites differs, but buildings serve a common use. What belonged to worship has departed from you; what belongs to the building has remained for the victors.”

When Caesar saw that not even these words, conveyed through Josephus, could recall the faction leaders—for they now thought that so frequent an appeal to desist showed lack of confidence rather than devotion—he returned unwillingly to the necessity of battle. He ordered the Romans to be ready, but because the narrow space impeded so great a multitude, he assigned a thousand warriors each to thirty chosen men. For the dense obstructions of the buildings would not admit the whole army. He too wished to descend with them, but his men held him back, lest he expose himself to danger in the confined space, often at night as well, when it was necessary to counter the guile of those lying in ambush. He would achieve more by being present as a spectator of the battle, since each man would think he must fight more readily when he was to fight under Caesar’s eyes. For everything being done around the temple could be seen from above, from Antonia’s position, as in a theatre. Won over to this view, Caesar entrusted the task to Cerealis: he was to fall upon the Jews posted around the temple at the ninth hour of the night. He exhorted the rest to press eagerly into the contest; he too would not fail to recognise the combatants’ deserts, as from above he judged the battle, a witness to each man’s cowardice or an arbiter of his valour.

Cerealis arrived promptly at the appointed time, but found the guards awake. Battle was joined, for those stationed inside the temple were not sleeping either, and when the men on watch engaged, the rest readily prepared for war. The Romans pressed forward in a dense formation. The Jews, relying upon enclosures and narrow passages to avoid being surrounded, ran in different directions, so that they were more often endangered by their own men, since they were not recognised in the darkness and were frequently run through by their comrades, who thought them enemies. For who could distinguish at night whether he met a comrade or an enemy, when questioning took too long, caution was useful and striking first prudent? And an error that wounded another was a more tolerable consequence of a mistake than neglecting one’s own danger where an enemy was feared. Thus throughout the night the Jews laboured under a twofold peril, either what the enemy inflicted or what a comrade did in error; nor were they afflicted with less destruction by day. At night there was more danger from their own men; by day the Romans attacked more fiercely, urged on, even in silence, by Titus, who watched the whole contest. They fought fiercely until the fifth hour, the Jews too battling stoutly, so that neither side yielded its ground.

While they fought these battles with one another, everything with which Herod had fortified the stronghold called Antonia was brought down to the very foundations in the space of seven days. The road leading to the temple was made wider, so that it would not only allow soldiers to run along it, but also provide as much space as was needed for setting up defences and heaping up siege banks, from which even the highest roofs of the temple could be struck. While the Romans were busily occupied with this, the Jews, pressed by unbearable hunger, began to lie in wait for the Romans’ beasts of burden. If anyone had let a warhorse loose to graze, or a mule needed to ease the burden of transport, they seized it and drove it away. Their food was obtained not only at the Romans’ expense but also to the disgrace of their military service. Caesar at once put an end to the reproach of such negligence by prescribing death as its penalty. Yet he did not check the guile of their obstinacy.

For, cut off from the food which this kind of plunder supplied to the starving, they sought help from vegetation and devised a plan to destroy the wall which Titus had drawn around the city boundary. This would give them greater freedom to range about and seek tree roots and fodder, for the circuit of the wall had shut them in like a prison, and they now had nothing with which to relieve their hunger. They therefore crept out in a sudden sortie and fell upon the men posted before the Mount of Olives. These did not fail in their assigned duty, but summoned others from the remaining fortified camps or towers with a trumpet blast to join the battle. A fierce struggle began at the outset, as shame drove the one side and hunger the other with a cruel and compelling command. But as the Romans converged, the Jews were repelled and driven back towards their city walls. Then one of the cavalry troop—his name was Pedanius—spurred his horse, stretched out his right hand and, leaning down a little, lifted up one of the fleeing Jews. He carried him captive to Caesar and, victorious with his glorious plunder, cast him down alive at Caesar’s feet, as an eagle does a little hare or a hawk a coot. Titus was greatly delighted by this and dismissed him with praise and honour.

The porticoes surrounding the temple were already burning. Everywhere there was grief, everywhere death; outside there was war, within there was fire as well as war. Yet the Jews were not broken in spirit. They thought that whatever they did without guile or insolence was lost to vengeance. Since they could no longer do otherwise, they provoked the Romans to hasten their destruction.

A certain Jonathan, small in body and more deserving of contempt, challenged the Romans beside John’s tomb, inviting anyone who wished to decide the matter with him in single combat. Some despised the man’s small stature; others scorned to fight someone whom they would shortly have as a captive. Others reflected that fighting men who, at the last extremity of survival, sought vengeance through mere rashness rather than any courage was a dangerous contest: there would be no glory in defeating a man already close to destruction, and very great disgrace if some mishap marred the common victory. This most insolent man vaunted himself and charged the victors with fear, pouring out abuse: the Romans relied on others’ help, not on their own strength, and the Jews had been afflicted by domestic seditions, not by an enemy’s warfare. Among the Roman soldiers was a man named Pudens. Stung by these empty insults, he rashly attended to his shame and neglected his safety. Made incautious by his very indignation, he exposed himself to a wound and, struck down to the ground, brought shame upon his comrades and left Jonathan cause both for exultation and for death. For Jonathan, delighted by the success of the contest and making a show of triumph, danced and exulted, brandishing his shield and sword in sport. He thus roused the centurion Priscus to wound him. Priscus could not endure his proud and swollen boasts and pierced him with an arrow as victory made him heedless. Laid low by this, Jonathan taught that no one should exult senselessly in battle, where the condition of victor and vanquished is uncertain until the war is ended.

But within the city, when they saw the enemy inside the walls, towering on the highest siege banks and threatening all the fortifications, they feared that the danger would advance inwards like a wound into the body. They cut through the northern portico at the point where it joined Antonia, lest the enemy ascend by it to the upper parts of the temple or, from above, press upon those stationed below. They cut down everything nearby, lest fires ravaging the buildings beside the temple consume the temple itself, and burned the parts they had cut off. Thus they were the first to begin what they feared from the enemy.

They also prepared Solomon’s portico for a deception, filling the interior of its roof with pitch and bitumen hidden within the vault of the upper roof. Pretending that they wished to defend it and repeatedly assailing the enemy, they drew the Romans on and stirred them up against themselves. The Romans brought up ladders and made for the top of the portico. The Jews gradually gave ground so that more Romans would climb up. The Romans competed in clambering up; the more prudent, however, suspected a trick and took care, while the multitude, intent on victory, pressed ahead. When the moment seemed ripe for the deception, with very many men caught as though in nets, fire was put to the inner vaults. Fed by pitch, bitumen and the other fuel, it spread through the whole portico. Flames surrounded the victorious Romans, leaving them neither the means to stand their ground nor a way to flee. They could not discover what to do. Titus watched his men in peril, angry indeed that they had climbed up without orders, but pitying them because they were perishing as victors. Many flung themselves down; yet, after escaping the fire, they died with broken legs and shattered bodies. It was more wretched still if they survived crippled. Caesar wished to help but could not. Nevertheless he urged those nearby and cried out that they should come to their comrades’ aid. They took these cries and this grief of Caesar as their final consolation. This was provision for their journey as they died; consoled by it as by a lofty tomb, they hastened to death, because they would be laid to rest in Caesar’s inward parts. The lives of those whose glory lived on would not perish: they were dying for Caesar and leaving triumph as their inheritance. Thus some were surrounded by the fires, others overtaken by them; nor was the enemy far away, ready to strike anyone fleeing the flames.

Longus, however, a man of outstanding valour, was urged by the Jews to entrust himself to them, with a promise of safety. He preferred to run himself through with his sword rather than stain the courage of his Roman character with disgrace. Artorius, for his part, very cunningly called loudly to Lucius, saying: “You will be my heir if you catch me as I fall.” The pitiable man ran beneath him as he fell and transferred to himself the death of the man who was about to die. Truly a testament of war, written not in ink but in blood, not on paper but on a sword’s point, which sent the heir ahead! A great ingenuity indeed, to find a willing substitute in death. The portico was therefore burned as far as the tower which John, when he was waging war against Simon, had built above the gates of the royal house that King Hezekiah had constructed for his own dwelling. The Jews themselves demolished the remaining part of it. On the following day the Romans also burned the whole northern portico as far as the eastern portico. For, by laying hands upon their own buildings, they taught the Romans not to spare those of others.

The face of the temple was now bare, and the people’s hunger was savage. They lay in wait for one another, each seeking to snatch food from another. Wherever food was suspected, war was fought among members of the same household for it. Those most dearly loved were killed; the dead were searched, lest food be hidden within their clothing. Some were thought to be pretending to be dead, so that they would not be suspected, as living people, of possessing any food. But even the living could neither discharge the functions of life nor feign death. Instead, with mouths open like rabid dogs, catching breaths of air, they wandered here and there with want as their guide. Often, too, they returned like drunken people to the same dwellings, to search again the places they had left empty. When they found no other relief for their hunger, they stripped the leather from shields, so that what did not protect them might feed them. They chewed footwear, unashamed to take into their mouths and lick with their tongues what had been removed from their feet. Old straw, too, which had long ago been thrown away, was sought with no slight eagerness; anyone who found some exchanged it for a great price.

How shall I begin to tell of Mary’s deed, at which the mind of any barbarous and impious person would shudder? She was one of the wealthy women of the region of Peraea, which lies beyond the Jordan. When the terror of war arose, she had withdrawn with the others into the city of Jerusalem to be safer. She had also brought her wealth there, and the faction leaders competed in seizing it. Even any food she had bought was torn from her hands. The villains harried her; she uttered dreadful curses and wished to die, but could find no one to strike her down. They preferred to torment her longer and afflict her more grievously rather than destroy her quickly. They thought that as long as she lived there would be plunder. Everything had now failed, and, accustomed to delicacies, she could not soften coarse straw or hard hides. Savage hunger poured into her innermost marrow, embittered her humours and agitated her mind. The woman had a little infant whom she had borne. Roused by his crying, seeing herself and her little one wasting away together, overcome by such horrors and unequal to so dreadful a calamity, she lost her affection. Forgetting the practice of a mother’s natural devotion, she swallowed her grief and took on fury. Turning towards the little one, now forgetful of being a mother and raging in mind, she spoke thus: “What shall I do for you, little one, what shall I do for you? Everything around you is savage: war, hunger, fires, brigands, ruins. To whom shall I entrust you as I die, or to whom shall I leave you, so tiny? I had hoped that, if you grew up, you would feed me, your mother, or bury me when I died; or at least that, if you died before me, I would enclose you in a precious tomb with my own hands. What shall I do in my misery? I see no means of life for you or me. Everything has been torn from us; for whom shall I preserve you? Or in what tomb shall I lay you, so that you are not prey for dogs, birds or wild beasts? Everything, I say, has been torn from us. Yet even so, my sweet one, you can feed your mother; your hands are fit for food. O your entrails, sweet to me, your delightful limbs, before hunger consumes you altogether, give back to your mother what you received; return to that natural hiding place. In the dwelling where you took on breath, a tomb is being prepared for you when dead. I myself shall embrace the one I bore, I myself shall cover him with kisses. Let the force of necessity have what the impatience of love has, so that I myself may devour my own limbs with bites that are not feigned but pressed home. Be food, then, for me, madness for the brigands and a tale for the living, the one thing still lacking to our calamities. What would you do, my son, if you too had a son? We have done what belonged to devotion; let us do what hunger urges. Yet your case is better, with some appearance of devotion, since it is more bearable that you should give your mother food from your entrails than that your mother can either kill or devour you.” Saying this, she turned her face away and plunged in the sword. Cutting her son into pieces, she set him on the fire, ate part and covered part, lest anyone come upon her.

But the smell of the roasting reached the leaders of the sedition. At once, following the smell, they entered the woman’s lodging and threatened her with death because she had dared to eat while they were fasting and to exclude them from the food she had found. But she said: “I have kept your portion for you; I have not been greedy or inhuman. Do not be angry: you too have something to eat. I have prepared food for you from my own entrails. Sit down quickly; I shall set the table. You will have cause to marvel at my service and to judge that you have never found such affection in any woman, who would not deprive you even of the pleasure of her sweet son.” As she spoke, she uncovered the scorched limbs and offered them to be eaten, with this exhortation: “This is my meal, this your portion. Look carefully, lest I have cheated you. Here is one hand of the boy, here his foot, here half the rest of his body. Lest you think him someone else’s, he is my son; lest you suppose it another’s work, I did it, I carefully divided it: what I should eat for myself, what I should keep for you. Never have you been sweeter to me, my son. I owe it to you that I still live. Your sweetness has kept my soul within me and postponed the day of death for your wretched mother. You have helped me in hunger, you are the gift of my last old age, you the restrainer of murderers. They came to kill; they have become guests. They too will have something to owe you when they have taken my feast. But why do you step back, why do you shudder in spirit? Why do you not feast on what I, his mother, have prepared? What has sated his mother can please you too. I am no longer hungry now that my son has fed me; I am abundantly satisfied, I know no hunger. Taste and see that my son is sweet. Do not become softer than a mother, weaker than a woman. Or if you are merciful amid the wounding and do not accept my victim but turn away from my whole burnt offering, I shall complete my sacrifice and eat what remains. Take care lest it be a reproach to you that a woman has been found stronger than you, to consume the feast of men. I indeed prepared such a feast, but you made a mother feast in this way. Affection held me too, but necessity prevailed.”

The enormity of so great a crime at once filled the whole city. Each person shuddered as though the serving of this feast of the murder of kin were set before his eyes. After this, even the instigators of the sedition began to inspect the food they stole, lest they find such fare and take it unawares. Everyone began to fear living long and to wish to die. The horror of this deed also reached the Romans, for very many, terrified by it, fled to the enemy.

On learning this, Caesar cursed the pollution of the unhappy land and, raising his hands to heaven, made this declaration: “We have indeed come to war, but we are not fighting human beings. We contend against all the rage of beasts and wild animals—why do I speak of creatures with feeling? Against all the savagery of rocks. Wild beasts love their offspring, which they nourish even in their own hunger; those that feed upon the bodies of others abstain from the carcasses of beasts like themselves. This exceeds every cruelty: that a mother has devoured the limbs she bore. I am clean of this pollution and declare myself free of it before you, whatever power you are in heaven. You know, you surely know that with heartfelt affection I often offered peace and, what I am not ashamed as victor to say, entreated them. I wished to spare even the authors of such monstrosities, to spare the people, to preserve the city. But what was I to do with those who resisted, what was I to do with those who raged against their own people? Often, after laying down arms, I returned to war because they would not desist from slaughtering their own, so that I might free the besieged, not destroy them. They themselves often urged us from the walls to fight, lest they perish more grievously at their own people’s hands. What sort of citizens are these, for whom an enemy is a remedy? I had indeed heard that this people’s ferocity was unbearable, that they roused themselves to every insolence through incredible beliefs: that they drew their lineage from heaven, first assumed bodily form there, had been inhabitants of heaven, had descended to cultivate the earth and returned from earth to heaven; that they had crossed seas dry-shod, that the waves of the sea had fled before them, that the Jordan’s streams had turned and run back to their source; that the sun had stood still so that they might defeat their enemies without the hindrance of night; that their people had been snatched up to heaven in fiery chariots, that the powers of heaven had fought for them, and that, while they were absent, all the enemy’s forces had been routed, and victory won while they slept. I had learned these things, but I thought that they boasted of divine benefits bestowed upon them, not that they would carry their audacity so far as to suppose that they could not be defeated even by the Romans. I therefore recognise that our battle is with those who believe themselves invincible, who boast that they are survivors of the flood, heirs of rivers, guests of the earth, travellers over the sea, climbers into the heavens, for whom water is a wall, air a road and heaven a dwelling, to whom flames yield and whom bonds do not hold. When they thirst, rock dissolves and pours itself out as drink; when they hunger, heaven opens, food is sent, the camp is filled with birds’ flesh, and man eats the bread of angels. Liquids are made solid, bitter things grow sweet, the sun is halted, darkness is illuminated. Finally, what can surpass this? When can audacity fail those who, as they say, live when dead and are raised again when buried? It is also widely believed that these people have conspired against divine powers, and their punishment is evidence. Lands burn even today because of their inhabitants’ impiety, and a chasm in the ground has swallowed very many of these people too. How long, then, do we linger in these places, where even the earth collapses? We have seen a dead sea; we have also seen the dead produce of the land, parched soil, empty semblances of green fruits, beauty outside and ashes within. Who can doubt that we are among the dead below, where even the elements themselves die? Indeed, among them even natural devotion, which usually lives on after death, has died, and so has the reverence that outlives the dead. For who does not love his parents even when dead? Who does not love even his lost sons and hold them still as his children? Affection remains even if the child has died; the name endures, the bond of nature does not fall away. Yet among these people a mother does not recognise even her living son, does not hear him calling or pity him crying, and lays murderous hands upon her child for the accursed food of a single hour. But why do I denounce this as something new, when they reckon the beginnings of their race from the murder of a brother? They praise the faith of Abraham himself, whom they call their father, the author of their teaching and the founder of their worship, chiefly because he thought that not even his son should be spared, brought him to the altar like a victim and did not hesitate to offer him as a whole burnt offering. I do not condemn devotion, but I ask for family devotion. They say that another of their people, victorious, also vowed to sacrifice to his god whatever first met him on his return home; that when he returned his daughter met him, and he laid hands upon her. They tell many other examples of this kind. What sort of nation is this, which assigns the killing of a human being to religion and thinks the murder of kin a sacrifice? What god could demand this, or what sort of priest could offer it? Indeed, they say that the earlier man, as the more prudent, did not do it but wished to, while the latter, as the less wise, persisted. Let them have their rites: yet they are hard people, among whom killing sons is a discipline; unhappy the city in which there is such a workshop, such a service. Let its own ruins cover and conceal it, so that the sun may not see this pollution of the world itself, nor the host of stars behold it; lest the breaths of air be defiled, let that purifying fire arise as well. We thought the feast of Thyestes a fable; we see the crime, we behold a truth more atrocious than tragedy. There it was the stronger sex and another’s offspring; here it is a woman whose own offspring became her food. There it was another’s deceit, here her own will. He grieved, she exulted. Food worthy of such men, who by their obstinacy in war have brought their women to such a feast!
