I indeed think that, afflicted by such bitter evils, they are now mad and have lost their minds, since they do not perceive these things. Let us therefore finish the war more quickly. Since they cannot be reformed, let us press upon them more urgently, so that we may flee the dying waters and collapsing lands of these regions.”

Having said this, he ordered battering rams to be brought against the temple, but their powerful blows achieved nothing. Nevertheless, very many, terrified, fled to Caesar from among the leaders of the seditions themselves. Titus hesitated to receive them, since they were driven by necessity rather than following his promise, but faith tempered his anger. Yet he did not hold them in the same regard as the earlier deserters, and began to press his men more urgently, so that all the enemy might depart, struck with fear. But when they saw that the walls stood unharmed by the blows of the rams through their sheer mass, their audacity grew. Caesar, however, forestalled them by his ingenuity and ordered the doors covered with silver to be set on fire.

When fire was applied, the silver began to run down; then gradually the wood too began to burn, and thus an entrance opened into the inner portico. But Caesar, moved by pity lest the adjoining porticoes of the inner vestibule catch fire and the temple burn down, called the commanders of the army to council. He said that he was not contending with things without feeling or waging war upon buildings, which would benefit the victors if they were preserved unburned.

The commanders, however, maintained that the strength of the walls and the fortification of the temple would continue to encourage the Jews, who delighted in insolence. The roots of rebellion must be torn out altogether, lest their rashness break out afresh.

Caesar nevertheless deferred discussion of the plan until the following day. The Jews, however, thought they should pour forth, but the Romans, though fewer, locked their shields together and sustained the first attack. Yet their line wavered under the onrush of the countless multitude. Caesar therefore came close with the cavalry, easily trampling those he met, and turned back the hostile column. Encouraged by this, since part of the vestibules was now open,

he planned on the following day to break in upon the enemy with a larger force of his men and enter the temple. This would have saved the city from burning, had not the people’s perverse mind provoked the enemy’s flames against themselves. For Caesar ordered the masses of fire to be extinguished, lest they obstruct those about to break in. Seeing this, the Jews lay in wait for those wishing to extinguish the temple fires and, by killing some, inflamed the enemy. One of the Romans therefore found a half-burned piece of timber which had fallen from the roof and, with its fire blazing, applied it to the gate called Golden because its doors were covered with gold. The solid gold, at once melted by the flames, laid bare the wood, which was exposed to the fire as though its flank were uncovered. When the doors had burned through, the fire made its way into the temple’s inner sanctuary. The vestibules of its gate were already glowing. All who defended themselves within the temple’s fortifications were thrown into confusion and at once began to tremble. Their minds were already inclining to the belief that this was the day of destruction, because on that same day the temple had once been burned when the Babylonians attacked. It was the tenth day of the month of Lous, which they had long counted among the ill-fated days. The fire, raised aloft by the breath of the air, poured joy into the victors and grief worthy of so great a calamity into the vanquished.

A cry also arose from everyone, and not long afterwards a messenger informed Titus of the enemy’s destruction. He rushed out and, as loudly as he could, ordered the fires to be extinguished. But in the tumult there was neither a chance to hear nor a wish to spare, since the Roman soldiers burned with zeal for vengeance, and Caesar’s known mercy took away his men’s fear of disobedience. It would bring no punishment upon his own men when even enemies were pardoned. Yet Titus called back those he could with nod and hand, and commanded some to restrain the soldiers’ assaults. But with anger as their leader, they fed the fire and pressed upon the enemy, who, despairing of safety, now squandered themselves and spent themselves wholly upon dangers. Above all the lowly multitude were struck wherever anyone encountered them, since they were protected by no weapons and could neither ward off a wound nor return it.

Caesar therefore withdrew, exhausted by shouting, while the flame was still devouring the temple’s chambers. When these had burned through, it rushed furiously into the temple itself. At this sight very many were struck with terror; others plunged into the very fires, for their eyes could not endure their being preserved alive after the temple. Titus ran back again, wishing to look about and see what sort of building it was. Moved by its beauty, he acknowledged that it had surpassed the workmanship of their own temples. He marvelled at the size of the stones, the gleam of the metal, the elegance of the work and the charm of its beauty. He declared that the place’s renown was not undeservedly so great that people gathered there from everywhere, for so great a dwelling was believed to belong to none but the highest God. The honour with which even barbarian nations revered that temple and brought gifts added credibility to its religion. Yet its own people, plunderers of religion, were then seizing and squandering these gifts. The brigands fell upon everything that had been deposited by widows or orphans, as though vengeance were taken upon the victors if the Romans’ booty were diminished at all. Seeing the temple burn, they themselves set the other buildings on fire, lest any building survive the temple’s destruction, thinking it an act of religion if everything perished with the temple.

Yet the Jews still did not lay aside their faithlessness, which caused greater destruction. For, when the minds of many were inclining towards forming a column and surrendering to the Romans, a certain false prophet began to proclaim in his ecstasy that God’s divine protection would not fail his temple. As though by an oracle, he declared that God was calling the people to himself, that he still remained in his temple and would immediately drive back the enemy’s ranks and the blazing flames. Thus the wretched people, faithfully believing false deceptions, were slaughtered like cattle, without honour or use. Had they been willing to believe, they had clear signs of their impending destruction, by which they were warned, as though by distinct voices, that their end was at hand.

For nearly a year a comet blazed above the temple itself, displaying a certain likeness to fire and a sword and foretelling that the nation, kingdom and city itself would be laid waste by sword and fire. For what could the likeness of a sword foretell but war, and what could fire foretell but burning? It was seen before the people separated themselves from the Romans. During the days of Passover, on the eighth day of the month of Xanthicus, and on each night at about the ninth hour, the temple and its altar shone with such light that it was as though day had come. This lasted for about half an hour each day. The multitude interpreted it as a visible sign of the nation’s increase, and were thereby emboldened, as though the time to recover their freedom were at hand. The more prudent held the contrary opinion, because this kind of star usually foretells war. Let no one suppose that we have spoken things alien to our worship and teaching: first, because we are not establishing what seems true to us, but what happened, what opinions existed at that time, what the prudent thought and what the imprudent thought. Nor, when anything is said about the Jewish sect, should it seem that we have written as though we were setting them within the truth of their worship, rather than as those sent ahead in shadow and figure so that more perfect things might follow. For concerning signs in the stars we are also taught in the Gospel that there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars. They also asserted that a heifer, standing at the altar to be sacrificed, gave birth to a lamb in the middle of the temple during the very sacred celebrations we mentioned above. They said too that the eastern inner gate, heavy with solid bronze, which twenty men used to close with great labour in the evening and which was secured with iron bars, opened of itself on several nights and was afterwards closed by the guards only with difficulty. Very many also thought this a sign of good things to come, for whose entrance the gate was opened. The more discerning, however, said that the temple’s protection seemed to have been removed, so that everything within would be plundered by enemies: worship would go out, devastation come in, the throng of worshippers be emptied away and sacrifice destroyed. The reading teaches that this was also clearly signified earlier, when they crucified Christ Jesus. After many days, too, a figure of immeasurable size appeared, which very many people saw, as the Jews’ books have made known. Before sunset, chariots and armed battle lines were suddenly seen in the clouds, attacking the cities of all Judaea and its region. During the very solemnity of Pentecost, the priests entered the temple’s inner parts at night to celebrate the customary sacrifices. They reported that first they had felt a certain movement and heard a sound, and afterwards also heard a sudden voice cry: “We are departing from here.”

Jesus too, the son of Ananias, a countryman, went up to the temple four years before the Jewish people undertook the war, when the city was in complete peace and abundance and the feast of Tabernacles was being celebrated with solemn sacrifices. He began to cry: “A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and against the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and against brides, a voice against all the people.” He cried this out by night and by day. Disturbed by this, the leading men of the place seized him, shuddering at the terrible portent of his voice, and subjected him to many torments, so that at least under the affliction of pain he might cease to announce things so terrible and full of foreboding. But he was frightened by no fear, blows or graver threats into changing his practice or his cry. With the same persistence in warning and the same sequence of words, without inserting any plea, he continued unchanged, heedless of injury and unmoved in feeling. They thought this was no casual utterance, but was being expressed in an ecstasy of mind, as indeed it was, and brought him before the local judge, who at that time conducted public affairs there on behalf of the Romans. To probe the truth, the judge tore him with the most grievous punishments. The more Jesus persisted, the more violently the judge ordered him to be scourged, so that he might reveal any hidden signs of future disturbance he had learned. Yet he neither wept nor begged, but at each blow mournfully lamented not his own destruction but his fatherland’s, saying: “Woe to Jerusalem.” Asked who he was, where he came from or why he said the same things, he gave no answer, but continued only that lamentation for his fatherland in a pitiable cry. Albinus—for that was the man’s name—therefore grew weary and dismissed him as one who, through madness of mind, did not understand what he was saying. But he neither conversed with anyone nor was heard to say anything else for the rest of the time. Singing this like a mournful funeral song, he continually made it resound by day and night: “Woe to Jerusalem.” He neither abused anyone who struck him nor thanked anyone who gave him food. To everyone he gave one and the same response, full of funeral wailing, especially at the celebrations of sacrifices. For seven years and five months, then, the same sequence of words and the same sound of his voice remained. Thus, unwearied for so long, when the siege began he ceased to cry out these things, as though warning ought to cease when what had been foretold was present. But when flame began to envelop city and temple together, he went around the wall and began to cry again: “Woe to the city and the people and the temple.” At last he added: “Woe also to me”; and, struck by a sling, he breathed his last with that same cry.

It had also been written in ancient writings that the city itself, together with the temple, would perish when the temple had been made square. Thus, whether forgetful or stupefied by the pressure of the evils assailing them, when Antonia was occupied they made the temple’s circuit square. Among these signs the most outstanding was what remained inscribed in equally ancient writings, which they called sacred: that about that time there would be a man from their region who would assume dominion over the whole world. This drove them into such frenzy that they promised themselves not only freedom but also kingship. Some thought this should be referred to Vespasian; the more prudent to the Lord Jesus, who, born in their lands according to the flesh from Mary, spread his kingdom through all the expanses of the earth. Thus, with so many things warning them, they could not avert what was being decreed by God.

Thus, as the instigators of the seditions fled while the temple burned, the Romans set up their standards within the temple’s circuit and sacrificed opposite the eastern gate, acclaiming Titus as imperator at the top of their voices. Meanwhile, a boy in the place where the priests too were suffering from thirst, wasted by lack of water and the heat of the neighbouring fire, asked one of the Roman guards to give him his right hand and offer him a drink. The guard at once held it out, pitying both his age and his need. The little boy drank; then, because his innocent age had been fully trusted, he snatched the water vessel and hurried away at a run, so that he might also provide the priests with a means of drinking. The soldier wished to follow but could not catch him. At his own peril, the boy relieved the priests’ thirst. A good deceit, which harmed no one and relieved necessity. Indeed, the soldier himself admired the boy’s devotion more than he detested his trick: at that age, amid the destruction of the whole city and the common peril, he had not left unexpressed, through whatever service he could render, the reverence owed to the priests. Not long afterwards, exhausted by hunger and thirst, the priests begged for their lives. Titus ordered them to be killed, replying that it showed a degenerate spirit to wish to survive their temple and their office.

John, Simon and the other leaders of the seditions asked him to order the missiles and the din to cease for a little while, to give them an opportunity to speak and not to turn away from clemency. When silence had been made, he gave this reply: “The time for mercy is late, most wicked men, when nothing remains to be preserved. It was offered to you and you despised it, thinking it want of confidence, not clemency. But I groaned that innocent buildings should perish through your crime; I grieved that the lowly multitude were driven to death. I wished to spare: you did not allow it. I suspended battles: you rushed in. I offered peace: you did not receive it. I addressed you often, approached you repeatedly—I am not ashamed to say that I made you more insolent by entreaty. What did you think? That the Roman battle lines would yield to you, and that by your numbers you would surround an army victorious over all lands? What a small part fought against you, since neither could your region contain the whole nor did necessity permit it! For our greater concern is to protect the world rather than extend our dominion. There is no new place to which we may advance; nothing is foreign to those whose possession is the whole earth. For a long time we thought we should overlook this brigandage like a blemish upon the body. At length, provoked, we judged that it must be removed, lest your disobedience obscure the splendour of Roman dominion like a cloud. You have felt Roman valour by dying, not by fighting. For we did not see your columns in the field but on the wall, though even your barriers did not avail to protect your safety. For what wall could withstand those whom the ocean did not withstand? What city, enclosed by the protection of walls, could be impregnable to our siege, when Roman arms have penetrated even the Britains, surrounded by the wall of the roaring element? That precipitous mountain of water was laid beneath us. Let the waters of the Red Sea, as Jewish tales relate, have surrounded your fathers as they crossed, like a wall: Roman courage broke through the ocean’s wall. I do not begrudge you benefits bestowed by another. Let the sea have seen you and fled, so that, hemmed in by the enemy, you might flee because you could neither break through nor withstand him. The ocean’s flight would have harmed us if it had fled. We first waged war with the waves; we conquered the raging sea before we reached the enemy. Britain received us already victors over the elements. We subdued what they trusted in, so that the ocean itself might be added to the fullness of our triumph. But perhaps you presumed upon bodily strength. Are you stronger than the Germans, whom Roman courage reduced to slavery though they were enclosed by the wall of the Alps? Those things are not like the hills of sloping Mount Taurus or the Canopean forces of the Egyptians, with whom you are accustomed to wage war. We climbed above the clouds and conquered peoples descending from the cloud; we opened a road through the air to all. We do not begrudge you one through the sea, provided that ours belonged to men in triumph and yours to men in flight. Thus mountains sank before Roman valour; rivers dried up, losing the course which nature had directed and bending it where the victors ordered. Let your Jordan, as you say, have turned and returned to its source to open a path for you: Cloelia, the Roman maiden, had no need of this. Breaking her bonds, she escaped the enemy and, making her way down the river, entered the Roman camp. Nor do we marvel at your fires, from which you are accustomed to sing at great length that the Hebrew youths escaped. Our Mucius, with no one compelling him, put his hand into the fire and did not withdraw it until, victorious over the burning, he filled the enemy with wonder at his courage, which had not felt the flames. Indeed, those who had hoped for triumph asked for peace. Or did that heavenly nourishment and food of rain exalt you against Roman valour? You ought to have considered that Africa herself, the nurse of the whole world, is subject to Roman courage. She who feeds everyone serves us; everyone’s hunger and everyone’s sustenance are in our power. What nature gave to all, Roman valour made its own right. It struck down Hannibal himself and drove him into exile: the world could not contain him, Africa was too narrow for him, the Spains seemed unsuitable for his stay, Gaul was cramped for his passage, and Italy unworthy of a treaty of friendship and shared alliance. You may boast that thunderbolts served you and heavenly powers fought for you: we conquered Hannibal riding upon thunderbolts and thundering amid the tempests of the world itself. The world was shaken, and he struck our walls with his arms. Nor was it necessary that our enemies, like your Assyrians, should be destroyed while asleep: they were destroyed while fighting. For victory is sought not in sleep but in battle; where there is a chance favour, there is no reward of valour. Our enemies did not fall heedlessly into our hands, deceived by the red gleam of waters reflecting the rising sun, thinking from the appearance of shed blood that we had been destroyed. Knowing what they did and prepared for war, they covered the plains of the earth with their bodies and filled them with their own blood. What courage has brought you to such insolence? Did you not see that those who ruled you serve us—Egypt, which used to afflict you, pays us an annual tribute and provides a road as far as the regions of India—and that we go beyond the world to seek another world, the sea’s hidden places and the furthest bounds of sun and ocean, and add the inhabitants of another world to our dominion? What of the kingdom of Antiochus, who afflicted you with grievous punishments and deprived you even of the right to practise your religion? Did we not restore it to Antiochus himself, judging it more glorious to command kings than to take away a kingdom? Did not Antioch herself, the seat of your masters, eagerly reject her own rulers and choose us as masters? Did you not yourselves flee to us to escape those masters? Did we not ourselves receive you and defend you against them? We preserved your right to live by your own laws; we gave you the power to devote yourselves to your own worship. We wished to know your sacred rites, but honoured them. Afterwards you thought you must rebel. Pompey captured the temple but did not destroy it; he occupied the city but preserved it; he kept all the offerings intact. In return for these things, grateful allies, you repaid us by waging war a third time. Nero may have deserved contempt, but Roman valour was not spent in one man. It had Vespasian as a soldier, who had already brought the Gauls back to peace, so brave in battle that through him even Nero conquered, through him Nero was formidable to the enemy; so faithful to his master that he alone did not seek the dominion which he alone deserved. But Cestius had done you harm. A complaint should have been brought, not arms employed. My father Vespasian was sent; he could have fallen unexpectedly upon you unprepared. He went about Galilee and burned distant places so that you might lay aside your insolence and ask pardon. He showed his valour and, when he held you all shut in, went to Egypt to give you a respite in which to regain your senses. Our absence made you more insolent, because you thought we were occupied elsewhere. But we are never so occupied that we are absent from the world. For even when absent we are present, and when far away we stand near. For, as the soul in the body gives life to all its members, so Roman providence is present in every part of its dominion and governs the whole Roman world as though present. For if that divine power gave individual souls the strength to govern a body, how much more has it supplied Roman vigour, by which the whole of our dominion is animated as one body, with a certain vital substance for its protection? You therefore renewed the suspended war. As my father was about to depart to recover the city of Rome from the tyrants, he separated me from his company so that you might not lack an executor of his mercy. I came to war with the appearance of one threatening, with the feeling of one entreating. How often did I call the army back from your walls? How often afterwards did I draw it back from the temple’s sanctuary? How often did I extinguish fires? How often did I warn you? But you never listened. Do you finally ask now, as though anything remained like what has already been consumed? Nevertheless, I have drawn the soldiers away from slaughter, burning and plunder. What do you desire? Why do you still stand armed, as though to give terms, not receive them—if you seek surrender, lay down your arms, no longer fearful to the victors but proud and full of insolence in the vanquished—so that you petition under arms as though either doubting our faith or still challenging our valour by threatening war? The people are destroyed, the temple burns, we hold the city. What hope remains to you except that your lives may be granted? Therefore lay down your arms as vanquished men. I shall grant you life, though you do not deserve it, because you were unwilling to preserve what was yours along with yourselves.”

Then they began to ask that, since they were bound by an oath never to surrender to the Romans, he should allow them to go out through the wall and proceed into the wilderness with their families, yielding the city to the Romans. Still more angered by this, Titus said: “Do you even impose conditions upon us? Rather defend your fatherland, stand by the temple, rise with all your valour and keep your oath of death, since you have rejected that of life.” At the same time he ordered the Romans to rise up and kill the enemy. Very many began to fall under the victors’ heightened indignation. Nevertheless, the sons and brothers of King Jaza surrendered, and very many of the common people with them. Out of regard for royal rank, Titus did not abandon his purpose, though roused to anger, but received those who fled to him. Yet he gained only the profit of mercy, which is the greatest gain. For the instigators of the sedition plundered all the royal household’s booty, so that none of it reached the Romans.

As soon as they rushed into the palace, they seized two Roman soldiers and killed the infantryman. The cavalryman, however, asked to be brought to Simon, claiming that he had something to disclose to that leader of the seditions. But when he was brought before him and spun out some empty tale, he was ordered to be killed. While the executioner delayed, though his eyes were already covered with a band, he dashed away to the Romans. They were fighting at close quarters and received the fugitive. When he was brought before Titus, Titus ordered him to be stripped of his arms and dismissed as a man unworthy of death, since he had allowed himself to be captured alive by the enemy. He preserved for him what the enemy’s cowardice had not taken away, but deprived him of the military oath which he had betrayed as a captive and dishonoured as a fugitive. This was a greater punishment for him, for among men the disgraces of military service are more grievous than the wounds of death.

The Jews, however, were at once driven back and withdrew to the upper parts of the city, abandoning the defence of temple and city. Great slaughter was inflicted upon those who remained; the streets were filled with the half-dead or with corpses.

Caesar ordered the engines to be brought against the upper parts as well. Seeing this, the Idumaeans chose men to send to Titus to ask for surrender. When Simon learned of it, he forestalled them and intercepted the men chosen to seek surrender. Yet not long afterwards, although deprived of their leaders’ support, the Idumaeans could no longer withstand the violence and surrendered to the Roman army. Thus hunger first, and finally despair of resistance, brought about their surrender. Nor did the Romans, now weary of much slaughter, refuse to spare their lives; their eagerness to sell captive slaves made them readier to preserve them. Very many were offered for sale, but buyers were few: the Romans disdained to keep Jews in slavery, and no Jews remained to ransom their own people, since each congratulated himself on having escaped, even destitute. Thus they surrendered everywhere with their fear removed, for the brigands were absent and the Romans granted pardon.

Indeed, Jesus too, one of the priests, the son of Thebutus, surrendered. Having received a pledge of safety, he willingly handed over the vessels of priestly service: two lamps, tables, mixing bowls and cups, and all the golden vessels, as well as hangings and the garments of the chief priests with their stones. Phinehas, the keeper of the treasury, was also captured and revealed the priests’ abundant purple cloth and scarlet and many other things reserved for use. Along with these he too handed over cinnamon, cassia, many spices and incense, many vessels for the sacred rites and a consecrated garment, but he was compelled by fear. Hence his disgrace was pardonable among his own people. Yet even if willingness was absent, courage ought not to have been lacking. Although we often judge more severely than we could take precautions if we ourselves were in such necessity, we ought nevertheless to refuse participation in the deed and treacherous disclosure.

The siege banks had now risen, and the rams had begun to strike the upper wall. On the seventh day of the month which they call Gorpiaeus, the final crisis was reached. Confused and terrified, even the faction leaders, who had exulted amid the greatest dangers, flung themselves at the knees of individuals, begging for help. One could see how pitiable was that change from their terrible and proud eminence to this humble and common abasement, to tears, weeping and fear. The wall of the upper city had not yet given way, but already they were running from one person to another, lamenting that no protection remained. They thought the enemy had entered; very many seemed to see the Romans already fighting from above. Their eyes pictured beforehand what their minds feared, and the mind’s terror became an image before their sight. Indeed, believing it certain that the enemy were already pressing upon their necks, though three towers stronger than the rest still remained to them—Mariamne, Phasaelus and the Equestrian—they abandoned the upper parts and fled to underground chambers or secluded caves.

Not long afterwards, however, John, wasted by hunger and exhausted by fasting, surrendered to Caesar. He was reserved for the triumph but bound in perpetual chains, drawing the breath of life until death rather than experiencing any pleasure in living; he escaped the axe.

Simon, however, remained hidden amid the ruins of the burned city, concealing himself underground with a few of his more faithful men. Caesar had already departed after the city was burned, believing that Simon too had been consumed by fire, crushed by a collapse or killed by some soldier. But as long as food lasted, Simon kept digging further inwards in the excavated caves. When the food failed and no way of escape opened, he suddenly crept up above ground, dressed in a white robe with a purple garment over it, to strike a certain terror into those who saw him. While the Roman soldiers were at first astonished, he instructed them to bring their commander. Rufus Terentius was there, whom Titus had left in command of the troops at the place. When he arrived and asked who he was, Simon at first gave other answers, then admitted that he was Simon. He was therefore sent to Caesar and himself reserved for the triumph. But because he had committed cruelties against the citizens and had not surrendered to Caesar, he was sentenced to death after the triumphal procession.

On the eighth day of the month of Gorpiaeus the city was burned. Countless thousands were slain throughout the siege—very many assert a hundred and ten myriads—all Jews, though not all from the same region and place, since they had gathered there from everywhere at the time of the Passover festival. About ninety-seven thousand were led away captive. Nearly all the brigands were immediately killed; the stronger men were led in the triumph and afterwards thrown to beasts and subjected to other punishments in almost every city through which Titus passed, so that by punishing rebellions he might spread fear among all.

At the same time the Alans, a savage nation long unknown to our people, inhabited the Scythian Tanais and its neighbourhood and the Maeotian marshes. They were confined in the interior with other savage and untamed nations by the difficulty of the inland places and the barrier of an iron gate which Alexander the Great had set upon the ridge of a precipitous mountain. By that king’s ingenuity they were shut in as though in a prison, to cultivate their own lands rather than raid those of others. But, whether because of the barrenness of the places, since the hoped-for fertility of cultivation did not answer the greedy farmer’s wishes, or from a desire for plunder, they urged the king of the Hyrcanians, who ruled the places, to open the gate and allow them to break out. Whether this was obtained by a payment or through dissension among the nations is uncertain. Having obtained this, they poured in upon the nation of the Medes, which was unprepared, and in a short time traversed almost the whole region on swift horses, with others likewise tethered on their right, onto which they could leap in turn whenever they wished. First they threw everything into confusion and gave the appearance of a greater multitude, before which no place of flight lay open; then, after surrounding everyone and inflicting as much slaughter as they wished, they carried off their plunder. For the region was populous and abounded in livestock, and lay easily open to pillage with no one resisting. Indeed, Pacorus himself, king of the Medes, withdrew into remote places, attending to his safety rather than his kingdom, so that his wife and children and concubines were captured by the Alans and afterwards ransomed for a hundred talents. Nor was Tiridates, king of Armenia, free from danger. Made more cautious by another’s misfortune, he foresaw the scourge and wished to meet it manfully, to turn the enemy from his borders. Yet while he fought, he was caught in a little noose and would have passed alive into the enemy’s power had he not quickly cut the misshapen knot with a very sharp sword. For, with a certain insolent pride in their own courage and arrogant contempt for others, and also to use this device as cover for their familiar practice of fighting at a distance and their opportunity of retreat, the Alans make throwing nooses and entangling the enemy their art and manner of warfare.

Tiridates therefore fled, content to have escaped, but left his kingdom to be ravaged. For, as though injured by his having dared to engage them, they devastated Armenia more fiercely than the kingdom of Media. Enriched with the spoils of both kingdoms, they returned to their own lands.

On learning of their incursion, Titus made for Antioch, but gradually, as befitted a triumphant commander. Concealing his reason, he celebrated the pageantry of victory in each city. Wherever he went, Jews were killed in the arena and, torn apart by beasts, paid the deserved penalty of rebellion.

At Antioch too the Gentile population pursued them with ancient hatred, because the kings of the Persians had bestowed upon the synagogues of Antioch the gifts which they had claimed from Jerusalem by right of victory, adding other gifts from their own possessions. The accumulated wealth therefore easily stirred envy. For, to omit for the moment what rivals for the priesthood had done against the Maccabees, and how great a calamity ambition had brought upon the citizens, as we mentioned above, Antiochus, a man of no obscure birth but depraved character, later fabricated a charge that the Jews had conspired to burn the city of Antioch. By the violence of the Gentile multitude he brought to death his own father, who was one of the leading Jews, and very many others whom he accused. Nor did he rest satisfied with that murder of kin and the slaughter of many. Afterwards too he found an opportunity when an accidental fire burned the porticoes, the square and a very great part of the buildings of the same city. Through the false charge of the conspiracy already mentioned, he again began to press and attack the Jews. He would almost have brought about the slaughter of them all had the investigation not been reserved for Titus’s arrival, from fear that Caesar might be angered if they took it upon themselves to punish so many. This saved the Jews.

At Masada too very many Jews gathered, trusting in the strength of the place. Titus considered the task of capturing it unworthy of detaining an imperator and entrusted it to Silva, to whom he had committed supreme command of the Roman troops in those places and responsibility for ensuring that no rebellion arose again. He himself made for Alexandria and sailed from there to Rome.

Silva vigorously pursued his assigned task and broke down Masada’s wall with a ram. They built an inner wall of wood, because wall material of this kind did not easily yield to such blows from engines. But the Romans changed their method of warfare and cast fire upon it, which readily caught the wood and blazed up without delay. As the fire grew, a great roar of flame arose. At first the breath of the north wind drove it away from the fortification and burned the Roman siege shelters instead; then, when the south wind arose, it turned back upon the stronghold, so that the whole wooden barrier of the wall burned up as its material was consumed. Since night had intervened, the Romans withdrew to their camp, confident of victory, intending on the following day to subdue men now exposed and stripped of every defence. But lest anyone slip away, they surrounded the stronghold with an interlocking cordon of guards.

Thus, with affairs desperate, Eleazar, the instigator of the disturbances, saw that no defence remained and began this speech. We have not omitted it, as a lamentable epilogue to close the work in the rhetorical manner: “What are we doing, men descended from Abraham, a royal race, invincible through the power of priestly grace? For valour is judged not by the outcome of victory, which is often uncertain, but by steadfastness of purpose. From this one may infer that subduing the enemy belongs to fortune, but not changing one’s mind belongs to valour. I may therefore rightly call you invincible if no fear of death has yet conquered you. But your father Abraham did not train you thus: in his only son he taught that, if he were sacrificed for religion, there would be not death but immortality for him. Why should I praise Josiah, than whom no one was a better interpreter of religion, despiser of death or champion of freedom? Placed on that royal eminence, he could have deferred death. Yet, because he saw that the captivity of the people of Israel would follow their grievous sins, he involved himself in another’s war and fled from life. Necho cried: ‘I have not been sent against you, but against the king of Israel.’ Yet Josiah did not withdraw before receiving a mortal arrow wound. Laid low by it, he shows us whether merit or chance carries greater weight in war. Josiah, the restorer of pious rites, was defeated; Necho, the most wicked of all men, won. But the defeated man is now with the angels, the victor in torment. For who does not know that the reward for human beings is stored up not in this life, but after this contest is completed? Here we run so that there we may reach the palm; here is the contest, there the reward. There is therefore no favour here in length of years. Indeed, Abel died early, Cain survived. Thus death fell to innocence and misery to life. Since then we have inherited the same lot: living has become most wretched, dying blessed. For what is life but a prison of the soul, which is shut within this slave-house and clings to companionship with the flesh? It is shaken by the body’s infirmities, afflicted by toil, crushed by anger, kindled by desires and harassed by fury. It cannot easily rise, bound to the ground, clotted with dust, fastened by a chain and entangled in sinews. Yet its power is no slight thing: it gives life to the body and pours the vigour of sense into insensible matter. Each person’s soul invisibly bestows this upon him, governs the whole man and carries him beyond mortal frailty, so that he may grasp the knowledge of heavenly secrets and direct his mind to the future. Thus, in the image and likeness of its ruler, it is not seen, though situated in the body. It is not perceived by bodily eyes, nor is its entry or departure caught by any gaze. Representing a certain likeness of the divine gift, it pours in life when it enters and brings about death when it leaves the body. Where the soul is, there is life; where it is absent, there is death. Whatever it visits it awakens; whatever it leaves is at once dissolved and immediately withers. By the soul’s infusion the dead man rises; by its departure the living man dies. Who then can doubt that immortality is seen to be at work in the soul, whose power is to avert death? Yet it is a burden to itself, though it abounds in service to another, and what it gives the body it takes away from itself. For it is weighed down and, as it were, bent towards the earth with this mortal body. Thus the body’s life is the soul’s death, and conversely the body’s death seems the soul’s freedom. For while we are in the body, our soul serves in slavery, a wretched slavery indeed, exiled from paradise and a stranger to its ruler. But when it is released from the bonds of this flesh, it flies back to that pure and shining place above, is present with the Lord its God, and enjoys the dwellings of the saints and the company of the blessed. It rejoices that it no longer has any fellowship with the dead and has left behind companionship with a corpse, that heavenly grace breathes upon it and no agitation of human cares troubles it. Sleep shows us how great a grace the soul resumes after the body’s death. For when the body sleeps and its desires and all its movements are as though dead, we often converse with the saints and receive those we have lost: the absent are present with us, the dead live, all grief is stilled, we approach God and converse with him, we know the future, the afflicted find rest and slaves freedom. What we dream in sleep we therefore attain in death; what is an image in sleep is in death the possession of truth and the grace of freedom. Hence some nations customarily greet people’s births with tears and their deaths with joy: they grieve that the former are born to misery and congratulate the latter on returning to blessedness; they lament that the souls of the former have come into slavery and rejoice that those of the latter have returned to freedom. The sages of the Indians too are said, when they have taken on the desire to die, to declare that they wish to depart, with no one raising a protest. Then, when the preparations for death have been made, they leap joyfully onto the burning pyre and bid farewell to those standing by. Women grieve as though about to be deprived of support, and little children because they are being left behind; others bless them and do not begrudge their hastening to better inhabitants, more splendid places and purer companions. What else, then, can I think of you, when even barbarian nations have the custom of pursuing freedom? I have long known you well and known you ready to answer to your ancestral institutions, holding that you should serve neither the Romans nor any nation, but God alone, who alone is the just and true Lord of all. The day has come which demands that you prove your will by deeds and not dishonour the splendour of your ancient character by subjecting yourselves, born in freedom, to human domination. You could previously have served without danger; now it is necessary to undergo harsh torments along with slavery if we offer ourselves to serve under Roman dominion, we who were the first of all to challenge them in war and the last still to hold them under arms. We did not surrender to the imperator when he offered peace; shall we surrender to Silva when he threatens cruelty? Wretched men, for what hope in this life shall we preserve ourselves? Granted, the enemy may pardon us. What will that avail when God’s offence is clear? The fires were turned from the enemy against us, the winds’ blasts changed, the flames bent back to burn our defences. Who can live with God opposed to him? There is no place for pardon, but a manifest command of voluntary death. Why did night intervene, except to keep the enemy from forestalling us and breaking in as soon as the wall’s protection was burned, to preserve time for us to kill one another and allow us to die with our children and kinsfolk, so that we should not see panting old men dragged away by the Romans or our dearest wives seized for the victor’s lust? Let us die with our fatherland and not survive the reproach of such disgrace. Where, then, shall we flee from the face of God, or where shall we go with the Lord of heaven hostile to us? If mountains fall upon us and hide us in hollow caves, how shall we nevertheless be able to evade the indignation of such power? Where shall we go where God is not, since he himself is everywhere? Are the examples slight which teach us that he has long been hostile, for our sins, to the nation he once protected? Who can doubt it when he sees that our hands have turned against ourselves and domestic sedition has killed more than war? I shall not grant the Romans that they have conquered; nor do they claim this for themselves, knowing that almost all of us have perished by our own arms rather than another’s. For what Roman arms did the Jews dwelling in Caesarea see? On the Sabbath holiday, amid the solemn observances of our sacred rites, the multitude of Caesarean Gentiles, inflamed by a sudden impulse and a fury sent from above, destroyed twenty thousand of them and drove all away, emptying the whole city. Did not a certain madness fill all Syria, so that Jews and Gentiles, living in the same cities and formerly bound together by the goodwill of shared residence, afterwards clashed with one another in arms, establishing for the Romans a ford to their future victory? For what shall I say of Scythopolis? The Jews had first hastened there to forestall the Gentile population, lest, following the example of the other cities, it devise anything against our people. Thus men who ought to have joined their forces and fought against foreigners instead fought against one another: some of the Jews battled alongside the Gentiles against their own kin and neighbours, and then were themselves killed by the Gentiles as the price of their labour and shed blood—the very thing they had prevented from happening to the Gentiles. The Damascenes struck down eight thousand Jews without any cause; the Ascalonites, two thousand five hundred. In the city called Ptolemais too, two thousand were killed. At Alexandria there was ancient hatred between the Jews and the Gentile peoples, ever since Alexander the Great had used the Jews’ zeal to subdue the Egyptians. Hence, when the city was founded, equal privileges were assigned to Jews and Egyptians, but separate dwellings, lest the worship of those who wished to preserve their purifications without any contamination be mingled. From this arose frequent clashes between them. Quarrels broke out and judgement was sought; yet it is clear that none of so great a king’s benefits was violated. But later, when a tumult arose from the Gentiles and some Jews were killed while others were detained for punishment, the Jewish people, provoked by the injury, rose against its authors. When they sought too obstinately to avenge themselves upon their fellow citizens, the Roman army was brought in and struck down sixty thousand Jews within the city. But why do I linger over lesser things, when we must lament the destruction of the whole world in the ruin of one city? Where is the great city Jerusalem, where beautiful Zion, where the wondrous temple, where that second tabernacle, the sanctuary of holiness, into which only the high priest was accustomed to enter once a year, not without blood which he offered for himself and for the people’s sin? It has been profaned by the Gentiles; those who destroyed the city dwell in its remains. Where, I say, are you, city crowded with people, revered by kings, acceptable to God, seat of grace? Your pavements were of marble, your walls gleaming with marble, your roofs shone with precious marble; your gates glittered with gold, others gleamed with silver. All have been killed, both those who continually dwelt in you and those who gathered to you from every part of the world, so that there can be no doubt that the whole world has perished in you. Bare, bare is everything, burned from the rooftops, demolished from the foundations; your dwelling has become deserted, and no one inhabits the tents. Does anyone still take pleasure in living, and not regret having lived? Hard are the eyes that can see these things, pitiless the souls that can wish anything to survive such griefs, not because the calamities have ceased, but because there is now no rest. Where shall we turn our eyes, or what can it delight us to see? The whole city is a tomb of the dead; ashes alone meet the gaze, streets empty of the living are filled with corpses. Wretched elders, with ash-covered grey hair and torn clothing, sit over the remains of the dead, covering bare bones to protect them from birds and beasts. A few women stand at the threshold, whom the impious soldier has preserved for dishonour, not for life. Who, seeing these things and thinking of postponing death, dares lift his eyes to heaven? Who is so forgetful of his fatherland, an enemy of his own people, estranged from family devotion, devoid of affection? Whose spirit is so effeminate and soft, who so fearful, that he is not ashamed to have been preserved for these things? If only we had died long ago, or, if life remained, lost the light of our eyes before we beheld the holy city demolished by enemy hands, this temple consecrated to God by our ancestors so impiously burned in flames, or priests lying slain in the temple. Let us therefore make amends for having survived these evils, so that we may seem to have deferred death not from a desire for life but from an intent upon valour. The enemy has surrounded the whole fortification; nothing remains but ourselves and our wives. They already set up our children for auction and contend among themselves over who shall take away whose wife, whether the women are to be distributed according to the claims of rank and station or forced to undergo a wretched drawing of lots. Monstrous punishments and the most elaborate torments are also being prepared for us: not only blazing flames or various deaths by the stroke of the avenging axe, a harsh punishment indeed after chains, prison and the yoke, but more tolerable to men because free from mockery; also limbs torn from the living and, above all, hands cut off. Not undeservedly, since they failed in their duty when they could have helped themselves. We must also undergo the bites of beasts as a spectacle for the victors. This has already been performed in the arenas of various cities, and ought to be shameful to us as an example or wretched as an experience: that we preserve ourselves to fight either beasts or brothers. Why then do we delay? We are no longer free to escape what we fear. If we are unwilling to kill our children out of mercy or ourselves through valour, we shall be compelled to kill our brothers or kinsmen in disgrace. The former affection urges; the latter the victors demand. If we are unwilling to perform the service of family devotion, we shall be forced to undergo the mockery of a pageant of the murder of kin. Let us therefore undertake what will benefit our children or wives. If they are weaker, let us remove them from the torments to come; if we are stronger, let us overcome parental compassion and the affections of kinship, and in this too conquer the enemy, whose booty we take away. Valour demands this, shame urges it. Not to fear death belongs to valour. For we are all born for death and beget children for death: their death is assigned to nature, their captivity counted as disgrace. Those whom we could not snatch from danger, therefore, let us snatch from mockery. Fathers, have mercy upon your children; husbands, upon your wives; all, upon the little ones. Let us have mercy, above all, upon ourselves while we have the power to show mercy, so that it may come from us, lest we seem both born and preserved for dishonour. For who could endure fathers killed before their sons’ faces and sons before their parents’ eyes, old men weary with grey age dragged away either to death or, worse, to slavery, women led away with dishevelled hair in their husbands’ sight and dragged by force to shame? Who could endure hearing the voice of a little child crying and calling his father to help him in his plea, when you now hear in vain, your hands bound and your captive neck beneath the yoke? Therefore, while our hands are still free, while we grasp the sword, let us undertake a work which the victorious enemy may admire. Let our wives receive the last gift of conjugal love as a dowry inheritance. We return these keys to them by a new testament of blood, so that they may be heirs of our freedom. They themselves urge this; certainly those who wish it deserve it, and those who shrink from it must be compelled. Nor will the little ones fear the sword which, because of their age, they do not understand and which they ought to receive from devoted parents, so that they may truly become free. What could be more excellent for us too than to burn the stronghold first, yet preserve the grain, lest they think that we undertook the service of mutual slaughter compelled by hunger rather than invited by a desire for valour? We give them food filled with blood; and if the flames consume it, the very smell of the burning grain will show that what the besieged had in abundance was lost to the besiegers. After this let each offer himself to the wound and, dying, cover his fatherland and clasp it in a final embrace. Let the fatherland which was the dwelling of our dignity become for us the tomb of freedom. This mound befits our dead, so that we may be covered by the enclosure of valour.”

Fired by such a speech, the others held drawn swords, kissed their wives and embraced their children, weeping and hurrying at the same time to forestall the enemy. “These tokens of love,” he said, “we give you as consolation in the utmost necessity.” Manfully suppressing affection, they shut out feeling and carried out the slaughter. Fearless, the women offered themselves to the wound to preserve their chastity. They too had put on the minds of their husbands. After killing their kinsfolk and children, they chose vigorous men to complete the remaining slaughter. Thus all were laid low, nine hundred and sixty with the little ones and women. Only one woman survived; she hid five sons in an aqueduct while the others attended to their final necessities. Roused by the voices of the Romans arriving at daybreak, she told them what had happened. A fire which they themselves had previously set consumed their wealth.
